title: Your daily coffee habit could be taking a toll on your bones, new study suggests
summary: A Flinders University study links high coffee consumption to lower bone density in postmenopausal women, while tea's catechins may promote bone health.
story: Dr. Alexa Fiffick, a board-certified family medicine physician and founder of Concierge Medicine of Westlake in Cleveland, Ohio, speaks about a new study linking hormone replacement therapy to lower dementia risk.
If you’re a woman who regularly reaches for coffee throughout the day, you may want to think twice about that next cup — or consider switching to tea.

Researchers at Flinders University reported in a study published in the journal Nutrients that high coffee consumption may be associated with lower bone mineral density (BMD) in older, postmenopausal women.

The scientists analyzed coffee and tea consumption among 9,704 women age 65 and older over a 10-year period. During that time, they also measured participants’ BMD at the femoral neck and hip, areas where osteoporosis-related fractures commonly occur.
The researchers found that drinking tea was associated with higher total hip BMD, while drinking more than five cups of coffee per day was associated with lower BMD.
COFFEE MAY HAVE POWERFUL EFFECT ON LIVER HEALTH, MAJOR STUDY SUGGESTS
Drinking more than five cups of coffee per day was associated with lower bone mineral density in older women, according to the study. (iStock)
Moderate coffee consumption — about two to three cups a day — was not associated with negative effects on bone health.

The study also identified differences based on other health and lifestyle factors. Coffee consumption was associated with lower femoral neck BMD among women with higher alcohol intake, while the positive association between tea and bone density was more pronounced among women with obesity.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS
The researchers wrote that osteoporosis, which is characterized by low BMD, "is a major global public health concern affecting individuals across all ages, genders and ethnicities."
About one in three women and one in five men age 50 and older worldwide experience osteoporosis-related fractures, according to the study.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER
Women face a particularly high risk because they generally have lower bone mass and experience accelerated bone loss after menopause.

In the U.S., the number of adults age 50 and older with low BMD in the hip or spine is projected to increase by 17.2 million by 2030, adding to the healthcare costs and long-term disability associated with osteoporosis-related fractures, the researchers noted.
Coffee lovers may not need to give up their daily brew, researchers said, but consuming more than five cups per day could be linked to lower bone density. (iStock)

The scientists wrote that they studied the relationship between coffee and tea and bone health because dietary factors play a "crucial role in the prevention of noncommunicable disease and may influence bone health," and these are two of the most widely consumed beverages globally.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Study co-author Ryan Liu told ScienceDaily "compounds called catechins, abundant in tea, may promote bone formation and slow bone breakdown."

"Coffee’s caffeine content, by contrast, has been shown in laboratory studies to interfere with calcium absorption and bone metabolism, though these effects are small and can be offset by adding milk," Liu said.
Older women who drank tea had higher bone density in the hip than those who did not, according to a study. (iStock)

"Our results don't mean you need to give up coffee or start drinking tea by the gallon," Liu added. "But they do suggest that moderate tea consumption could be one simple way to support bone health and that very high coffee intake might not be ideal, especially for women who drink alcohol."

"This study offers an interesting look at how everyday beverages might relate to bone health, but the findings should be interpreted with caution," Lisa Young, registered dietitian and adjunct professor of nutrition at New York University, told Fox News Digital.
"Because it followed women over time without assigning them to drink coffee or tea, it can only show associations, not prove that coffee weakens bones or that tea strengthens them."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The study had limitations, including differences in participants’ lifestyles, its focus on bone density rather than fractures and relatively small effects seen mainly in older women, Young noted.
Symptoms of osteoporosis and early bone loss include back pain, loss of height over time and stooped posture, according to the Mayo Clinic.
"The bottom line for the public is reassuring: Moderate coffee intake appears fine, and there is no need to switch drinks for the sake of your bones," Young said.
"The most proven ways to protect bone health remain getting enough calcium and vitamin D, staying physically active and avoiding smoking and excess alcohol," she added.
"With that said, I do make a case for moderate amounts of coffee for good health. Too much of anything is never a good thing."
Teresa Mull is a freelance writer with the Lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

title: ‘Quiet quitting’ could silently destroy your marriage — 4 ways to bring the spark back
summary: From flirting and dating to spending quality time without phones, experts share how small daily gestures can reverse quiet quitting in a marriage.
story: James Sexton explains how emotional withdrawal develops between couples and why renewed attention, affection and mindfulness can reveal whether both partners remain invested.
Much like the workplace term that means doing the bare minimum, "quiet quitting" could also happen in marriage, sometimes gradually.

The informal term, which is not a clinical diagnosis, refers to spouses who remain together while reducing their emotional effort, communication or involvement in the relationship, according to experts.
New York City divorce lawyer James Sexton described what "quiet quitting" can look like at home and at work.
"I'm not going to go through the dramatic gesture of ending this thing," Sexton said. "I'm just going to stop. I'm going to stop paying attention. I'm going to stop participating."
‘QUIET QUITTING’ IN MARRIAGE: THE SUBTLE SIGNS A SPOUSE HAS EMOTIONALLY CHECKED OUT

Silently pulling away from the relationship may seem to be easier than going through the "trauma" of divorce, Sexton told Fox News Digital, and the person avoids looking like the "bad guy" for ending the relationship.
"Very often, you actually receive more sympathy because you're perceived as the victim of the breakup as opposed to the perpetrator," he added.
A mature couple looking despondent after having a fight with one another at home (iStock)
A lack of effort in a relationship can be a bigger warning sign than frequent conflict, according to Sexton.
"When people are fighting, it kind of means there’s still skin in the game," he said. "The opposite of love is not hate … it’s indifference."
NEARLY 1 IN 3 MARRIED AMERICANS AREN'T HAVING SEX — EXPERT REVEALS HOW TO BRING BACK THE SPARK
Dr. Mindy DeSeta, a clinical sexologist and licensed mental health counselor in Miami, said some couples seek help after about 30 years of marriage, when the demands of family life have eased.

"The kids are gone, or they're hitting that retirement age, so they don't have the life distractions, and they're realizing, ‘Wow. I actually quiet quit my relationship when my kids were toddlers,’" she told Fox News Digital.
Some couples realize they've been out of their marriage since their children were young, an expert said. (iStock)
DeSeta identified four relationship principles, including the following:
Learning how to discuss physical and sexual intimacy
Focusing on teamwork
Staying autonomous
"Learning and earning" your partner through constant dating
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Couples experiencing quiet quitting may continue to function well as a team, managing the household and other responsibilities while becoming emotionally disconnected.
DeSeta said this disconnection can develop gradually as spouses begin living increasingly separate lives.
"Quiet quitting" your relationship can show up in subtle signs like taking interests in different things or going to bed at separate times. (iStock)

"When you stop spending the evenings together … you each are kind of doing your own thing. Your shows are different. You're going to bed at different times. … You may have different friend groups. You're working out at different times," she said.
4 tips to turn it around
Both experts shared tips for addressing emotional disconnection between romantic partners.
Reconnection often requires small, active steps that restart the momentum, rather than making grand gestures, Sexton suggested.
"Every single person in your life is not permanently gifted to you. They're loaned."
The divorce lawyer encouraged revisiting the simple acts and gestures that both partners enjoyed early in the relationship.
His suggestions included sending sweet "good morning" texts, writing a note complimenting a partner or sharing a song that sparked a romantic memory.

"It costs nothing, takes 30 seconds to do it," he said. "What does it cost to write an email with a list of 10 things I like about you? These are not only things we welcome receiving under any circumstances, but they're actually reminders."
Oftentimes, quiet quitting looks like zoning out during moments of quality time, DeSeta said.
If one partner scrolls on a phone while watching a movie together, the device can become "the third member of the relationship," signaling where that partner’s attention lies, the expert cautioned.
"When you're on your phone, you're just actually saying, ‘I'm choosing to do this versus spending this quality time with you,’" an expert said. (iStock)
"When you're on your phone, you're actually saying, ‘I'm choosing to do this versus spending quality time with you,'" she added.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
In addition to paying attention during one-on-one activities, the act of asking personal questions — as simple as "how was your day?" — can also help to restore a connection, DeSeta said.
Instead of leading with a complaint about the relationship, Sexton suggested using a positive approach.
For example, instead of saying, "We never spend time with each other anymore," try calling back a positive memory and suggest recreating it.
Communicating positively is more likely to receive a positive response, experts advise. (iStock)

"Focusing on what we need to work on is harder than focusing on what it is that we really like about this person, what drew us to them to begin with," he said. "Chances are, they might feel far away from who they were at the beginning of the relationship.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"And maybe our job in a relationship is to try to remind each other of the 'you' and the 'me' before we became the 'we.'"
Making an active effort to flirt with a partner can boost your mood while signaling continued romantic interest, according to DeSeta.
"Let your partner know that you are there to earn them every day," she said, emphasizing the importance of continuing to learn about and pursue a partner throughout the relationship.
The relationship expert emphasized the importance of consistently "learning and earning" your partner. (iStock)

"Let them know in the most subtle ways every single day that you care about them, that you're thinking about them. And if you do that, you kind of break this cycle of the quiet quitting, and, eventually, it starts coming back to you."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Sexton reminded couples that their time together is limited, so illness or tragedy should not be the catalyst for renewed effort.

"Every single person in your life is not permanently gifted to you. They're loaned," he said. "There’s a finite number of times that you're going to be with this person, see this person, tell this person that you love them."
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Top GOP senator reveals what Dem colleagues are fretting about behind closed doors
summary: Senate Republican John Barrasso says Democratic senators privately admit the progressive wave led by Abdul El-Sayed and others is their future.
story: Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo., revealed to Fox News Digital that his Democratic colleagues quietly worry about their party's "far, far left" future.

DALLAS — As Republicans huddle for a last show of unity before the home stretch of the midterm elections, a top Senate Republican revealed what his Democratic colleagues are predicting about the future of their party.

Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo., told Fox News Digital that in private, his colleagues across the aisle are wringing their hands over the insurgent progressive wave that has fast become the standard-bearer of the Democratic Party during this election cycle.
"It's surprising how the energy of the Democrat Party has moved to the far, far left," Barrasso said during an interview at the Republican National Committee midterm convention.
TOP REPUBLICAN NAMES WHO HE SAYS IS REALLY LEADING DEMOCRATS — AND IT'S NOT SCHUMER OR JEFFRIES
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., departs after a weekly Senate Democratic Policy luncheon at the US Capitol in Washington, DC on July 29, 2026. (Alex Wroblewski / AFP via Getty Images)
"Those are the people that are driving the party. And the concern that I have, talking to other colleagues in the Senate, who they’ll say that is the future of their party," he continued.
Republicans are trying to fight against history and anxious voters feeling the crunch on their wallets, and as the war in Iran continues to sputter on without a clear end in sight.
The convention in Dallas is meant to hammer home that while President Donald Trump’s name isn’t on the ballot, his agenda, and the incumbents and fresh candidates that could execute it, are.
TRUMP'S $5,000 DIVIDEND CHECKS WOULD COME WITH A MAJOR CATCH UNDER GOP SENATOR'S PLAN

While that push to energize Trump’s base to hit the polls in November ensues, key races across the Senate map have seen progressive and far-left candidates emerge as the standard-bearers for the party during this cycle.

Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, James Talarico in Texas and Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota all bucked expectations, and the Democratic old guard in Washington, D.C., including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., to earned the nomination in their respective races.
REPUBLICAN SOUNDS ALARM ON RISING DEM STAR: 'THIS GUY’S GOING TO BE A PROBLEM'

Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo., speaks to reporters after voting at the U.S. Capitol on March 4, 2026. Senate Republicans rejected a Democratic-backed war powers resolution aimed at limiting President Donald Trump's military campaign against Iran. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

El-Sayed and Talarico, in particular, have been targeted heavily during the convention, which Trump declared was, in part, dedicated to ensuring Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton would win out and prevent the Lone Star State from turning a shade of purple.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"And we cannot allow that to become the future of our country," Barrasso said. "So that's, to me, the reason that we need to win all of these races, why it's so critical, is that these people that are winning the Democrat primaries, I believe, would be terrible for our nation."
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Vance declares Democrats ‘party of hatred,’ says party has moved beyond big government, censorship
summary: Vice President JD Vance will use a deeply personal speech to reflect on the legacy of late friend Charlie Kirk, the joys of fatherhood and the future he hopes America can provide.
story: Vice President JD Vance says the Democratic Party is no longer the party of FDR or even Bill Clinton anymore at the Republican midterm convention.

FIRST ON FOX: Vice President JD Vance argued Thursday that Democrats have moved so far to the left that they no longer resemble the party of past Democratic presidents, branding the modern Democratic Party the "party of hatred" in a fiery convention address first obtained by Fox News Digital.

"They're not the party of FDR or JFK. Hell, they're not even the party of Bill Clinton anymore," Vance said. "The Democrats are the party of hatred. They're the party that despises America and the people who built it."

Vance used the closing night of the Republican convention to build that charge across a series of cultural and economic flashpoints, pointing to a Democratic candidate's attack on the nuclear family, his own clash with Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed and what he cast as a broader Democratic message telling American children "who they ought to hate."
TRUMP DANGLES $5,000 CHECKS AS DEBT SURGES — BUT ONLY IF GOP CAN CLEAR MAJOR MIDTERM HURDLE
Vice President JD Vance speaks at the Lake Lucerne Summit at the Buergenstock resort in Obbuergen, Switzerland June 21, 2026.  (Urs Flueeler, Pool Photo via AP)

The vice president contrasted that portrait with what he called Americans' "birthright" — the opportunity to build a family, own a home, find meaningful work and pass a better country to their children — while honoring his late friend Charlie Kirk one year after his assassination.
On the anniversary of Turning Point USA's co-founder Charlie Kirk’s death, Vance honored his friend.

"I was elected Vice President of the United States one year ago today, on September the 10th of last year, that good friend was taken from us when Charlie was assassinated. Now, Charlie left behind two children, two little kids. They were too young to fully understand," said Vance.

Vance recalled Kirk’s message to young men that few callings are greater than falling in love, starting a family and becoming a father — words that have taken on new meaning for the vice president since he and Second Lady Usha Vance welcomed their son Alec in July.
Vice President JD Vance speaks with Breitbart News Washington bureau chief Matthew Boyle at Andrew W. Mellon Auditorium Nov. 20, 2025, in Washington.  (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo)
He used Kirk's legacy to transition into touting what he called Americans' "birthright" exceptionalism.

"I believe the Founders built this nation on a promise that echoes our Creator: That every American child is born an heir, born with a birthright," said Vance. "Born with the right to inherit the blessings of this country. Not because of who their parents are. Not because of what they look like or where they come from. But because they are Americans."
Vance used the opportunity to outline his vision for rebuilding the nuclear family, while taking shots at Democrats.

"I think about what the Democrats have said about our shared birthright as Americans, or frankly, the lack thereof in Michigan. One Democrat in particular, one candidate has said, and I quote ‘f the nuclear family.’ What are you even talking about?" said Vance.
"They come not from a desire to serve you or our fellow Americans, but they come from a very deep emptiness in the soul," he added.
CROWD ERUPTS AS VANCE SMACKS DOWN PROTESTER WAVING MEXICAN FLAG: ‘GET YOUR A-- OVER THERE’

Vance used the opportunity to outline his vision for rebuilding the nuclear family – taking shots at Democrats. "I think about what the Democrats have said about our shared birthright as Americans, or frankly, the lack thereof in Michigan." (RONALDO SCHEMIDT / AFP via Getty Images)
A protester emerged carrying Mexican and Palestinian flags, prompting Vance to respond, "What the people at home missed is that we just had a protestor interrupting us and waving the Mexican flag."
"Well. Well, my friend, if you love Mexico so much, get your ass over there. I'll buy you the plane ticket," the vice president said.
Vance said the protester should have been waving the American flag, adding that it is a symbol of the fight for the American dream.

"This fall, the Democrats are running candidates who will tell your children what they're allowed to say, how they're allowed to live, and importantly, who they ought to hate. Because that's what the Democrat Party is about in 2026. It's not about you, it's about foreign fraudsters, and it's about who they hate," said Vance.

A protestor throws a Mexican flag as US Vice President JD Vance speaks during the second day of the Republican National Committee midterm convention at the American Airlines Center in Dallas, Texas on September 10, 2026. US Republicans are betting that putting President Donald Trump at the center of their campaign can rescue a party facing grim election forecasts, despite the president's negative approval ratings. (Brendan SMIALOWSKI / AFP via Getty Images)
Vance spoke about the economy former President Joe Biden left, pointing to housing costs and Americans competing against illegal immigrants in the job market.
"Our nation became a place where you had to be rich to enjoy what used to be the birthright of every ordinary middle-class life," he said.
Vance touted his wins from leading the White House Task Force on fraud and calling out Democrats for "refus[ing] to prosecute the crime."
He said the task force has found $250 billion of fraud just since he was appointed fraud czar.
Vance took aim at Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, with whom he has sparred in recent weeks after El-Sayed made comments about the second family.

"He saw me describing what a decent man and my papa was genuinely a decent and good man. He saw me talking about my papa and his work and his history and what he loved and what he cared about. And you know what old Abdul did? He asked mockingly whether I'd be willing to bring Usha back in time to meet Papa," Vance resurfaced.
Vance said El-Sayed saw "the color of his skin, sees his background, and decides that he could never have loved my wife."

"Abdul himself was raised by his own white step-grandparents. He knows exactly that kind of bond and what it looks like in a family, and he chose any way to say that a man like my grandfather couldn't have love from the bottom of his heart," Vance added.
Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.

title: Top Trump official reveals how 30-minute military op unlocked Venezuela oil windfall for US buyers
summary: Energy Secretary Chris Wright says the Trump administration is tapping Venezuela's 300 billion barrels of oil reserves to expand supply and cut prices.
story: Energy Secretary Chris Wright told Fox News Digital the military actions in Venezuela helped open the door for a major increase in oil production while on the sidelines of the RNC Midterm convention.

DALLAS, Texas — The 30-minute U.S. military operation that removed Nicolás Maduro from power has helped clear the way for a sweeping expansion of Venezuela’s battered energy sector, Energy Secretary Chris Wright said, sharing that the country’s national energy production will more than double by the end of 2027.

"Chevron is going to more than double their energy production. In fact, that national energy production in Venezuela will more than double by the end of next year from the intervention on Jan. 3 this year," Wright told Fox News Digital on the sidelines of the RNC Midterm Convention.

Wright said the military actions in Venezuela helped open the door for a major increase in oil production as the administration has increasingly taken an active role in the socialist country as part of a broader push to expand U.S. influence and investment.

U.S. forces entered Venezuela for Operation Absolute Resolve Jan. 3, capturing Maduro and his wife Flores. War Secretary Pete Hegseth said the attack was part of "massive joint military and law enforcement raid" and lasted less than 30 minutes.
TRUMP TOUTS ACCESS TO 65 BILLION BARRELS OF VENEZUELAN OIL IN DEAL HE SAYS WILL SLASH GAS PRICES
A view of the town of Agua Santa Rosa, on the shores of Lake Maracaibo, among dilapidated houses in Maracaibo, Venezuela, July 27, 2026. (Jose Isaac Bula/Anadolu via Getty Images)

"You had 25 years of communist dictatorship. The standard of living has just plummeted in Venezuela. Eight million Venezuelans fled. About a million of them, and not all of them good actors, came to the United States of America. People tried to beg, borrow, bribe, anything they could to change the Venezuelan government. No luck," Wright said.
"President Trump is an out-of-the-box, bold foreign policy leader.
"A brief military operation, arrest two criminals and now we have leverage over the government. It’s an existing government. Are they perfect? No. But we have a lot of leverage."
Chevron scored an investment of more than $7 billion over five years and more than double its Venezuelan oil production to 600,000 barrels per day, according to its press release.

Venezuela controls more than 300 billion barrels of crude reserves, roughly 20% of the world’s total. Despite holding an estimated 17% of the world’s oil reserves, Venezuela produces only about 1% of global output after years of political instability and deteriorating infrastructure undermined its energy industry.
TOP ENERGY TRADER HAILS TRUMP'S VENEZUELA OIL DEAL AS A 'GENERATIONAL WIN' FOR GAS PRICES
President Donald Trump takes questions from members of the press aboard Air Force One Jan. 11, 2026, while traveling from Palm Beach, Fla. (Samuel Corum/Getty Images)

Wright said shifting the center of global energy production toward the Western Hemisphere will put the U.S. at the center and major producers, including Canada, Guyana and Mexico supplying more of the world’s oil and gas.

Millions of barrels of new Venezuelan production would be processed through U.S. refineries and produced using American rigs and infrastructure, creating thousands of American jobs, according to the White House.
STATE DEPARTMENT ANNOUNCES 'TOTAL COMPLIANCE' FROM VENEZUELAN GOVERNMENT IN RELIEF EFFORTS AFTER MADURO ARREST
Secretary of Energy Chris Wright speaks to Fox News Digital at the RNC Midterm Convention in Dallas, Texas. (Fox News Digital)
The administration’s emerging approach to Venezuela could use U.S. leverage with energy investment to prompt political change.

That deal comes with added importance as the war with Iran disrupts oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. The average U.S. price for regular gasoline rose to about $4.22 a gallon Wednesday, according to AAA, up from roughly $3.19 a year earlier.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"We're solving a 47-year conflict with Iran. We cannot have a nuclear-armed Iran. This is a nation sounding death to America and doing everything they can to implement it. But we've massively grown United States natural gas exports, good for our economy, good for the world economy," Wright said.
Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.

title: WATCH: Socialist protester blames 'provocateurs' after assaults at 'closest entry point' to Trump convention
summary: A socialist protester blamed right-wing provocateurs after Dallas police in riot gear arrested two near the Republican National Committee convention.
story: A socialist anti-Trump protester blamed ‘right-wing provocateurs' for a confrontation with police that led to two arrests just outside President Donald Trump's midterm convention in Dallas.

A socialist "Never Trumpers" protester blamed "conservative provocateurs" for a tense confrontation with police that resulted in multiple arrests just outside the Republican National Committee's midterm convention in Dallas.

Videos posted on social media Thursday afternoon showed what appeared to be hundreds of Never Trumpers confronting Dallas police just blocks from where the president was set to deliver his convention-closing speech. Authorities responded with a strong show of force that included officers in apparent riot gear.

The Dallas Police Department confirmed with Fox News Digital that two protesters were arrested on charges related to their actions during the protest. The department said that officers assigned to the area arrested the two protesters after it said they "assaulted a counter-protester" and "obstructed a road."
The department said the suspects’ names and specific charges will be released after they are booked into jail.
CAN THE 'BEST SHOWMAN IN POLITICS' DELIVER AGAIN? GOP BETS ON TRUMP AT HISTORIC MIDTERM CONVENTION

Law enforcement officers detain a demonstrator during a protest ahead of the second day of the Republican Midterm Convention in Dallas, Texas, Thursday, Sept. 10, 2026. (Leah Millis/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Fox News Digital spoke with a protester named Rick Majumdar, who was wearing a shirt with the initials for the Freedom Road Socialist Organization (FRSO), which, according to its website, is a "national organization of revolutionaries fighting for socialism in the United States."

Majumdar said that the protest was organized by the Dallas Against the Trump Agenda Coalition, which, he said, consists of 16 "faith-based organizations, pro-immigrants’ rights groups and labor organizations."

"We're here to protest the Republican agenda, the Trump agenda and all its policies that it has enacted over the last few years," he explained. "The march is an important event, we feel, against this convention that's happening for the last two days."
REPUBLICANS HEAD TO DALLAS WITH ONE MISSION: DEFY HISTORY AND WIN BIG
Demonstrators march during a protest ahead of the second day of the Republican Midterm Convention in Dallas, Texas, Thursday, Sept. 10, 2026. (Leah Millis/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
He said that, during the group's march, "we encountered some street closures by the police" and that officers arrested a couple of protesters who "were at the front of the group."

Pressed on why the protesters were arrested, Majumdar said, "Those people were trying to draw people away from rioting provocateurs, and I think the police heard something. And they immediately tackled two of them and arrested them, and some of them even pulled out their guns as well."

The protest came amid heightened concerns over political violence and the targeting of public figures. It also coincided with the first anniversary of the assassination of conservative activist and Turning Point USA co-founder Charlie Kirk.
CHARLIE KIRK CONTINUES TO INSPIRE REPUBLICANS AS PARTY RALLIES FOR MIDTERM BATTLE: 'HAVE COURAGE'

title: Federal appeals court compares Trump migrant detention policy to Japanese American internment
summary: The 4th Circuit rejected Trump's mass detention policy, comparing it to Japanese Americans' World War II internment, setting the stage for a Supreme Court showdown.
story: DHS Chief Counsel James Percival said a group of federal district judges — not the judiciary as a whole — is repeatedly blocking deportations and temporary protected status rollbacks despite SCOTUS rulings, calling it ‘naked political activism.’
A Trump administration policy to detain migrants on bond without a chance for release harkens back to the mass detention of Japanese Americans during World War II, a federal court said Thursday.
In a 2-1 decision, the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals rejected the administration's mass detention policy, a major part of President Donald Trump's mass deportation agenda.
"Mass detention of marginalized individuals without due process harkens back to some of the darkest moments in our country’s history," the court wrote.
BIDEN JUDGE OVERRULED ON KEY TRUMP IMMIGRATION POLICY

A group of undocumented migrants is deported by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents across the McAllen–Hidalgo–Reynosa International Bridge in McAllen, Texas. A federal appeals court blasted the ICE policy of holding immigrants on bond without a chance for release. (Felix Marquez/AP Photo)

Nine federal appeals courts have now separately ruled that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement's (ICE) new mandatory detention policy is illegal, concluding it could apply to recent arrivals at or near the border but not to migrants determined to be living elsewhere within the country.
Two other appeals courts have upheld it, meaning the U.S. Supreme Court is likely to take up the case in its upcoming term.
TRUMP SCORES SCOTUS ASYLUM WIN — BUT LIBERAL JUSTICE WARNS IT COULD BACKFIRE AT BORDER
Federal agents detain a man after attending a court hearing in immigration court at the Jacob K. Javitz Federal Building June 30, 2025, in New York City. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)
Immigrant rights groups say basic due process is being violated when longtime residents are denied bond hearings during removal proceedings.

"The courts have resoundingly rejected the administration’s cruel policy and its blatant disrespect for the rule of law," said My Khanh Ngo, senior staff attorney with the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project. "We are thrilled for our clients and their families."

Mass arrests of suspected illegal immigrants during President Donald Trump's second term have prompted widespread protests, particularly in Democratic-led cities like Chicago. In July 2025, the administration announced it would detain every migrant found anywhere in the U.S. whom ICE determines was not granted permission to enter.
A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said the agency was disappointed with Thursday's decision but said it recently sought a Supreme Court review of a similar decision from the 6th Circuit.
FEDERAL JUDGE IN NEW YORK TIES TRUMP ADMIN HANDS ON ARRESTS AT IMMIGRATION COURTS

"Opinions from the Board of Immigration Appeals and two other federal courts of appeals reflect the soundness of DHS’ legal position," the spokesperson said. "This legal position was the nail in the coffin for Biden’s catch and release policies. That is why the left and their activist proxies on the judiciary are resisting it so vigorously.

"President Trump and Secretary Mullin are now enforcing the law as it was actually written to keep America safe," the spokesperson added. "As our record in the U.S. Supreme Court demonstrates, the law is on our side."

Writing for the majority, 4th Circuit Judge Nicole Berner invoked the mass internment of Japanese Americans during World War II as a warning against sweeping executive detention authority without due process.
"The stain of these detentions on our nation — and the judiciary’s abdication of its obligation to protect basic freedoms — continues to haunt us," Berner wrote.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the White House and ICE.

title: Bioweapon threat exposed as Anthropic sounds alarm on foreign actors plotting virus experiments
summary: Researchers outside the United States used Anthropic's Claude to plan gain-of-function experiments on bird flu, chikungunya and dangerous toxins.
story: Former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon discusses his resignation from the company and concerns over artificial intelligence safety on ‘Special Report.’

Researchers outside the United States used frontier AI models to plan experiments involving highly pathogenic bird flu, chikungunya and other biological agents with potential weapons applications, according to a new threat report from Anthropic.

The researchers used AI to study viruses’ transmissibility and immune evasion, investigate orthopoxvirus immune-response genes and help design novel toxins at times while taking steps to evade safeguards meant to restrict access to dangerous biological capabilities.

Anthropic detailed five cases in the report published Thursday but withheld the countries, institutions and specific biological agents involved. The company stressed that it is not claiming the researchers intended to develop biological weapons.
AI KILL SWITCH BILL COULD SHUT DOWN ROGUE MODELS
Staff prepare samples for DNA sequencing at the new offices and laboratories of Othram, a DNA forensics lab, in The Woodlands, Texas, on Nov. 6, 2023. (Michael Wyke/Houston Chronicle)

The findings offer a concrete glimpse at a threat that has largely been discussed in hypothetical terms. Scientists who already possess biological expertise, materials and laboratory access are using increasingly powerful AI systems to accelerate sensitive dual-use research.

They also land amid a renewed debate over catastrophic AI risks. Jacob Coxon, a former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher, recently resigned while accusing the companies of "racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives." His warning drew more than 100 million views on X.
SEN BERNIE SANDERS: YES, WE MUST HIT THE PAUSE BUTTON ON AI BEFORE IT IS TOO LATE
Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s alignment science lead, separately said he personally believed there was a greater than 10% chance AI could kill all humans within the next decade.

But Anthropic’s report points to a threat that is already taking shape: researchers using frontier AI for potentially dangerous biological work, circumventing geographic restrictions and adapting when the models’ safeguards get in their way.
Pages from the Anthropic website and the company's logos are displayed on a computer screen in New York Feb. 26, 2026. (Patrick Sison/AP Photo)

In one case, Anthropic blocked a grant application for chikungunya gain-of-function research at a military research institute. The proposed work focused on identifying mutations that could increase the virus’s transmissibility and ability to evade the immune system.
The researchers planned to engineer those mutations into infectious clones and repeatedly pass the virus through live animals, selecting for variants that caused the most severe disease.

That work could help scientists develop better vaccines and treatments for chikungunya. It could also produce a more dangerous pathogen that would be difficult to distinguish from a naturally occurring outbreak, Anthropic said.

The researchers accessed Claude through a life sciences platform that tunneled traffic through U.S. infrastructure to evade Anthropic’s regional restrictions. When Claude refused to answer sensitive prompts, the platform routed those requests to another model with more permissive safeguards.

Anthropic said the research continued after the company banned accounts connected to the activity. The platform operator reestablished access within days using new identities, while Claude continued to provide editorial assistance on research materials.
In another case, a researcher spent weeks using Claude to plan experiments involving mammalian adaptation and airborne transmission in highly pathogenic avian influenza.
FDA APPROVES FIRST-EVER MRNA FLU VACCINE FOR MILLIONS OF OLDER AMERICANS

The researcher was studying viral traits that could allow bird flu to spread more effectively among mammals and cause severe disease outside the respiratory system. A version capable of efficient human-to-human transmission would pose a significant pandemic threat, according to the report.

Anthropic said the researcher appeared to have access to virus isolates and animal-model facilities. The company confined the work to weaker models, limiting the assistance primarily to study design, data analysis and editorial support.

The company said the case provided evidence of an active research program developing the knowledge and biological materials needed to create pathogens with enhanced pandemic potential. The researcher also took steps to hide his identity while accessing the models from an unsupported region.
A separate user connected to a state-associated infectious-disease laboratory used Claude to draft an orthopoxvirus research grant from start to finish in about an hour.

Orthopoxviruses include variola, the virus that causes smallpox, as well as mpox. The grant application proposed studying viral genes that disable the human immune response and included the central hypothesis, experimental design, dosing, statistical plans and contingency strategies.

Because the work was framed around weakening the virus, Claude’s safeguards did not block the assistance. But Anthropic said the same knowledge could also help a researcher preserve or enhance the virus’ immune-evasion capabilities.
The final two cases involved venom peptides and toxins.
One researcher used Claude to build an atlas of toxin peptides from multiple venomous animal lineages and then created a generative pipeline to optimize their characteristics.
A researcher in a lab drops a blood sample into a Petri dish. (iStock)

The stated goal was to develop new painkillers, antidepressants and other treatments. But the atlas also included structures associated with paralytic toxins that could potentially be used as incapacitating agents. Anthropic said the work was part of a state-supported research program.

In the other case, a researcher used Claude to computationally redesign several toxins, including a bacterial toxin and a protein from a hemorrhagic fever virus identified by the World Health Organization as a priority disease threat.
The researcher used Claude to help prepare progress reports but instructed the model to keep the identities of the toxins deliberately vague.

The cases illustrate why biological misuse can be difficult to prevent through automated filters alone. Anthropic’s safeguards blocked the clearest attempts involving enhanced pandemic pathogens, but they were less effective when users framed their work as medical, defensive or therapeutic research.

"Biological capabilities are dual use," Anthropic said in the report. "The same information that can be used to develop a biological weapon could also be used to develop, for example, a vaccine or a cure for a disease."
Dario Amodei, co-founder and chief executive officer of Anthropic, during the company's Builder Summit in Bengaluru, India, Feb. 16, 2026.  (Samyukta Lakshmi/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The company said it recently reviewed 30 days of activity associated with adversarial state institutions and found roughly 35 distinct biological research efforts. Most involved ordinary civilian science, but some had "notable dual-use potential."
Anthropic said the findings do not show that Claude has enabled an imminent biological attack.

They do show, the company said, that researchers tied to state-associated programs are attempting to evade access controls and use frontier AI models in biological research that could have weapons applications.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The company said future safeguards will likely require more than content filters, including identity verification, institutional vetting and closer monitoring of users seeking access to advanced biological capabilities.

title: Prosecutor Joseph diGenova resigns from DOJ role investigating Trump-Russia probes
summary: Joseph diGenova resigned from his Justice Department role investigating the alleged "Grand Conspiracy" surrounding the Trump-Russia investigations.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

Joseph diGenova has resigned from his Justice Department role investigating the alleged "Grand Conspiracy" surrounding the Trump-Russia investigations, according to two sources familiar with the matter.

Fox News has learned diGenova lost the confidence of both the Justice Department and the White House. According to sources familiar with the matter, he had been effectively sidelined well before his departure.

His resignation comes after months in which his role had diminished internally, ending his involvement in the investigation amid questions about his standing within both the administration and DOJ leadership.
DOJ ORDERED TO FREEZE ANTITRUST WORK WITH CANADA AS TRADE TENSIONS INTENSIFY
ABC News first reported his resignation.
"It was an honor and a privilege to serve the president and the department," diGenova told CBS News.
He declined to comment further about the circumstances surrounding his departure.
DiGenova’s wife, attorney Victoria Toensing, who also joined the federal prosecution team in South Florida, is expected to leave the Justice Department on Friday, according to CBS News.
Joseph diGenova, who has resigned from his role at the Department of Justice. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

The so-called "Grand Conspiracy" investigation is based out of the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Fort Pierce, Florida. It examines whether Obama- and Biden-era officials were involved in a long-running effort to prevent Trump from returning to political office.

The probe has scrutinized officials involved in past investigations of Trump, including former CIA Director John Brennan and former FBI Director James Comey. DiGenova was also overseeing a separate criminal investigation into whether Brennan lied to Congress about the intelligence community’s assessment that Russia interfered in the 2016 election.

Rudolph Giuliani, left, and Joseph diGenova, center, attorneys for President Donald Trump, conduct a news conference at the Republican National Committee on lawsuits regarding the outcome of the 2020 presidential election on Thursday, November 19, 2020 (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call/Getty Images)
MAJOR BLUE STATE HOSPITAL PULLS PLUG ON CONTROVERSIAL CHILD TRANSGENDER TREATMENTS AFTER DOJ INTERVENTION

The investigation has issued dozens of subpoenas over the past year. Lawyers for some witnesses were recently notified that their clients would receive grand jury subpoenas, while investigators also sought voluntary interviews with former FBI agents involved in the Mar-a-Lago investigation, according to CBS News. Prosecutors have not filed charges in either case.

DiGenova was tapped to oversee the probe in April after career prosecutor Maria Medetis Long was removed from the case. He had criticized delays in the investigation and said indictments could have been brought within 30 days.
His departure, along with Toensing’s expected exit, leaves the future of the investigation uncertain.
Joe Digenova on Fox News in 2019.  (Fox News)

The longtime Washington attorney previously served as U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia from 1983 to 1988. He later represented Trump’s campaign during its unsuccessful effort to challenge the 2020 election results.

title: Fatwas, holy wars and socialism: Inside the Islamic conference where El-Sayed drew a hero’s welcome
summary: Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed headlined an ISNA conference where an attendee called for a fatwa against members of Congress.
story: Fox News Digital captured video and audio documenting statements made by speakers and panelists at the Islamic Society of North America’s annual conference.

DETROIT – Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed headlined an Islamic conference over Labor Day weekend where the United States was described as an empire in decline, early Islamic conquests were praised and the aftermath of 9/11 was framed around Islamophobia and discrimination.
The event, held annually by the Islamic Society of North America, featured a range of speakers discussing topics from Muslim civic participation to the ongoing conflict between Israel and Hamas.

Over the course of the conference’s speeches and panel discussions, participants took positions that were generally critical of the United States and the broader Western world and expressed opinions that some may regard as extreme.
EXILED MUSLIM SCHOLAR WARNS FAR-LEFT–ISLAMIST ALLIANCE BEHIND ANTI-ISRAEL PROTESTS ECHOES IRAN’S RISE

Fox News Digital attended the event over the weekend, sitting in on many of the panels held on Saturday and Sunday before and after El-Sayed's speech. The Michigan Democrat is running in one of the most hotly contested Senate races of the 2026 cycle, the outcome of which may decide control of the Senate.

At one panel, "Rising Islamophobia in the U.S.," a speaker described recently passed legislation that could bar colleges participating in certain commercial boycotts of Israel from receiving some federal higher education funds as "an anti-Muslim bill."
Abdul El-Sayed's campaign running a booth at the Islamic Society of North America's annual conference.  (Robert Schmad/Fox News Digital)

Shortly after that, a man in the audience wearing a Pakistani flag pin stood up and called for a fatwa to be issued against the bipartisan group of lawmakers who voted for the bill. A fatwa is a religious ruling or opinion that can range from a formal condemnation to, in some cases, a call for or justification of violence.
The legislation was introduced by Rep. Virginia Foxx, R-N.C., and co-sponsored by Rep. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J.
After the man called for a fatwa against members of Congress, members of the audience — and one panelist — applauded.
Earlier, during the same discussion, a panelist criticized Congress for moving to censure Reps. Ilhan Omar and Rashida Tlaib for making "​​the most lighthearted comments"

Tlaib was censured in part for endorsing the phrase "from the river to the sea, Palestine will be free," which calls for the destruction of Israel as bounded by the Jordan River in the east and the Mediterranean Sea in the west. Critics characterized the phrase as a call for ethnic cleansing, while the congresswoman defended it as "an aspirational call for freedom, human rights and peaceful coexistence."

ISNA is a nonprofit Muslim religious organization established in 1981 to provide America's growing Muslim population with a platform for civic coordination and education. Detroit, where the event took place, is situated in a metropolitan area that has a significant Arab American population concentrated in areas such as Dearborn and Hamtramck.
EL-SAYED CAMPAIGN BACKED BY OVER $100,000 FROM DOZENS OF MEMBERS OF GROUP WITH ALLEGED TERROR TIES
A breakout session at the ISNA's annual conference.   (Robert Schmad/Fox News Digital)

Panelists also accused billionaire Elon Musk of funding a White supremacist global anti-Muslim movement, suggested that some of the narrative regarding 9/11 taught in American schools has been "debunked" and asserted that Muslims were treated unfairly in the wake of the 2001 attacks.

Criticism of America’s response to 9/11 surfaced repeatedly across the conference’s events and breakout sessions. One speaker asserted that one of the most important things to reflect on as the 25th anniversary of 9/11 approaches is that "Islamophobia is at an all-time high." Another called the War on Terror, a series of post-9/11 military operations that claimed the lives of over 7,000 U.S. military personnel, the "War of Terror."

El-Sayed has sought to moderate his public image since launching his Senate campaign, even as he has maintained ties to prominent socialists and socialist-aligned activists. His attendance at the recent ISNA conference is the latest in a series of associations that have drawn criticism, including ties to Nation of Islam figures, Muslim clerics accused of expressing support for terrorist organizations and activists on the socialist left.

In response to these charges, the Democrat has pointed out that GOP Senate nominee Mike Rogers has links to individuals who echo conspiracy theories about the 2020 election or who have called for bans on gay marriage.
EL-SAYED’S HASAN PIKER PROBLEM FOLLOWS HIM TO DEM CONVENTION AS JEWISH VOTERS BREAK RANKS
A speech being delivered at the Islamic Society of North America's annual conference.   (Robert Schmad/Fox News Digital)
Before the event, El-Sayed’s campaign moved to distance the candidate from other conference speakers.
"Abdul is not affiliated with and does not endorse any other participant of the conference," a spokeswoman for his campaign told media outlets in the lead-up to the event.

The statement followed reports that he would appear alongside Islamic clerics who defended child marriage and praised U.S.-designated terrorist organizations, including al Qaeda. Of the controversial speakers, only the cleric who had defended child marriage was ultimately disinvited, The Washington Free Beacon previously reported.

ISNA appeared to anticipate scrutiny over some of the speakers it invited to the conference. In the conference venue’s main hallway, the organization posted a prominent sign which says, "ISNA does not endorse the actions of convention participants and explicitly disclaims any responsibility for the views expressed, information provided, or materials displayed, sold or distributed by convention speakers, performers, exhibitors, vendors, or attendees."
COUNTERTERRORISM EXPERT WARNS ABDUL EL-SAYED SENATE BID RAISES HOMELAND SECURITY CONCERNS
Disclaimer placard at the ISNA's annual conference.  (Robert Schmad/Fox News Digital)
While ISNA sought to distance itself from the controversial views expressed by some conference speakers, the organization itself took actions that also drew scrutiny.

Fox News Digital spoke to three Christian evangelists outside the conference who claimed they were removed from it without warning. Each of them said they were simply having conversations with individuals who wanted to speak with them before they were escorted outside by security.
Attendance at the conference was open to people of all faiths, and registration did not require attendees to be Muslim. The conference also held an interfaith banquet on Sunday.

The disclaimer took on added significance in light of books available for purchase at the conference’s on-site bazaar. Fox News Digital found books that defended Islamic warfare while portraying Christianity as uniquely violent.

"Christians are the last people on earth who should bring the charge of bloodshed and cruelty against followers of any other system, for it is a well-established fact that no religion known to history has such a horrible sanguinary record as church Christianity," one book sold at the conference reads.

Another book argued that all Islamic warfare is defensive, defended non-Muslims being forced to pay a discriminatory tax and claimed that Christian civilization has killed nearly 200 million people by attributing wars that did not have religious motivations or were not initiated by Christians.

The French Revolution, which was instigated by individuals hostile to Christianity, for instance, is counted toward Christianity’s death count. The Korean War, which was launched by communist North Korea, is also counted toward the body count of Christianity.
UNEARTHED INTERVIEW REVEALS EL-SAYED’S SHARIA ‘OBLIGATION’: ‘NOT BECAUSE OF FEAR’
A selection of books at the ISNA's annual conference.  (Robert Schmad/Fox News Digital)
The conference also featured advertisements for "Sharia-compliant" mortgages and other financial products.

El-Sayed held a quasi-celebrity status among the conference’s attendees. Campaign buttons were nearly ubiquitous at the conference, and his campaign’s booth was easily the busiest of those located in the main hall, Fox News Digital found.
When the Senate hopeful walked on stage to address the conference, he was greeted with a thunderous standing ovation. Calls of "we love you" rang out from the crowd.
El-Sayed’s speech was ultimately measured and largely focused on unity, representation and the idea that Muslim and American identities are compatible.
"As we leave here tonight, I’ve got a challenge for each and every one of you," El-Sayed said with a measured cadence reminiscent of former President Barack Obama.

"It’s the question of how you show up in the spaces in which you show up everyday, as wholly and 100% yourself. Because we are a community as Muslim Americans who believe in the rhyming of our Muslim ideals and our American ideals. That those two things are not mutually exclusive, in fact, that at their best being Muslim makes us better Americans and being Muslim enables us to be better Americans."
‘DESTROYING THE AMERICAN WAY OF LIFE’: EL-SAYED’S POLITICAL ORBIT COMPLICATES EFFORT TO MODERATE HIS IMAGE
Attendees look on as a cleric in traditional garb speaks.   (Robert Schmad/Fox News Digital)
But elsewhere at the conference, speakers offered a markedly different assessment of America and its place in the world.

"The world has become multipolar, and we see almost like the fear and insecurity that the empire has at this moment if we think through the lens of the U.S. So, I like to think that we are on the very end of an ending empire," an academic speaking at a session about the conflict between Israel and Hamas said. "I'm very positive about it."
The same panelist later argued that referring to the river next to Detroit as the "Detroit River" was an immoral act of colonialism because Native Americans had a different name for the waterway.

In a similar vein, a speaker at one of the conference’s main sessions criticized American foreign policy after the 9/11 terrorist attacks, then credited the "TikTok generation" with mobilizing in favor of Palestinians following the Oct. 7 terrorist attacks.
Some speakers, however, made a clear effort to connect El-Sayed’s socialist project with his Islamic faith.
"Islam historically was not just spread by the instance of Dawah. It was spread by socialism," said a cleric who would go on to speak positively about early Islamic conquests.

ISNA declined comment. The El-Sayed campaign did not respond to requests for comment after being reached by Fox News Digital Wednesday.

title: Trump administration accuses prestigious law school of favoring Black applicants over White, Asian peers
summary: Federal officials allege a major California law school favored Black applicants over Asian and White students, but the university denies violating admissions laws.
story: Fox News senior correspondent Claudia Cowan has the latest on the Justice Department's investigation into violent riots outside a Turning Point USA event at UC Berkeley on 'America Reports.'

The Trump administration on Wednesday blasted the University of California, Berkeley, School of Law for allegedly favoring Black applicants while discriminating against Asian and White students, marking its latest federal action targeting race-conscious admissions policies at universities.

The Department of Justice (DOJ), along with the Department of Education, found Berkeley Law in violation of Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibits racial discrimination in programs and activities receiving federal funds.
"The data produced by Berkeley Law demonstrates a strong bias against Asian and White applicants, with a corresponding bias in favor of Black applicants," the DOJ said.

The findings came after officials launched a compliance review of Berkeley Law in March 2025, roughly two years after the Supreme Court struck a major blow to affirmative action programs many universities used in admissions for decades. California had already banned affirmative action in public education under Proposition 209, enacted in 1996.
JUSTICE DEPARTMENT ZEROES IN ON UCLA FOR ALLEGED ILLEGAL DEI ADMISSIONS AS ELITE SCHOOL CRACKDOWN EXPANDS

Berkeley Law in Berkeley, Calif., on June 4, 2021. Federal officials allege Black applicants had higher admission odds than comparable White applicants at Berkeley Law. (David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
According to the DOJ's analysis, Black applicants in 2025 had "5.8 times higher odds of admission than comparable white applicants."
An analysis of LSAT scores for admitted students in 2024 and 2025 found that 37% of Black admitted applicants scored below 99% of admitted White applicants.
In addition, half of the school's admitted Black applicants had LSAT scores "below 95% of the admitted white applicants."

According to figures cited by the DOJ, median LSAT scores from 2021 through 2025 showed a persistent disparity between racial groups, with Black admits scoring around 165. Asian and White admits scored around 172, while Hispanic admits had median scores around 169.

"The median Black admit consistently has an LSAT score about 5 points lower than the median white or Asian admits," the department said in a letter to attorney Tania Faransso, who is representing the law school.

An aerial view of the University of California, Berkeley, campus in Berkeley, Calif., May 2, 2024. The DOJ cited LSAT score disparities among law school admits. (Jane Tyska/Digital First Media/East Bay Times)
DOJ OPENS PROBE INTO PRESTIGIOUS COLLEGE OVER ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION FAVORING MINORITY STUDENTS
As of October 2025, Berkeley Law had 1,128 students enrolled. Of those, 516 were White, 293 were Asian, 51 were Black and 130 were Hispanic.
In a statement to Fox News, Berkeley Law firmly rejected the allegations, saying its admissions decisions comply with federal law and Proposition 209.
However, the school noted that the laws still allow institutions to build diverse student bodies by considering race-neutral factors, which can include socioeconomic status and personal experiences.

"Our admissions policy is clear that race is not considered in any way in admissions decisions," the school said. "Proposition 209, federal statutes and the Supreme Court’s decisions do not preclude schools from pursuing diversity so long as they give no preferences based on race. Berkeley Law does not do so."

UC Berkeley’s central administration also said the school is "committed to ensuring that every student is admitted based on their merit, and not on their race, sex, color, ethnicity or national origin."

Students walk past Sather Gate at the University of California, Berkeley, on Feb. 19, 2026. The school maintains that it complies with California’s Proposition 209 and federal law. (Christina House/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"UC Berkeley will spare no effort to provide ample evidence showing that the university complies with all relevant laws, policies and rules governing admissions," the school said.
Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

title: Trump signs act clearing the way for Medal of Honor monument on National Mall
summary: Trump signed the act at the National Medal of Honor Museum in Arlington, Texas, after meeting 15 living recipients and touring the facility.
story: President Donald Trump shakes hands with Medal of Honor recipients during a visit to the National Medal of Honor Museum in Arlington, Texas, Sept. 10, 2026.

President Donald Trump signed legislation Thursday authorizing the future National Medal of Honor Monument to be located within the Reserve of the National Mall in Washington, D.C., near the Lincoln Memorial, during a ceremony honoring Medal of Honor recipients in Arlington, Texas.
Trump signed the Hershel "Woody" Williams National Medal of Honor Monument Location Act at the National Medal of Honor Museum after touring the museum and meeting more than a dozen recipients.

The legislation does not create the monument itself, which Congress previously authorized in 2021. Instead, it allows the future monument to be located within the Reserve, a protected area of the National Mall that includes some of Washington's most prominent monuments and memorials.
EXCLUSIVE: NEW AMERICA 250 MONUMENT LETS FAMILIES FIND MILITARY RELATIVES IN SECONDS: 'I HAD TEARS IN MY EYES'
President Donald Trump takes the stage during an event at the National Medal of Honor Museum on Thursday in Arlington, Texas. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
Trump greeted and shook hands with recipients before taking the stage for the signing ceremony.
"We're privileged to have with us 15 of the 65 living recipients of the Congressional Medal of Honor," Trump told the audience.

"When I see the recipients of the Congressional Medal, those that are living, many are dead. They died. And they died in battle. Some of the battles are … I read inscriptions of what took place. That level of bravery is incredible," Trump said.

The act is named for Williams, a Marine who received the Medal of Honor for his actions during the Battle of Iwo Jima and was the last surviving World War II Medal of Honor recipient when he died in 2022.
HEGSETH UPGRADES ABBEY GATE MARINES' VALOR AWARDS AFTER 5-YEAR DELAY: 'THOSE DAYS ARE OVER'
Congressional Medal of Honor recipient Hershel Woody Williams salutes while standing at the new Gold Star Families Memorial Monument in downtown Pensacola Nov. 10, 2020. (Gregg Pachkowski/Imagn)
Trump recounted Williams' heroism before recognizing members of his family who attended the ceremony.
"In the Battle of Iwo Jima, he carved a path to American victory, literally carved a path so soldiers could get in and win through a deadly gantlet of enemy strongholds," Trump said.

"And back and forth, he went. He just kept going back and forth," Trump continued. "And one machine gun nest after another. He knocked [them] out, and he did it for hours and hours. People said they've never seen anything quite like it."
National Medal of Honor Museum Foundation Chairman Charlotte Jones said 16 of the nation's 65 living Medal of Honor recipients were present at the museum Thursday.
SIX AMERICAN HEROES EVERYONE SHOULD KNOW THIS MEMORIAL DAY, FROM DELTA FORCE TO A WWII BOMBER CREW

The coffin of Hershel Woodrow "Woody" Williams is carried down the East Front Center Steps of the U.S. Capitol during a ceremony after lying in honor in Washington, D.C., July 14, 2022. (Anna Rose Layden)
"This is not a war museum. This is a museum about heart, about courage, about sacrifice and patriotism," Jones said.

The museum foundation said the effort to create and locate the monument has received eight votes in Congress over six years, all unanimously. The location act itself also passed both chambers without opposition, according to the foundation.
Jones said that bipartisan support reflected the significance of the Medal of Honor and the values associated with it.
"That is the inspirational power of the Medal of Honor," Jones said. "And that is why this project matters."
'BLACK HAWK DOWN' SNIPER SHINES LIGHT ON BRUTAL REALITY OF VIOLENT COMBAT

President Donald Trump signs the Hershel "Woody" Williams National Medal of Honor Monument Location Act during an event at the National Medal of Honor Museum in Arlington, Texas, Thursday. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

The future monument will be located near the Lincoln Memorial, though its precise site has not yet been selected. The National Park Service will award the specific site, after which the foundation said it will launch a design competition.
No federal funds will be used to construct the monument, according to the foundation, which will raise the money needed for the project.
Trump also reflected on the sacrifices represented by the recipients gathered for Thursday's ceremony.

President Donald Trump signs the Hershel "Woody" Williams National Medal of Honor Monument Location Act at the National Medal of Honor Museum in Arlington, Texas. (Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images)
"People like this, they stood tall when their country needed heroes," Trump said.

"They carried the wounded out of battle and on their own backs and carried them back and forth," he continued. "They gave their bodies the shields for their brothers at arms. They stood in the way of bullets, purposely standing just like this and taking bullets. And it's amazing. These are amazing."
Trump said the future monument, together with the museum, would provide a permanent way to preserve those stories.

"With this museum and a new monument in Washington, D.C., America will never, ever forget what they did and what they risked and how much they risked, what they meant to their families and what they've meant to our country," Trump said.
