title: Trump faces reckoning as GOP figures label $5K promise a 'socialist vote-buying scheme'
summary: President Donald Trump's $5,000 dividend proposal could cost over $1.2 trillion, sparking a fierce GOP debate over tariff revenue and national debt.
story: President Donald Trump promised $5,000 dividends for adult U.S. citizens if Republicans keep majorities in Congress. 'America's Newsroom' and 'Fox & Friends' weigh in on the proposal.

President Donald Trump’s proposal to send $5,000 checks to American adults if Republicans win both chambers of Congress is forcing Republicans to debate an idea more commonly associated with the Democratic side of the aisle: sending direct government payments to voters.

Called a "socialist vote-buying scheme" by former GOP Rep. Bob Good of Virginia, the so-called Trump Dividend would only be handed down if Republicans keep the House and Senate in November, the president announced at the party's midterm convention in Dallas.
Good warned that the checks would add to the national debt, which has topped $40 trillion.

The plan could cost more than $1.2 trillion, based on estimates of roughly 240 million eligible adults. The president cannot direct the Treasury to issue the checks without a law providing that authority, so Congress would need to authorize the spending plan.
TRUMP MAKES STUNNING FIRST-OF-ITS-KIND CASH PROMISE IN BID TO RALLY GOP VOTERS AT DALLAS MIDTERM CONVENTION
President Donald Trump speaks on stage on the first day of the 2026 Republican National Convention at the American Airlines Center on Sept. 9, 2026, in Dallas, Texas. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)

"If the Republicans win the House of Representatives and the United States Senate, both of them … I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000," Trump said during his keynote address Wednesday night.
He compared the payment to a cash distribution from a successful company to its shareholders and said the money would have to be spent domestically.
"The only caveat I have is that the dividend that we're making must be spent in the United States of America," Trump said. "We don't want you going to Canada to spend the money."

"If you keep us in power and allow us to continue to do these things, then you’re going to share in some of the benefit of this incredible wealth that we’re creating in the United States of America," Vice President JD Vance said after Trump unveiled his new idea.
Conservative commentator Matt Walsh called the plan "flagrant bribery" and said Republicans could help working Americans by allowing them to keep more of their own money through tax cuts.
"Holding it as a carrot on the stick for after the election is just shameless," Walsh wrote.
Vance and Trump both pointed to tariff revenue as a potential funding source for the payments, and questions emerged over where the money would come from to fund the dividends.
"The reason the Democrats can’t do that is because they don’t do tariffs. They don’t take in money. All they know is poverty," Trump said Wednesday night.

Treasury data show the federal government collected about $154.4 billion in customs duties from Oct. 1, 2025, through July 31, 2026, which would cover roughly 13% of the estimated $1.2 trillion cost of sending $5,000 checks to about 240 million adults.

The administration has not provided an income threshold for the proposed middle-class payments or explained how much tariff revenue would be dedicated to the program. The remaining cost would have to be covered through other federal revenue, spending reductions or additional borrowing.
CONGRESS SPENDS $7 TRILLION; HERE’S HOW THAT MATH WORKS OUT IF YOU THINK OF JUST $100
President Donald Trump speaks on stage on the first day of the 2026 Republican National Convention at the American Airlines Center in Dallas, Texas, Sept. 9, 2026. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)

Vance also suggested in an interview after the president's speech Wednesday that the proposal could be limited to middle-class Americans rather than every adult citizen, potentially lowering the cost.

The VP defended the idea as "fundamentally a dividend for American workers," arguing that tariffs have generated revenue from foreign companies and countries that have taken advantage of American workers.
The proposal’s funding and eligibility questions have fueled criticism from fiscal conservatives, who say the plan would create a new government benefit while adding to the national debt.
Rep. Chip Roy, R-Texas, said the estimated $1.2 trillion cost of the dividend proposal could instead be used to eliminate taxes for married parents with dependents earning up to $200,000.
"Or maybe some of us think dependency is evil & soul-sucking in all its forms," Roy wrote in a follow-up post.

That criticism from Republicans reflects a broader conservative argument that tax cuts are preferable to direct payments because they reduce the government’s role rather than create a new reason for Americans to rely on it.

James Fishback, a former Florida gubernatorial candidate who previously proposed a $5,000 DOGE dividend, said his plan would have returned savings generated by spending cuts. Meanwhile, he argued Trump’s proposal would add to the debt without a comparable reduction in government spending.
Investor Joe Lonsdale called the idea "bread and circus bribes." Former Arkansas Gov. Asa Hutchinson urged Republican leaders to reject it and focus on reducing the debt.

President Donald Trump greets attendees as he walks on stage on the first day of the Republican National Convention at the American Airlines Center in Dallas, Texas, on Sept. 9, 2026.  (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)
Other Republicans and Trump allies are moving in the opposite direction.
Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, said he would prepare legislation to pass the dividend after the election, while Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., asked voters how they would spend their $5,000.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The reactions show a Republican Party split between treating tariff revenue as money to return to Americans and preserving the party’s traditional emphasis on lower taxes, limited spending and less government dependence.

title: Trump's $5,000 dividend checks would come with a major catch under GOP senator's plan
summary: Trump's $5,000 tariff dividend plan could cost $1.2 trillion as Sen. Bernie Moreno pushes legislation to fund checks through market access fees.
story: Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, says his plan to make President Donald Trump’s $5,000 tariff-funded dividend checks law would require congressional approval, with payments restricted to spending in the U.S.
DALLAS — There’s a push in the Senate to turn President Donald Trump’s pitch of $5,000 checks for Americans into a reality, with a couple of caveats along the way.

Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, plans to introduce legislation that would codify the dividend checks and wants it done as soon as the upcoming midterm elections are over, when the balance of power could tilt in favor of Democrats.

But the money, Moreno told Fox News Digital, wouldn’t come from taxpayers’ coffers. Instead, he wants to approve certain structural tariffs to act as a "market access fee" that would find its way back into the pockets of Americans.
TRUMP DEFENDS $5,000 DIVIDEND PROPOSAL, PRAISES 'BEAUTIFUL' TARIFFS ON 'INGRAHAM ANGLE'
President Donald Trump speaks during the Republican convention at American Airlines Center on Sept. 9, 2026, in Dallas. (The Dallas Morning News via Getty Images)
And it can only be spent in the U.S.

"This dividend would be something that is allowing working Americans to share in the prosperity of this country," Moreno said. "The money would be used only here in the United States, so it's not to be used outside the United States. I think it would provide a big economic boost to our economy."

"So, if you're a company out there, anywhere in the world, you want to sell your products in America, you either make it here in the United States, or you pay a fee to enter our market," he continued. "That money goes to funding this one-time dividend."

Trump floated the plan Wednesday night during the Republicans’ midterm convention in Dallas, where the GOP and several — but not all — vulnerable incumbents and candidates flocked to energize their base and pitch why they should maintain control of Congress.
TRUMP JUST EXPANDED HIS TARIFF PLAYBOOK WITH A POWERFUL TRADE WEAPON NO PRESIDENT HAS EVER USED

The cost, however, could be an eye-popping $1.2 trillion. Moreno argued that the cost was worth it and noted that despite the steps Republicans have taken to lower costs, Americans are still feeling the crunch.

"It's about providing relief," Moreno said. "It's acknowledgment that during the Biden years, it was so bad for working families, that, despite what we've already done in 18 months, it just isn't enough to get working families to basically so that they're level, right?"
"Because they're underwater right now," he continued. "I think it's extremely important for us to understand in elected office that working families are struggling."

For the plan to work, Republicans would need to maintain their control of both chambers of Congress, and it comes as the nation’s federal deficit skyrocketed to $40 trillion last month and as the GOP has consistently pitched itself as the party of fiscal responsibility against Democrats’ wanton federal spending.
Trump's plan scored one unlikely ally in House Freedom Caucus Chairman Andy Harris, R-Md., leader of a pack of fiscal hawks who routinely scoff at Congress’ inability to tackle the nation’s debt.

"Hardworking American taxpayers probably deserve a tax rebate. We're gonna have to discuss, you know, how large a rebate that would be. But I think, again, American taxpayers deserve relief from taxation. I think that's a good idea," Harris told Fox News Digital in an interview during the GOP midterm convention.
REPUBLICAN SOUNDS ALARM ON RISING DEM STAR: 'THIS GUY’S GOING TO BE A PROBLEM'
"I think it would provide a big economic boost to our economy," Sen. Bernie Moreno said of the dividend. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)
Harris said such a plan "would have to go through Congress," and he suggested that the party-line budget reconciliation process would be needed to skirt Democratic opposition.
The Senate’s top Republican agreed with Harris.
"It smells very much like a reconciliation issue," Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told Fox News Digital.

Thune said Senate Republicans would be willing to work with Trump and his team to get the dividends done, but noted that until Wednesday night it was a proposal that "we hadn’t heard before." He argued that the idea showed the difference between the GOP and Democrats seeking power.

"I think it illustrates the clear contrast between us and the Democrats about how you want to, how you see government functioning," Thune said. "And one is in giving more power, control, money in the pockets of the American people, and the other, giving more power to, you know, for people in Washington to tell you how to run your life."
And Republicans will likely have to rely on reconciliation to do it, given that Democrats are already slamming the idea.

"Donald Trump is a known liar. This is the biggest liar to ever serve in government, period. And look, the dividend is not happening," Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., told Fox News Digital. "He promised a dividend on tariffs, that didn't happen. He promised a dividend on Doge, that didn't happen. He promised some strange new dividend from Air Force One, what, six months ago. That never happened."

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., recoiled and slammed the move as emblematic of Trump’s presidency being "so failed and broken, he is resorting to trying to bribe the American people for their votes."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"An insult to Americans, to democracy, and an admission of how absolutely screwed he is," Schumer said on X.

Moreno countered that when it comes to dumping tens of billions of dollars outside the U.S., Democrats were all on board but didn’t show the same vigor when it came to seeing money flow back into America.

"So look, at the end of the day, these politicians are all hypocritical. They love helping anybody on earth except for working Americans," Moreno said. "They love giving money to foreign countries. They love funding endless wars. They love having us solve the entirety of the world's problems. When it comes to helping working Americans, all of a sudden, there's no money. What we're saying is no."
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Illegal convicted of assaulting high school girls thought he was free — then DHS dropped the hammer

story: Fairfax County leaders face harsh criticism for allegedly prioritizing illegal criminals over the safety of young girls. story: Biblical economist reveals why higher education is failing on wisdom and how new TPUSA program prepares young people for life

For decades, aspiring young Americans have followed a predictable formula: high school, college, debt. But at the Turning Point USA prep year program, 18-year-old students are encouraged to pause, learn how to think, and discover their true purpose before committing to that considerable investment.
Charlie Kirk speaks at CPAC in Oxon Hill, Maryland. (Kevin Lamarque/Reuters)

Dr. David Arnott, dean of the program, reflects on why the biggest problem in America isn't merely economics: it's character and wisdom. The mission is bold: use a year of classical, liberal arts education to mold the next generation of America's conservative leaders.
CHARLIE KIRK'S 10 MOST POWERFUL MOMENTS FROM COLLEGE CAMPUSES TO THE REPUBLICAN NATIONAL CONVENTION
Dr. Arnott sat down with Fox News at FreedomFest in Las Vegas to discuss how TPUSA's prep year is fulfilling Charlie Kirk's educational vision for America's youth:

"It is an ‘education about economics’ problem. I started my lecture here yesterday at FreedomFest asking the question, ‘why do we keep falling for socialism?’ And I tried to answer that question. And that's what I've been studying over the last 12 years as a Christian economist.

"How do we distribute goods in a fallen world? And so, I was asked by the people at Turning Point USA to be their dean of the prep year program in Fort Worth. Charlie Kirk's first book in 2022 was called ‘The College Scam.’ In 2026, he implemented his idea for education.

Dr. David Arnott speaks at a Turning Point Education event.

"We're having this interview at FreedomFest. So I think people should have the freedom… they should have the freedom to go to college. They should have the freedom to go into the trades. The problem is the government puts their thumb on the scale by supporting the price of college and, of course, forgiving the debt, which they shouldn't do anyway. If the government would just leave it alone, we'd be happy."
TPUSA's prep year program recently graduated its first class.

"We just dismissed our first class of 34, our inaugural class of prep year. It started Sept. 2, 2025, and ended May 22, 2026. Thirty-four students, about a third will be in college this fall. About a third will go into the trades. I just filled out an application the other day for one of the students to get a Mike Rowe scholarship. And about a third will go on to other things that we don't know yet.

The launch of the program was immediately prior to Kirk's tragic assassination on the campus of Utah State University.

So that's what we do. We'll take in 35 to 50, maybe as many as 80 students in Elgin, Illinois, and Fort Worth this fall. CHARLIE KIRK SAYS 'UNDER NO CIRCUMSTANCE SHOULD A MAN EVER LET A WOMAN PAY FOR A DATE'

"And the real secret sauce that I can't explain to you because it's so hard to explain is the effect of being with 35 to 50 other committed Christian conservative 18-year-olds who are highly intelligent. The way in which they learn from each other and gain from each other is just spectacular."
As AI radically transforms education, learning, and the very face of knowledge itself, Arnott emphasizes that the program seeks to instill wisdom, not merely mastery of academic subjects:

Dr. David Arnott and a Turning Point Education representative stand at a podium during an event.

title: Pentagon witness blasts Virginia school district's 'vanilla' 9/11 teacher guide
summary: Fairfax County, Va., schools face criticism over its new 9/11 guide, which identifies al Qaeda but emphasizes Muslim sensitivities and warns teachers not to “center the extremists."
story: Retired Vice Admiral Lou Crenshaw, who was inside the Pentagon when the hijacked plane struck, describes the building shaking and smoke rising as Fairfax County, Va., schools emphasize Muslim sensitivities over the attackers’ ideology.

A wealthy Washington, D.C., suburb's public school district is advising teachers not to link 9/11 with radical Islam and to be sure to create "safe spaces" for Muslim students as the nation somberly marks the 25th anniversary of the terror attacks that killed nearly 3,000 Americans.

The guardrails in a six-page instructional guide, "25th Anniversary and Commemoration of 9/11" and distributed to teachers, has prompted critics to accuse Fairfax County (Virginia) Public School's liberal leaders of coddling post-9/11 sensitivities rather than teaching history.

s"It's sort of a vanilla way to do things," retired Navy Vice Admiral Lou Crenshaw, who was stationed inside the Pentagon when al Qaeda terrorists crashed a hijacked passenger jet into the building. "Everybody can go through the deal and feel good about it. And at the end of the day, nobody complains.
CBC TELLS JOURNALISTS NOT TO CALL 9/11 ‘TERRORIST ATTACKS’ IN INTERNAL GUIDANCE

"To me, that's not exactly what we need to do. We need to make sure that the kids have learned a lesson here. And that's not going to happen if we try to shave the facts to the point where it's hard to figure out what we're talking about."

A digital content analysis reveals that about half of the 1,740-word document is devoted to tips for creating "safe spaces for Muslim and Middle Eastern students," about 15% spells out specific 9/11 instruction and the rest of the document tip-toes around managing "emotional responses" to the lesson.
In northern Virginia, Fairfax County Public Schools distributes a guide for 9/11 lessons, with a list of "Do's and "Don'ts" (Fairfax County Public Schools)

The guide by the school district, which sits only a few miles from the Pentagon and several military bases, mentions military families only three times and first responders only once, saying at one point, "Many families of military personnel and first responders experienced loss and hardship."

Meanwhile, it has 30 references to Islam, "Muslim families," "Muslim students," "anti-Muslim racism," "anti-Middle Eastern" rhetoric, "Islamophobic rhetoric" and "Middle Eastern students" and families. It includes a bulleted list of "critical considerations" to challenge anti-Muslim bias.

The curriculum guidance speaks to a wider tension about how the 9/11 attacks are described by influential figures from teachers, journalists and politicians to social media influencers as a network of powerful Muslim organizations have built educational programs over the past 25 years downplaying discussions about the extremist interpretations of Islam that motivated al Qaeda and the 19 hijackers involved in the 9/11 attacks.

On Thursday, New York Police Department Commissioner Jessica Tisch called for "moral clarity" about what happened on 9/11, saying in a speech, "The men who attacked this city were terrorists. The men and women who ran into the towers to save innocent lives were heroes.
"Twenty-five years cannot be allowed to blur that distinction, and shame on those who do."
Last month, after a major public backlash, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation reversed earlier guidance that instructed journalists to avoid calling 9/11 a "terrorist attack."

Fairfax County Public Schools provides teachers a guide that includes "critical considerations" to avoid discussing the extremist interpretation of Islam that motivated the 9/11 hijackers. (Fairfax County Public Schools)

In a statement provided to Fox News Digital, Fairfax County Public Schools said the school community has a "deeply personal connection to September 11 because of our proximity to the Pentagon and the many military-connected families we serve.

"On the 25th anniversary of the terrorist attacks, we remember the nearly 3,000 people who were killed, including 184 at the Pentagon. We remember the victims, their families, the survivors, and everyone whose lives were forever changed. We honor the first responders whose courage and sacrifice continue to inspire us," the school district said.
"FCPS remains committed to creating an inclusive environment in our schools where all students feel welcome and respected as we strive to provide a world-class education and workplace."
LIZ PEEK: WE CANNOT LET THE LEFT REWRITE WHAT HAPPENED ON 9/11
Smoke pours from the twin towers of the World Trade Center after they were hit by two hijacked airliners in a terrorist attack Sept. 11, 2001, in New York City. (Robert Giroux/Getty Images)

Crenshaw saw the effects on military and civilian families impacted by the attack. On the fateful morning, Crenshaw was stationed on the Pentagon’s E Ring. He watched the TV footage of two airplanes crashing into the World Trade Center.
"I thought, 'This is not a good thing,'" Crenshaw recalled.
He then continued with a scheduled appointment, but as it began, the Pentagon was struck.

"Just about the time they sat down, and we started the interview, there was tremendous noise," Crenshaw said. "Bang! The entire building shook, and we knew right away that something bad had happened."

Crenshaw, who served in the Navy from 1974 to 2007, was on the fourth floor of the Pentagon on the same side of the building hit by the plane. His work area did not immediately collapse, although he said it was later destroyed by fire.
He looked outside and saw smoke billowing from the area where the airplane had hit. He also remembered seeing a chief petty officer crying as windows shattered and glass scattered across the floor.

Our Flag Was Still There features flags related to 9/11 as the nation marks 25 years since the 2001 terrorist attacks and celebrates its 250th anniversary. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images; Craig Ruttle/Pool/Getty Images)

The reality of the attack soon became clear to Crenshaw and the rest of the country. Al Qaeda, an extremist terrorist organization led by Usama bin Laden, had carried out a coordinated assault. The group used an extremist interpretation of Islam to justify the attack, portraying it as retaliation for the presence of U.S. forces overseas and American foreign policy. Bin Laden associate Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, who took credit for planning the attack, awaits a trial in Guantánamo Bay, Cuba.
Crenshaw said students should understand that 9/11 was not simply "a coordinated terrorist attack on the United States," as the FCPS script describes it, but a strategic act of war.
"What we saw in 9/11 was a religious extremist group, al Qaeda, who did not tolerate what the United States was doing around the world and decided to react violently," Crenshaw said.

Teachers should be prepared to discuss the Islamist extremism behind the attack without collectively blaming all Muslims, he said, noting that he agreed it is important to make sure Muslim students aren't shamed.

"They are a branch of Islam, but they certainly do not espouse any of the values that we know of Islam worldwide," said Crenshaw. "And, therefore, they really shouldn't be considered to be part of that mainstream religion."
Fairfax County Public Schools provides teachers guidance on teaching about the 9/11 attacks with an emphasis on challenging "anti-Muslim racism." (Fairfax County Public Schools)

The guide includes a section titled "Responding to Racism, Hate, and Bias against Muslims and Middle Eastern People," telling teachers that Muslim students experience "the worst anti-Muslim racism" during Sept. 11 lessons.

FCPS instructs teachers the anniversary "may intensify anti-Muslim and anti-Middle Eastern rhetoric." They are told that speaking out against anti-Muslim bias is part of their "sacred role as teachers."
The guide also says that if educators hear students or colleagues using "Islamophobic rhetoric," "it is up to you to disrupt."
Under a list of "Do" and "Don’t" instructions, FCPS explicitly tells teachers don't "associate the 9/11 attacks with Islam or Muslims" and don't "center the extremists or the acts of the extremists."
The guide says the commemoration should focus on "those whose lives were lost and those who sacrificed to help others – not those who attacked the United States."
Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the accused mastermind of the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks, has been held at Guantánamo Bay since 2003. (AP)

The guide says teachers should not focus a commemorative lesson on "an examination of Islam." It argues that doing so could send the "harmful message" that "Islam, or all Muslims, are responsible for these terrorist attacks."

Crenshaw said not explaining the ideology of the hijackers and how al Qaeda interpreted Islam to justify the attacks means the guide fails to deliver "a sense of urgency or the evilness of what actually happened."

title: Trump administration proposes ending 60-day grace period after job loss for H-1B, other visa holders
summary: USCIS and DHS propose eliminating the 60-day grace period for H-1B visa holders who lose their jobs, requiring foreign workers to leave immediately.
story: A federal judge in Boston ruled against the Trump administration's $100,000 fee for H-1B visas, deeming it an unauthorized tax. The fee, which was significantly increased from a typical $2,000 to $5,000, aimed to prioritize U.S. citizens in the workforce. The administration is appealing the decision.

U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) are preparing to propose a rule that would eliminate an existing grace period for visa holders who can't find a job, according to an unpublished document posted to the Federal Register.

Under current immigration laws, holders of certain visas, particularly H-1B visas, which are non-immigration visas that allow employers to sponsor skilled workers with Bachelor's degrees or higher, get a 60-day grace period to find a new job if they lose the employment tied to their visa.
The new rule proposal would eliminate that grace period, according to the document.
FEDERAL JUDGE STRIKES DOWN TRUMP’S $100K H-1B VISA FEE, RULING IT AN UNCONSTITUTIONAL TAX

"This proposal restores a direct relationship between an alien’s nonimmigrant status and the specific employment or activity that formed the basis of his or her admission or grant of status in the United States and reduces administrative burden," the document reads.

People wait inside a U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services office. The Trump administration is preparing to propose a new rule rescinding the 60-day grace period allotted to non-immigrant visa holders with visas tied to employment if they no longer work at the place of employment tied to their visa. (John Moore/Getty Images)
A noncitizen would have to immediately leave the U.S. if no longer working for an employer linked to a visa status if the rule were to be implemented.
US STATE DEPARTMENT HAS YANKED MORE THAN 175K VISAS UNDER TRUMP ADMINISTRATION SO FAR

"DHS believes that restoring the expectation that aliens depart the United States upon cessation of the employment or activity upon which the alien’s status was based, would better promote program integrity and be more consistent with statutory purpose," the rule proposal reads.

The agency also claimed that eliminating the grace period would greatly reduce administrative burden "as the process of determining when the up to 60-day grace period may apply, reviewing the information submitted, and determining whether to shorten or eliminate the grace period may be time consuming and complex for the agency and confusing or unpredictable for the petitioner, alien and the alien’s dependents."
AMERICA’S BROKEN LEGAL IMMIGRATION SYSTEM IS REPLACING US WORKERS BY DESIGN

Before 2017, the document states, there was no 60-day grace period. But in 2016, DHS established the grace period in a rule that came into effec Jan. 17, 2017, three days before President Donald Trump first took office.

President Donald Trump signed two executive orders Sept. 19, 2025, establishing the Trump Gold Card and introducing a $100,000 fee for H-1B visas. The Trump Gold Card is a visa program that allows foreign nationals permanent residency and a pathway to U.S. citizenship for a $1 million investment in the United States. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
DHS also wrote that the rule's elimination would favor U.S. workers because employers who previously filled jobs with foreign workers would have less foreign-born labor to choose from.

"DHS assumes that almost all these entities would offer the same jobs to equally qualified U.S. workers, go through the I-129 petition process to sponsor nonimmigrant workers, or reassign the work to other current employees. DHS acknowledges that some of these petitioners may incur a temporary loss of productivity due to labor turnover," the rule proposal reads.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin speaks during a news conference at the Eisenhower Executive Office Building July 17, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Jim Lo Scalzo/EPA/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The unpublished rule is scheduled to publish Friday, Sept. 11, 2026, according to the Federal Register. It will then be subject to a two-month period of public comment before becoming law.
Fox News Digital contacted DHS and the White House for further comment.

title: Outgoing Rep Chip Roy says the GOP has already 'delivered significantly,' but must 'finish the job'
summary: Outgoing House Republican Chip Roy of Texas said that while Republicans have "delivered significantly," they still must "finish the job."
story: During an interview with Fox News Digital on Sept. 9, 2026, outgoing Rep. Chip Roy of Texas gave his analysis of the GOP ahead of the midterm elections.

Rep. Chip Roy, R-Texas — who lost the Lone Star State GOP attorney general primary runoff in May and will depart the U.S. House of Representatives when his current term expires — said Republicans have "delivered significantly" but "need to finish the job."

"Well, we've done so much that frankly, it kinda gets lost in a lot of the noise," Roy told Fox News Digital during an interview on Wednesday, pointing to issues such as tax provisions in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act signed by President Donald Trump last year.
The Texan pointed to the nation's border as the "biggest example" of Republicans' achievements, saying that "we've literally shut down the flow across the border" through enforcing the law.

He also pointed to the passage of the "Laken Riley Act," a measure named after the 22-year-old woman murdered in 2024 by Jose Ibarra, a man who, according to a 2024 statement by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), had previously been "arrested by U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP)" after illegally entering the U.S., but was "paroled and released for further processing."
Roy said Republicans "need to unite with a singular vision about where we wanna take the country if we wanna be... rewarded in November... and then frankly looking ahead to 2028."
TEXAS MAGA BATTLE ENDS WITH MIDDLETON VICTORY AS CHIP ROY FALLS SHORT IN AG RACE
Rep. Chip Roy, R-Texas, talks with reporters outside the U.S. Capitol after the last votes of the week on July 16, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
"Have we done everything we should do? No," Roy said, claiming that "Congress has fallen short" regarding some of what they "should do."
But he still believes the GOP could potentially retain their majorities in both congressional chambers during the midterms.
"I think right now Republicans are staring at barely holding onto the Senate and slightly losing the House, but I still think we can win the House," he said.

The House is now only scheduled to work for several days next week before a lengthy break until after the Nov. 3 elections. Roy indicated that Republicans should get back to work after the midterms "to do our part to finish the job."

"Obviously I'm not campaigning. So I'm thinking a lot about what we could do with another reconciliation package or what we might be able to do in the lame duck or in January, when I'm not in office," he noted.
FENTANYL DEATHS COULD NOW COST DRUG DEALERS THEIR LIVES UNDER NEW GOP PROPOSAL

In a Sunday post on X, Roy wrote, "Government does not fund anything. It takes money from people under force of law and distributes it to other people very inefficiently and usually tyrannically. Child care is unaffordable because government (& corporate cronyism) has made life unaffordable. Stay out."

The New York Times reported last week that the Trump administration is moving to enable some married people with a stay-at-home parent situation to receive a childcare subsidy from a federal program that was meant to help parents who work.

The proposal "creates the option for a new category of care, parent-based child care, that will allow one married parent to receive C.C.D.F. [Child Care and Development Fund] assistance to care for their own child, while a spouse works at least 35 hours per week," the outlet reported, citing a draft document.

Roy said during the interview on Wednesday, "I just don't believe that it's good for the human soul to have the government coming in with a grant and making you dependent on government. I just don't philosophically think that that's freedom. I think freedom, non-dependence, independence is what makes America great."

A White House official said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital on Thursday that the Trump administration "has not announced any such proposal. Until and unless it does, any discussion about potential policies is baseless speculation."
CHIP ROY FIELDS PROPOSAL TO BLOCK PAY AND POWER FOR LONGTIME LAWMAKERS
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

As for whether he has any interest in running for office again, Roy said the matter is "up to God" and to Texans, adding that he has "a calling for service" and his current focus is on attempting to "solve the big problems for" Americans.
Alex Nitzberg is a writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Republican sounds alarm on rising Dem star: 'This guy’s going to be a problem'
summary: Mike Collins claims Jon Ossoff is using the Georgia Senate race as a Democratic Party springboard for a 2028 presidential run as a DSA candidate.
story: Rep. Mike Collins, R-Ga., told Fox News Digital that he believed Sen. Jon Ossoff’s bid for re-election in Georgia was the first step on his way to a 2028 presidential bid, and that he was the only one who could stop the Democratic star’s rise.

DALLAS — There’s a rising star in the Democratic Party that is generating buzz for a possible presidential run, but one Republican argues he’s the only thing standing in the way of a future "DSA candidate" in 2028.

Rep. Mike Collins, R-Ga., is running to unseat Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., in one of the most closely watched contests of this midterm election cycle. Ossoff has sought to nationalize their battle, focusing more on President Donald Trump and leaning into viral clips on social media to sell his message.

But Collins told Fox News Digital during the GOP’s midterm convention that Ossoff’s intentions extended beyond a second term representing the Peach State. Instead, Collins charged that Ossoff is eyeing the White House and using this cycle as a springboard to get there.
TRUMP-BACKED CANDIDATE SURVIVES GRUELING RUNOFF, ADVANCES TO HIGH-STAKES SENATE RACE
Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., speaks to members of the media during the opening of the Democratic Party of Georgia's South DeKalb Field Office on May 23, 2026. (Elijah Nouvelage/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"This guy is nothing but a trust fund kid who's never had a real job in his life," Collins said. "And at the end of the day, and I think the whole puzzle has been put together now, you can put the pieces of this thing so easy."

"He caters to that far-left base, and at the end of the day, we've got to stop him in Georgia," he continued. "If we don't stop him in Georgia, this guy's going to be a problem for the entire country in 2028."

Those puzzle pieces were scattered throughout his voting record, which Collins said aligned over 90% of the time with Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., through his support of progressives, like former Maine Senate Democratic nominee Graham Platner and Michigan Senate Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, and because the bulk of his campaign donations are from out-of-state.
'JESUS WAS A RADICAL': PROGRESSIVES INVOKE CHRIST TO SELL LEFT-WING AGENDA ON CAMPAIGN TRAIL
Collins contended that the final piece was when the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) opened their first permanent field office in Atlanta last month. The organization has not endorsed Ossoff.
"That just tells you, yes, Jon Ossoff is really running for president," Collins said. "He's going to be the DSA candidate. He uses Georgia as a platform to raise money."
Ossoff’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
OBAMA STRATEGIST TURNS ON RISING DEM STAR OVER VIRAL TRUMP ATTACK: 'GRATUITOUS AND UNNECESSARY'
Republican Senate candidate Rep. Mike Collins speaks to supporters at a primary night event on May 19, 2026, in Jackson, Georgia. (Jason Allen/Getty Images)

He has previously thrown cold water on the notion that he was chasing the White House and told MSNOW last month, "I have zero interest in running for president in 2028, and, frankly, zero interest in the 2028 fantasy football right now."

The first-term senator is considered one of the most vulnerable incumbents on the Democrats’ Senate map this cycle, running in a state that Trump won in 2024 over former Vice President Kamala Harris by nearly three points.

Still, he has gained national attention over the summer for his speeches on the campaign trail, particularly when he needled Trump in a viral social media clip bringing into question his relationship with his executive assistant, Natalie Harp.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"He doesn't want to do the job," Ossoff said. "He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the Emir of Qatar."

That remark stoked a news cycle and earned him accolades from the likes of Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., who noted that Ossoff was one of the top communicators on the trail when it came to targeting Trump.
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Zohran Mamdani urged to skip New York City's 9/11 memorial: 'Vile antisemite'
summary: Rep. Mike Lawler demands Zohran Mamdani skip the 9/11 memorial, citing the NYC mayor's ties to terror sympathizers and antisemitic rhetoric.
story: Reps. Mike Lawler and August Pfluger spoke with Fox News Digital on the sidelines of the Republican midterm convention in Dallas.
DALLAS – A House Republican representing the New York City suburbs is calling on Mayor Zohran Mamdani to skip the Sept. 11 memorial in downtown Manhattan.

"From my vantage point, I don't think he should be there, and I think most New Yorkers agree that he should not be there," Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., told Fox News and Fox News Digital. "Certainly, the 9/11 families and the first responders believe he should not be there."

Political rancor is threatening to cast a long shadow over this year's Sept. 11 remembrance events, marking 25 years since the tragedy that rocked the United States. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's past rhetoric and links to terror sympathizers are spurring intense backlash ahead of the city's events memorializing the World Trade Center attacks, with Republicans and people whose lives were changed by the attacks demanding he not show his face.
MAMDANI FACES GROWING 9/11 BACKLASH AS OLD POST RESURFACES AHEAD OF GROUND ZERO CEREMONY: 'IS THIS REAL?'
Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks to the media regarding the attempted bombing at a right-wing protest in front of Gracie Mansion on March 8, 2026, in New York City. (Ryan Murphy/Getty Images)

"I think Mayor Mamdani has proven himself to be a vile antisemite. I think he has associated with people who believe America deserved 9/11, and it's not just Hasan Piker. If you go look at many of the people that support his administration, they agree with that rhetoric. They agree with that philosophy," Lawler said.
An online petition led by family members of people killed on Sept. 11 — signed by over 100,000 people — has called on Mamdani to skip the memorial.
9/11 FAMILIES PUSH TO BAN MAMDANI FROM 25TH ANNIVERSARY REMEMBRANCE OVER 'HOSTILE' RECORD

"Mr. Mamdani has praised Brooklyn Imam Siraj Wahhaj, who has been linked to radical Islam, was named as an alleged co-conspirator in the 1993 World Trade Center bombing, and served as a character witness for the 'Blind Sheikh,' who was convicted in 1995 of plotting terror attacks against the United States," the petition said. "Mr. Mamdani has endorsed candidates such as Aber Kawas, who described 9/11 as an attack 'a couple of people did in the context of U.S. capitalism, racism, white supremacy, and Islamophobia,' and who also expressed sympathy for Ahmed Ferhani, who pleaded guilty to plotting to blow up a Manhattan synagogue."

Mamdani and other socialist candidates' association with far-left activist Hasan Piker has also seen intense scrutiny over Piker's past comments that the United States "deserved" the attacks, remarks that he promptly walked back at the time but continue to haunt him and his political circle. Mamdani himself has also condemned the comment.
A firefighter walks through the rubble of the World Trade Center as an American flag hangs from a traffic light post on Sept. 11, 2001, in New York. (Doug Kanter/AFP via Getty Images)

Republican Study Committee Chairman August Pfluger, R-Texas, told Fox News Digital that Mamdani should not attend Sept. 11 memorial events "until he can... actually call out terror groups around the world for what they want to do to this country, and that includes Hamas."
Hamas was not responsible for the Sept. 11 attacks, for which al Qaeda took credit, but Hamas has recently been front-and-center for perpetuating the Oct. 7, 2023, terror attack in Israel.

"These people are really a cancer to the freedoms that we fought for, and they do not represent the American values that our founders set up and that we have had for 250 years," Pfluger said of Mamdani and his allies.
MAMDANI DROPS MASSIVE 9/11 RECORDS TROVE AS OLD CLAIMS ABOUT GROUND ZERO COME UNDER FIRE

Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., speaks with local law enforcement about the rise of antisemitism in New York City during a campaign endorsement event at Haverstraw Elks Lodge No. 877 in Haverstraw, New York. (Kyle Mazza/CNP)
Both he and Lawler spoke with Fox News Digital on the sidelines of the 2026 GOP midterm convention in Dallas.

Mamdani's office recently launched an online portal allowing city residents to access roughly 170,000 pages of local government records on Sept. 11, which appear to show city officials misled the public about air quality following the attacks.

Fox News Digital reached out to the New York City mayor's office for comment.
Elizabeth Elkind is a politics reporter for Fox News Digital leading coverage of the House of Representatives. Previous digital bylines seen at Daily Mail and CBS News.

title: For 'horrible moment,' Bush White House thought US military shot down Flight 93
summary: Condoleezza Rice recalled the tense moment she and George W. Bush believed Flight 93 had been shot down while coordinating responses in a bunker.
story: Former President George W. Bush recounted the "horrible moment" on 9/11 where the White House thought the U.S. military had shot down Flight 93.
Former President George W. Bush discussed his memories of 9/11 with his former secretary of state, Condoleezza Rice, ahead of the 25th anniversary of the attacks this week.

Bush and Rice said they both remember sitting in a bunker in the hours after the attacks, coordinating the U.S. domestic response. Rice recounted how they were working to ground civilian flights across the country and said at one point they thought the U.S. military had shot down United Airlines Flight 93.

"I do want to say one thing to Gen. [Daniel] Caine, because something in what you said, our paths crossed in a strange way. So you mentioned that you heard that as the president, you have to understand the hard decisions that this man had to make, just like that. And one of them was what would happen if a plane was not properly identifying itself, because every plane had become a missile," Rice said.
FLIGHT 93 HERO'S DAD WARNS 'ENEMIES FROM WITHIN' AIM TO DESTROY AMERICA AT THE BALLOT BOX
President George W. Bush discusses creating the Department of Homeland Security following 9/11. (Getty Images)

"And so we were trying to land, I remember Norm Mineta, the transportation secretary, trying to land planes on a legal pad, yellow pad, legal pad. But you'd given the order through the vice president that should a plane not squawk properly, it should be shot down. Gen. Caine, we thought initially, standing in that bunker, that Flight 93 had been shot down," she continued.
9/11 MUSEUM UNVEILS EXHIBITION FOR GENERATION TOO YOUNG TO REMEMBER THE ATTACKS: 'CALLED EVERYBODY TO LEAD'
"Yeah, I thought it was the same thing," Bush said.
Former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice joins "Special Report" for an interview on June 26, 2025. (Fox News/Special Report)

"And there was this horrible moment where the vice president kept trying to get confirmation as to what had happened. And for about 10 minutes we thought we'd shot down a civilian aircraft. And that always, to me, represented just how hard the decisions were that you had to take under a lot of pressure," Rice said.
The event, called, "A Legacy of Service: America at the 25th Anniversary of 9/11," saw Bush host many members of his 2001 administration in Texas.

President George W. Bush, first lady Laura Bush, Vice President Dick Cheney and his wife Lynne Cheney participate in a moment of silence on the south lawn of the White House in Washington, D.C., Sept. 11, 2005, to honor the fourth anniversary of the terrorist attacks. (Brooks Kraft LLC/Corbis via Getty Images)

As part of the 25th anniversary commemoration, Bush painted 16 works of art that "reflect on the courage, sacrifice, and resilience that emerged from one of the most defining moments in American history," that will be displayed at Freedom Hall at the Bush Museum through September.
Fox News' Peter D'Abrosca contributed to this report.
Anders Hagstrom is a reporter with Fox News Digital covering national politics and major breaking news events.

title: 9/11 hero’s memory preserved through massive effort to ‘do good’ for vets, first responders: ‘His legacy’
summary: Tunnel to Towers' 343 Homes Initiative honors Stephen Siller and the 9/11 firefighters with mortgage-free homes for fallen first responders' families.
story: Tunnel to Towers Foundation CEO Frank Siller shares the inspiration behind his new memoir, 'Let Us Do Good.' Siller reflects on the sacrifice of his FDNY firefighter brother, Stephen Siller, and how their parents' lessons of service guided their family's mission.

On one of the darkest days in America’s history, New York City firefighter Stephen Siller strapped on his gear and ran through the Brooklyn Battery Tunnel to the collapsing Twin Towers, ultimately giving his life to save those caught in the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks. Two and a half decades later, Tunnel to Towers, founded by Siller’s family, has continued his legacy through its commitment to "do good" for veterans and first responders and their families across the country.

Since its founding, inspired by Siller and his favorite quote, "While we have time, let us do good," Tunnel to Towers has provided more than 1,700 mortgage-free homes to the families of fallen service members and first responders, as well as to disabled veterans and first responders. The organization has also delivered housing assistance and support services to more than 20,000 homeless veterans and holds hundreds of events nationwide to honor America’s heroes and preserve the memory of those who lost their lives for future generations.

Tunnel to Towers CEO Frank Siller, the brother of the 34-year-old firefighter who gave his life on Sept. 11, previously warned in 2020 that America was "very close to forgetting the impact 9/11 had on our nation." Now, with anti-American sentiment on the rise and some online commentators belittling the Sept. 11 attacks or even justifying them, many worry the legacy of those who lost their lives, including the 343 members of the New York City Fire Department who made the ultimate sacrifice, will be forgotten.
Siller, however, has vowed that "Tunnel to Towers will never let that happen."
9/11 IS BECOMING HISTORY. MY GENERATION MUST MAKE SURE AMERICA NEVER FORGETS
The Tunnel to Towers Foundation was started in honor of  FDNY firefighter Stephen Siller, who died responding to the attacks. (Tunnel to Towers Foundation)

The Tunnel to Towers 9/11 Institute has helped to educate students from kindergarten through 12th grade on the "extraordinary heroism and goodness of everyday people" on Sept. 11, "while demonstrating the strength and resilience of America’s spirit." Its mobile 9/11 exhibit has traveled to nearly all 50 states as well as Canada.

This year, Tunnel to Towers launched its "Steel Across America" display, in which a 16,000-pound steel beam pulled from the wreckage of the World Trade Center traveled more than 10,500 miles to 35 stops across 21 states and the District of Columbia, culminating in New York City.
NEW 9/11 MUSEUM EXHIBIT AIMS TO CONNECT YOUNGER AMERICANS TO THE ATTACKS THROUGH POWERFUL ARTIFACTS

Frank Siller, CEO of the Tunnel to Towers Foundation, stands near a piece of World Trade Center steel that will be featured during the foundation's effort to honor and remember the victims of the 9/11 attacks as the 25th anniversary approaches. (Courtesy: Tunnel to Towers Foundation)

To mark the 25th anniversary, Tunnel to Towers also launched its 343 Homes Initiative this year to honor the 343 New York firefighters who died on Sept. 11. According to the group, this initiative will deliver 343 mortgage-free homes to the families of fallen service members and fallen first responders as well as to catastrophically injured service members across the country.

This initiative builds on Tunnel to Towers' "In the Line of Duty Programs," which have provided more than 1,700 mortgage-free homes to the families of fallen service members and first responders, as well as to catastrophically injured veterans and first responders. More than 220 of those homes have been custom "Smart Homes," modified to be fully accessible to catastrophically injured veterans and first responders.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

A firefighter walks through the rubble of the twin towers of the World Trade Center as an American flag hangs from a traffic light post on September 11, 2001, in New York. (DOUG KANTER/AFP via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

In a recent Fox News opinion piece, Siller put it simply: "Stephen’s life and heroic death serve as a reminder to us all to live life to the fullest and to spend our time here on earth doing good—this is his legacy."
Peter Pinedo is a politics writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Supreme Court again blocks Missouri from using Trump-backed congressional maps
summary: The Supreme Court blocked Missouri's Republican-backed congressional map for a second time as a contempt hearing looms for Denny Hoskins this week.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
The Supreme Court turned back another effort to use Missouri congressional maps supported by President Donald Trump.
"The application for stay presented to Justice [Brett] Kavanaugh and by him referred to the Court is granted," Thursday's ruling read.
The court's brief order was unsigned and gave no explanation, as is common when the justices handle emergency matters. No justice publicly dissented from the decision.
While the Missouri Supreme Court’s ruling paved the way for use of the old maps, the state’s Aug. 4 primary was already held under the new maps.
MISSOURI AG FILES PETITION ASKING SUPREME COURT TO REVIVE TRUMP-BACKED REDISTRICTING MAP
Facade of the Supreme Court. (Valerie Plesch/picture alliance via Getty Images)

"After repeated legal victories defending Missouri’s fair and lawful map, this 11th-hour ruling pulls the rug out from under voters who already cast their primary ballots," RNC Election Integrity Communications Director Ally Triolo wrote in a statement. "Changing the rules mid-election is reckless and wrong."

The court’s decision came after U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark ordered Missouri to use the new map, conflicting with a unanimous ruling by the Missouri Supreme Court that said the districts had not legally taken effect and that the state’s older map should be used unless voters approve the changes.
Following the U.S. Supreme Court's stay, Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins said his office is directing local election authorities to use the 2022 congressional map.
MISSOURI HIGH COURT BLOCKS GOP-BACKED CONGRESSIONAL MAPS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS; TRUMP BLASTS 'RIDICULOUS' RULING

"Following the United States Supreme Court's stay, the only governing court order in effect is from the Missouri Supreme Court. In accordance with that order, my Office is directing local election authorities to use the 2022 congressional map," Hoskins said in a statement.
Republican state officials have argued it would violate voters' federal rights to switch districts before the general election.

The Missouri Supreme Court also ordered Republican Secretary of State Denny Hoskins to appear at a contempt hearing Thursday, after he instructed local election officials to use the new districts. A federal judge declined to halt that hearing before the Supreme Court issued its order.

The redrawn map was approved by Missouri Republicans in 2025. It dismantles the Kansas City-based 5th Congressional District held by Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, D-Mo., by shifting portions of the seat into neighboring districts and extending the remainder into heavily Republican areas.
The way the map was designed gave Republicans a strong chance of winning seven of Missouri’s eight House seats, compared with the current six-to-two Republican advantage.

Opponents of the map, including the group People Not Politicians, submitted hundreds of thousands of petition signatures seeking a statewide referendum. The Missouri Supreme Court ordered that referendum to appear on the November ballot, meaning voters will decide whether the redrawn map can be used in future elections.

The Missouri Supreme Court has ordered Republican Secretary of State Denny Hoskins to appear at a contempt hearing Thursday, after he instructed local election officials to use the new districts. A federal judge declined to halt that hearing before the Supreme Court issued its order. (Nick Wagner/The Kansas City Star/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Republicans currently hold a 219-214 majority in the House, including one independent who caucuses with the GOP.
The Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report.

title: Mamdani, touting RI socialist’s victory, answers question of ‘What is the Democratic Party?’
summary: David Morales' rent control platform powered his upset of Providence's incumbent mayor, and Zohran Mamdani says it signals a national shift.
story: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani says Rhode Island State Rep. David Morales’ Providence mayoral primary victory as evidence voters support rent stabilization policies.

Democratic socialist David Morales’ victory in Rhode Island's mayoral primary Wednesday night got the attention of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who says it is evidence of where the party as a whole is headed as November's midterm elections draw near.

"I think it comes back to what I’ve said before, which is what is the Democratic Party, if not its voters?" Mamdani asked during a Thursday morning news conference on the first day of school in his city.

"We’re seeing that the voters across this country are eager for not only a change, but also for a vision of something that we are fighting for," Mamdani added. "And, you know, I've spoken a lot about childcare this morning. I've often couched it as the second driver of the cost of living crisis. The first driver is housing."
MAMDANI CLAIMS DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS CAN WIN ‘ANYWHERE’ AS DEMOCRATS FEUD OVER PARTY’S FUTURE
Mayor Zohran Mamdani has promised to enact a four-year rent freeze on rent-stabilized units in New York City. (Yuki Iwamura-Pool/Getty Images)

Mamdani was hailing a new free education program for 2,000 needy families, as Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul unveiled a pledge for $425 million more in next year’s state budget to expand early childhood programs, including services for families with disabilities.

At the end of Thursday's news conference, Mamdani responded to a question about Morales, a 27-year-old state representative and Democratic socialist who defeated one-term Providence Mayor Brett Smiley, 47, in the Democratic primary.

Republicans hold no seats on the Providence City Council, and Democrats make up a majority of registered voters in the city. Former Vice President Kamala Harris beat President Donald Trump in the city by 51 points in 2024.
Mamdani hailed Morales’ campaign for rent stabilization and affordability in the deep-blue city.
MAMDANI RIPPED OVER RECORD-HIGH NYC RENTS WITH CRITICS POINTING TO POLICY THEY SAY IS FUELING CRISIS

title: What your HOA may be putting online about you
summary: Homeowners association meeting minutes and membership lists can expose names, addresses and emails that scammers use to craft convincing phishing scams.
story: California homeowners Amy and Chris Cooke discuss their homeowners association allegedly threatening them with fines over displaying a U.S. flag on ‘Fox News @ Night.’
A scammer doesn't need to hack your homeowners association. They may only need to look at information your community already makes available.

Meeting minutes, membership records and other association documents can contain details about the people who live in a community. Depending on the HOA and state law, some records may be available to association members while others could appear on an association website or another online system.

You probably didn't put the information there yourself. You may have no idea how much someone can learn about you. Yet a name tied to an address or community can give a scammer useful details for making a call or message sound legitimate.
What your HOA puts online could reveal more about you than you realize. Here's what to look for and what you can do about it.
THE ONE THING SCAMMERS CHECK BEFORE TARGETING YOU ONLINE
Homeowners associations may publish records that expose names, addresses and contact details scammers can use to make fraud attempts more convincing. (Jordan Vonderhaar/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. How HOA records can expose your personal information
HOA records can contain details about homeowners, association business and community disputes. What members can access and what an association can publish depends heavily on state law.

HOA meeting minutes and other association records can reveal more than homeowners expect. How much information appears depends on the association and state law. Some states give HOA members broad rights to inspect association records. Sensitive disciplinary, collection and payment issues can receive additional privacy protections.

California provides a useful example. State law treats board meeting minutes as association records available for member inspection but excludes minutes and other information from executive sessions. Those closed sessions can cover matters such as member discipline, certain payment issues and other sensitive association business.

California law also allows an association to withhold or redact information when releasing it could reasonably lead to identity theft or fraud or compromise a member's privacy. The privacy concern grows when an association includes unnecessary personal details in records or makes information available more broadly than required.

HOA membership lists can contain information that scammers and data brokers would find useful. In California, state law defines the membership list as including a homeowner's name, property address, mailing address and email address as collected by the association. Members can request access to association records under state law.

Homeowners also have an important privacy option. California law allows members to opt out of sharing their name, property address, mailing address and email address through the membership list by notifying the association in writing. The law also restricts association records from being sold, used for commercial purposes or used for purposes unrelated to a member's interests as a member.

Rules differ from state to state, so check the laws where you live and ask your HOA exactly what information it collects, who can access it and whether you can opt out. The concern extends beyond the HOA itself. Once personal information appears publicly online, it can be indexed or copied and combined with information already collected from public records and other sources. Data brokers and people-search sites build profiles using many of those sources.
FIVE DATA BROKER OPT-OUT MYTHS THAT LEAVE RETIREES EXPOSED
Experts warn homeowners to review what their HOA publishes online and understand available privacy protections. (PC Photography / Getty Images)
How HOA information can make scams more convincing

Personal information gives scammers context they can use to make a fraudulent message feel legitimate. The Justice Department has already prosecuted companies that supplied consumer information to fraud operations.

Epsilon Data Management, one of the largest marketing companies in the country, agreed to pay $150 million after federal prosecutors said it sold consumer data to operators running fraudulent mass-mailing schemes involving fake sweepstakes and astrology solicitations. The government said many victims were elderly and vulnerable. A related company, Macromark, pleaded guilty after lists it provided to fraudulent clients resulted in at least $9.5 million in victim losses.

Those cases involved marketing databases rather than HOA records. Still, they demonstrate why personal details can become valuable to criminals. Names and addresses helped fraudsters identify and target potential victims.

HOA information can give scammers another source of context. A scammer who learns your name, street address and community can weave those details into a phone call, text or email. A message claiming to involve an assessment or another issue connected to your property can sound far more believable when the person contacting you already knows where you live.

Older adults remain especially attractive targets for financial scammers. The FBI says criminals may target older Americans because many have accumulated significant savings. Older victims can also be more likely to engage with unsolicited phone calls, texts or emails.

In 2025, Americans over 60 reported more than $7.7 billion in internet-enabled fraud losses. The FBI received more than 201,000 complaints from people in that age group, which reported the highest total losses of any age group.

Those numbers don't mean everyone living in a retirement or 55+ community will encounter fraud. They do show why reducing unnecessary personal information online deserves attention. The fewer details scammers can easily connect to you, the harder you make their job.
How to reduce your HOA privacy exposure
You may have more control over your HOA information than you realize, but your options depend on where you live and how your association handles its records.

Start by seeing what someone outside your community can find. Search your HOA's name along with terms such as "minutes," "directory," "membership list" or your own name. Check whether documents appear directly in search results without requiring a resident login. Pay particular attention to documents that connect your name with your address or other personal information.

Contact your board or management company and ask which records anyone on the internet can access. Find out which documents require a resident login and whether search engines can index anything posted on the association's website. If a document contains personal information that has no reason to appear publicly, ask whether the association can remove it, redact the information or restrict access.

Privacy rights vary by state, so find out what options apply where you live. California homeowners, for example, can opt out of sharing certain information through the HOA membership list. Other states may have different rules covering association directories and member records. Ask your HOA or management company how its opt-out process works and whether you can limit the contact information available to other members.
WHY CAREFUL PEOPLE STILL END UP ON DATA BROKER SITES
Homeowners can reduce privacy risks by reviewing HOA policies, opting out where allowed and removing data from broker sites. (David Ryder/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Even if your HOA removes information from a public page, your name, address and other details may already appear elsewhere online. People-search sites and data brokers gather personal information from public records, websites and other sources, then combine those details into profiles.

Start by searching for your name, phone number, email address and home address on major people-search sites. If you find a profile, look for the site's opt-out or removal process and submit a request to have your information deleted.

You can also use a data removal service to automate some of this work. These services send removal requests to data brokers on your behalf and may continue monitoring for information that reappears later.
Whichever route you choose, check back periodically. Personal information can resurface as data brokers refresh their databases or pull from new sources.

Kurt's key takeaways

I doubt most HOA boards are thinking about scammers when they post meeting minutes or maintain a community directory. They are focused on running the neighborhood. The problem comes when information collected for one purpose becomes useful to someone with very different intentions. That is why I would spend a few minutes searching your HOA's name along with your own. See what a stranger can learn about you without logging in or proving they live in your community. You may be surprised by how quickly a name, home address and neighborhood can be connected. I would also ask your HOA what stays behind a resident login, what appears on the open web and what you can opt out of sharing. Laws vary by state, but there is no reason to make a scammer's research easier than it already is. And remember, removing something from an HOA website may only solve part of the problem. Once personal information spreads to people-search sites and data brokers, cutting down those profiles can help put some distance between you and anyone trying to build a convincing story around your life.

title: Floating solar panels could save cities millions. Is your town next?
summary: Lima, Ohio, has installed 3,120 floating solar panels on its Twin Lakes Reservoir, projecting nearly $10 million in electricity cost savings.
story: Fox News host Will Cain discusses Cowboy Space Corporation’s plans to launch solar-powered data centers into orbit by 2028 as demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure grows. Cain explains how the technology could use solar energy to power AI chips in space.

What if your town could build a solar farm without giving up acres of valuable land? Lima, Ohio, is trying something different. The city has completed a 2-megawatt solar array that floats on the Twin Lakes Reservoir, its primary drinking water source.

More than 3,000 solar panels now sit on the water and feed electricity to the nearby water treatment plant. The city projects the system will save nearly $10 million in electricity costs over its lifetime. That kind of savings could get the attention of cities far beyond Ohio.
So, could floating solar panels eventually show up on a reservoir near you? Here's how the technology works, why cities are interested and what it could mean for your community.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com
WHO PAYS FOR US POWER BOOM? BLUE, RED STATES OFFER STARKLY DIFFERENT WAYS TO LOWER UTILITY BILLS AMID AI SURGE
An Ohio city is using floating solar panels on its drinking water reservoir to power its water treatment plant and cut millions in projected energy costs. (D3Energy)
Ohio puts 3,120 solar panels on a drinking water reservoir

Lima officially celebrated the completion of its Twin Lakes Floating Solar Project on Aug. 12. The final system includes 3,120 solar panels spread across about 3.6 acres of water, according to developer D3Energy. The 2-megawatt array sits on Lima's primary drinking water reservoir. That reservoir serves roughly 35,000 residents.

Next door, the city's water treatment plant processes about 14 million gallons of water each day. It also consumes more electricity than any other city facility. That makes the plant an obvious place to look for energy savings. Lima projects the floating solar system will save nearly $10 million in electricity costs over its lifetime. Earlier city estimates put first-year savings at roughly $200,000. For a city utility, that is serious money. Actual lifetime savings will depend on factors including future electricity prices and how the system performs over time.
How floating solar panels work
Instead of attaching panels to racks planted in the ground, engineers mount them on floating platforms. Anchors and mooring lines keep the array in position.

Lima uses Ciel & Terre's Hydrelio floating system. Its anchoring setup connects to the banks and reservoir bottom. The design also allows the array to move as water levels change. The project uses bifacial solar panels, which can capture light on both sides.

Electricity travels from the array to eight inverters onshore. From there, the electricity helps power the water treatment plant. The result looks a bit like a traditional solar farm that traded grass for water.
Why cities may want solar panels floating on water

Here is where the idea gets particularly interesting. Land costs money. It also competes with housing, businesses, agriculture and other development. Reservoirs already occupy space. Lima's floating array covers about four acres.

A land-based system producing the same amount of electricity would reportedly need at least 10 acres. That could make floating solar attractive to cities with limited open space. The panels can also sit near the facilities that need the electricity. In Lima, the water treatment plant sits right beside the reservoir. That reduces the need to find a distant solar site and then figure out how to move the electricity where the city needs it.

Researchers have also studied whether floating solar can help reduce evaporation by shading portions of the water surface. Of course, every reservoir comes with different conditions. Water depth, changing levels and recreational use can affect whether a project makes sense. Federal researchers also consider existing dam operations when evaluating potential sites.
LAWMAKERS TARGET ENERGY AFFORDABILITY THROUGH SWEEPING PERMITTING OVERHAUL IN NEW HOUSE BILL
Floating solar could help cities generate clean energy without using valuable land, but questions remain about long-term costs and water safety. (D3Energy)
What about putting solar panels on drinking water?

This was one of my first questions. These panels are floating on the same reservoir that provides drinking water to about 35,000 people. Lima's system uses Ciel & Terre Hydrelio floats made from high-density polyethylene, or HDPE.

Ciel & Terre says its floating system complies with the BS 6920:2000 standard for nonmetallic materials that come into contact with water intended for human consumption. Still, communities considering floating solar have more to evaluate than whether the structure can float safely.

The National Renewable Energy Laboratory has examined environmental and regulatory questions surrounding floating solar. Its research notes that projects can affect water bodies differently depending on the location. That means a system that works well on one reservoir may require a different design somewhere else.
The project cost millions before it could save millions

There is another number worth paying attention to. The Lima project cost about $5.3 million. Federal support played a substantial role in making the numbers work. The city received a $2.4 million Department of Energy grant. Combined with almost $900,000 in federal direct-pay tax credits, that support helped offset roughly half of the project's cost.

Those incentives covered a significant share of the upfront expense. That context is important when another city looks at Lima's projected $10 million in savings. A town considering floating solar would need to look at construction costs, financing and expected electricity production. Available incentives could change the calculation as well.

Lima began considering the project years before crews put panels on the water. City Council approved moving forward with the project in 2023. Construction began in 2025 before the system came online this August.
Could floating solar panels spread across America?

Lima may look unusual today, but floating solar has substantial room to grow. Ohio already has more than one project. D3Energy and ARP Solar completed a 1.5-megawatt floating array for Del-Co Water in Delaware, Ohio, in 2024. A 6-megawatt system in Monroeville is expected to come online before the end of 2026.

The bigger opportunity stretches far beyond Ohio. National Renewable Energy Laboratory researchers studied federally owned or regulated reservoirs across the U.S. They estimated those reservoirs have technical potential for 861 to 1,042 gigawatts of floating solar capacity.
That figure represents technical potential rather than a prediction that thousands of reservoirs will soon disappear under solar panels. Plenty of locations would never make sense.

Still, the scale helps explain why energy developers and local governments are taking a closer look at water. CyberGuy has covered this idea before on a much larger scale. India's Omkareshwar project showed how enormous floating solar installations can become. We have also seen developers rethink the shape of solar installations on land. One Texas company is building vertical solar towers designed to produce more power from a smaller footprint.
AMERICA’S BROKEN PERMITTING SYSTEM IS QUIETLY RAISING YOUR COST OF LIVING
Cities across the U.S. are exploring floating solar as a way to reduce utility costs while making use of existing reservoirs. (D3Energy)
Will floating solar panels lower your utility bill?

Here is the part I would keep an eye on. Lima expects to save nearly $10 million in electricity costs over the project's lifetime. But that does not mean residents will suddenly see a cheaper water bill. The city could use those savings in different ways. Lower energy costs could help cover other expenses, pay for infrastructure upgrades or ease pressure on future rate increases.

So, if a floating solar project comes to your town, there is one question worth asking: Will any of those savings eventually make their way back to you? That answer could determine how much this technology really helps the people paying the bills.
What this means to you

You probably do not spend much time thinking about how much electricity your local water plant consumes. Yet you ultimately help pay for that electricity through taxes, utility rates or both. Floating solar gives cities another way to attack that expense without buying a huge parcel of land.

It also raises questions you should ask before cheering on a project. How much will it cost? How much electricity will it realistically generate? What happens to the savings? You should also ask what testing and monitoring will protect the water supply. Those answers will tell you whether a floating solar project makes financial sense for your community.
Kurt's key takeaways

What I like about Lima's floating solar project is how practical the idea feels. The city already owns the reservoir, and its water treatment plant right next door uses a huge amount of electricity. So instead of finding another piece of land for solar panels, Lima put them on the water. Then there is the projected $10 million in savings. That certainly gets my attention. I want to see whether those savings hold up over time and, more importantly, whether residents eventually benefit from them. Lima also gives other cities something real to look at. We are seeing communities experiment with new ways to generate and store energy, from floating solar to massive battery projects. And who knows? The next solar project in your town may end up floating right on the water.

Would you be comfortable with thousands of solar panels floating on your town's drinking water reservoir if officials said the project could save millions, or would you need to see more long-term evidence first? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com.
