title: Amazon's Alexa for Shopping can now verify suspicious messages
summary: Amazon's Alexa for Shopping now lets customers verify suspicious emails, texts and phone calls against the company's own communication records.
story: Artificial intelligence is rapidly accelerating elder fraud schemes across the U.S., targeting older Americans who hold a significant share of household wealth. ScamSkeptic founder Matt Sanner joins 'America's Newsroom' to highlight how fraudsters utilize AI to mimic voices and create deepfakes. Sanner provides key strategies for families to identify these scams and protect their vulnerable loved ones.
We have seen plenty of scams borrow Amazon's name, and some of them look convincing enough to make almost anyone hesitate.

Earlier this summer, we showed you a fake Amazon email that claimed there was unusual activity on an account and pushed the recipient to "Sign In to Verify." The message even suggested a document might need to be uploaded. We have also warned about fake Amazon recruiting texts promising hundreds of dollars a day for easy remote work.
The stories change, but scammers keep coming back to Amazon because so many of us use it. A delivery warning or account alert can feel believable when you are already expecting a package.

Now Amazon is giving customers a new way to answer the question we keep asking when these messages arrive: Did Amazon actually send this? The company says about 360,000 customers contact Amazon customer service every year asking whether a message is real. Its latest answer is built into Alexa for Shopping.
AMAZON JOB SCAM TEXTS ARE SPREADING AGAIN WITH A NEW TWIST
Alexa for Shopping can now help U.S. customers check whether a suspicious text, email or call actually came from Amazon. (Amazon)
Here is how the new verification tool works, what it can tell you and why you should still keep your guard up when an Amazon message feels suspicious.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com
Amazon Alexa scam verification checks suspicious messages

Amazon says U.S. customers can now ask Alexa for Shopping whether an email, text, phone call or other message actually came from Amazon. Alexa for Shopping is Amazon's AI shopping assistant. It helps customers find products, compare items and manage shopping through natural conversation. Prime membership is not required to use Alexa for Shopping, but if you are considering joining, see our guide on how to get a cheap Amazon Prime membership at Cyberguy.com.

Now, you can also use Alexa for Shopping when something suspicious lands on your phone or computer. Instead of trying to judge a message by appearance alone, you can describe it to Alexa for Shopping.

You might ask: "Did Amazon send me a text about a delivery problem yesterday?" Or you could ask whether a Prime membership email came from Amazon. You can even provide details about a phone call from someone claiming to offer an Amazon refund. The verification tool then checks the information you provide against Amazon's own communication records.
How Alexa for Shopping checks an Amazon message

When you ask Alexa for Shopping about a suspicious communication, provide details about where it came from and when you received it. You can also tell the assistant what the message said. Amazon then compares those details with its records.
According to the company, its technology looks at information such as the sender and message content. It also considers timing and formatting.

That gives Amazon an advantage over tools that simply search for suspicious wording or potentially dangerous links. Amazon can compare the communication with messages generated through its own systems. The company says it only confirms a message as legitimate when the tool has complete confidence.
What Alexa tells you after checking a message

The answer depends on what Amazon finds. If Amazon can match the communication to its records, Alexa for Shopping tells you it came from Amazon. It can also provide details about the communication and account security advice.
If the message does not match Amazon's records, the tool tells you that the information provided does not appear to correspond with an official Amazon communication.
At that point, Amazon may advise you to check your orders directly in the app or contact Amazon through its official support channels. You should also avoid clicking links in the suspicious message.

There is another possibility. Alexa may tell you that it cannot verify the communication with certainty. If that happens, Amazon provides additional steps. You can submit more detailed information or use another Amazon verification option.
AMAZON RECALL TEXT SCAM COMES WITH RED FLAGS
Alexa for Shopping now offers Amazon customers another way to check suspicious communications without relying solely on appearances. (Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
You can also forward a suspicious Amazon email

Alexa for Shopping is only one of Amazon's verification options. Earlier this year, Amazon launched verify@amazon.com. Anyone worldwide can forward a suspicious message to that email address and receive a response about whether Amazon sent it. You do not need an Amazon account or the Amazon app to use the service.

Amazon also offers a communication verification form through its customer service pages. So, if Alexa for Shopping cannot give you a firm answer, you still have another way to check before taking action.
Amazon reports suspicious communications you submit

There is another interesting part of the new feature. When you ask Alexa for Shopping to verify a communication, Amazon says it automatically reports that submission to its customer protection and enforcement team.

Those reports can help Amazon identify developing scam campaigns and bad actors impersonating the company. That means the suspicious text sitting on your phone could potentially help Amazon spot a larger scam targeting other customers.
Why fake Amazon messages keep fooling people

Amazon scams work because they often start with something completely believable. You ordered something last week, so a delivery problem sounds possible. You have a Prime membership, so an account warning gets your attention. Then the scammer adds pressure.

A fake email may claim your account has been locked. Another message might say someone placed an expensive order using your account. That urgency can push you toward a link before you have time to think.

We saw exactly that pattern in the fake Amazon account email we investigated. The message used Amazon branding and warned that the account had been placed on hold. The safest response remains simple. Do not use the link in the message to investigate the warning. Open Amazon yourself and check your account.
FBI HELPS TAKE DOWN AI PHISHING RING
Amazon is expanding its anti-scam efforts with a new Alexa verification tool designed to help customers identify fake emails, texts and calls. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How to protect yourself from fake Amazon messages
Amazon's new verification feature gives you another way to check suspicious communications. However, scammers will keep changing their tactics, so these steps can help you stay safer.

Be cautious when a message pressures you to act immediately or threatens consequences if you do not respond. Scammers want you reacting quickly because slowing down gives you more time to spot something suspicious.
If a message claims your account will close or a package requires immediate action, avoid clicking its links. Check your Amazon account through the official app or website instead.

Watch for anyone claiming to represent Amazon who asks you to buy gift cards as payment. Amazon warns that it will never ask you to purchase a gift card to resolve an account problem or make a payment. If someone makes that request, stop communicating with them.

Be especially careful if a caller asks for sensitive account information. Amazon says it will never ask for your password or one-time passcode over the phone. If someone claiming to represent Amazon asks for those details, end the conversation and contact Amazon through an official channel.

Phone scams deserve extra caution because the number on your screen can look convincing. Scammers can spoof caller ID information and make a call appear to come from a familiar company. Seeing "Amazon" on your phone does not prove Amazon is actually calling. If someone unexpectedly calls about a refund or account problem, avoid giving them information. Hang up and check your Amazon account independently.

Phishing messages can expose you to malicious websites and dangerous downloads. That is why I recommend using strong antivirus software on your devices. Strong antivirus software can warn you about known phishing sites and suspicious links. It can also help detect malware if a scammer tricks you into downloading something dangerous. Of course, antivirus software cannot replace good judgment. Avoid clicking links in unexpected Amazon messages whenever possible. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com.

Amazon also points U.S. consumers toward the Better Business Bureau's Scam Tracker at bbb.org/scamtracker. Amazon has partnered with the BBB so consumers can search reports involving suspicious communications. You can search using details such as an email address or phone number. However, a lack of reports does not prove a message is safe. New scams can appear before anyone reports them. When in doubt, verify directly with Amazon.
Kurt's key takeaways

We have spent a lot of time showing you convincing Amazon scams because they keep arriving in inboxes and on phones. Scammers understand that Amazon feels familiar, which can make an urgent message easier to believe. That is why I think this verification feature has real potential. Instead of staring at an email wondering whether the logo looks right, you can ask Amazon whether the communication lines up with something it actually sent. Still, I would keep one habit above everything else: go around the message. Open Amazon yourself. Check your account from there. If something looks suspicious, use Amazon's official verification tools before you respond. The more ways we have to interrupt a scammer's sense of urgency, the harder it becomes for that scam to work.

title: Innocent woman says police use of Flock camera led to 13 days in jail
summary: Lindsey Brooke Isaacs spent 13 days in jail after a Flock camera flagged her Dodge Durango near a fatal Florida crash that killed three people.
story: Lindsey Isaacs spent 13 days in jail after license plate reader data wrongfully linking her to a crash that killed 3 people. Prosecutors dropped all charges after investigators identified another suspect. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

Lindsey Brooke Isaacs was asleep at home when police arrived and told the 23-year-old that her car had been involved in a crash that killed three people. She knew they had the wrong person. Her black Dodge Durango showed no obvious collision damage, and she had a receipt showing where she had been.

Still, the investigation eventually led to her being arrested and 13 days in jail. "My heart was in my stomach," Lindsey told me on The CyberGuy Report Podcast at Cyberguy.com/podcast/. "I didn't know what was going on."

Months later, prosecutors dropped all eight felony charges against her and investigators arrested another woman in connection with the crash. Her case now raises a bigger question about how much weight investigators should give license plate camera data when a person's freedom is on the line.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com
LICENSE PLATE CAMERAS ARE TRACKING DRIVERS EVERYWHERE

Lindsey Isaacs says the ordeal left her shaken after she was arrested in connection with a deadly I-4 crash and later cleared of all charges. (Volusia County Division Of Corrections; The Law Offices of Patrick J. McGeehan, P.A.)
How a Flock camera became a major lead

The deadly crash happened on Oct. 4, 2025, along eastbound Interstate 4 near DeBary, Florida. Motorcyclist Joaquin Deno died. Flagler County Deputy Administrator Jorge Salinas and his wife, Nancy Salinas, also died. Witnesses reported that a Dodge Durango was involved.

Investigators found Lindsey's black Dodge Durango through a Flock automated license plate reader. The camera recorded her vehicle traveling eastbound near the Seminole and Volusia county line at 9:51 p.m. That camera was about three miles west of the crash scene. The crash happened around 9:53 p.m. That timing became especially important later.

Lindsey's attorney, Patrick McGeehan, said his team performed a time-distance analysis and concluded Lindsey was already beyond the crash location when the collision occurred. So the camera really did capture Lindsey's vehicle. The problem came from what investigators concluded from that sighting. Lindsey put it more bluntly during our conversation. "They just picked up my car off a camera and called it the end of the day. We got her."
Other evidence pointed toward a different Dodge Durango

The Flock camera hit was far from the only information investigators had. A 911 caller described a maroon Dodge Durango and provided part of its license plate number. Later, investigators also found red or maroon paint transfer on a Ford Focus involved in the crash.

Meanwhile, Lindsey drove a black Dodge Durango. A specialized Florida Highway Patrol team later inspected Lindsey's vehicle and reported finding no damage suggesting it had been involved in a collision with another vehicle.

That finding lined up with something Lindsey said she had been telling investigators from the beginning. "Where is the damage on the vehicle?" she recalled asking police. "Because I'm standing right in front of it and I don't see any damage." Still, authorities impounded her SUV. Months passed.
Lindsey Isaacs is arrested on charges seven months later

On April 17, 2026, Lindsey got a call from her attorney. She had to surrender that day. "They are arresting you for this crime," Lindsey recalled him telling her. She faced eight felony charges: three counts of vehicular homicide, three counts of leaving the scene of a crash involving death, leaving the scene involving serious bodily injury and reckless driving causing serious bodily injury. Lindsey spent 13 days in jail.

During our podcast conversation, she described spending her first several days in solitary confinement. She said she had a toilet, a sink and a metal sleeping slab covered by a thin mat. Her charges were so serious, she said, that jail officials initially kept her separated from other people.
Later, Lindsey was transferred to other sections of the jail. After her first bond hearing, she remained behind bars. "I was devastated, I was scared," she told me. "I thought my life was over."
HOW SURVEILLANCE TECH LED POLICE TO ACCUSE THE WRONG PERSON
Flock cameras helped identify a vehicle, but Lindsey Isaacs says investigators treated the camera hit as proof instead of a lead. (Lori Van Buren/Albany Times Union via Getty Images)
A new investigation changes the case

The case finally began moving in a very different direction after prosecutors and a specialized Florida Highway Patrol team took another look. That team found no meaningful crash damage on Lindsey's Durango. Investigators revisited witness information and followed evidence pointing toward another vehicle.

On May 22, the State Attorney's Office formally declined to prosecute Lindsey on all eight charges. Authorities then arrested Alisa Lee Montalvo on charges connected to the crash. Prosecutors allege Montalvo was driving a maroon Dodge Durango. She faces nine charges, including three counts of vehicular homicide and tampering with physical evidence. She has not been convicted, and the charges remain allegations.

For Lindsey, the news brought enormous relief. "I felt like a new woman," she told me. "I felt free." Lindsey told me she later received an apology from the head of the Florida Highway Patrol. "It felt like a miracle," she said. "Another miracle from God that I was hearing it in person, face to face."

However, she also said the experience left lasting emotional and physical effects. "This took and is going to take maybe years to get better mentally, physically, emotionally," Lindsey said. Lindsey has since filed a federal civil rights lawsuit against two Florida Highway Patrol troopers involved in the investigation, alleging false arrest, wrongful imprisonment and malicious prosecution. Those claims have not been proven in court.
Flock Safety responds
We reached out to Flock Safety and the Florida Highway Patrol for comment. Flock Safety responded with the following statement:

"Flock cameras provide investigative leads; they do not identify perpetrators, determine guilt, or make arrest decisions. In fact, the complaint itself calls the Flock evidence 'exculpatory, not inculpatory,' meaning the evidence pointed away from Ms. Isaacs rather than implicating her: it accurately placed her vehicle three miles from the crash scene just two minutes before the crash. Characterizing her arrest as the result of Flock technology fundamentally misrepresents both the allegations and the role our technology played in this case."
The Florida Highway Patrol did not respond to our request for comment.
What a Flock camera can record

Flock cameras are automated license plate readers, often called ALPRs. They capture images of passing vehicles and use software to identify license plates. Flock systems can also capture vehicle characteristics including make, model and color. Each camera sighting can create a record linking a vehicle with a particular place and time.

For police, that can become an extremely useful investigative tool. A stolen car can appear on a camera. A vehicle connected to a missing person case could produce a lead. However, Lindsey's experience raises another question. What happens when investigators put too much confidence in one search result? We previously explored that concern after surveillance technology helped police accuse a Colorado woman of stealing a package. Her own phone location history eventually helped show where she had really been.
Lindsey blames how investigators used the Flock data

One of the most interesting moments in my conversation with Lindsey came when I asked whether she blamed the Flock technology or the way police interpreted its data. Her answer was clear. "I 100% think the second one you said, how police interpret the camera footage," she told me. That gets to the heart of this story.

The Flock camera captured Lindsey's vehicle traveling on I-4. The machine did what it was designed to do. Human judgment came next. Investigators had to decide what that sighting meant. They also had to weigh it against witness accounts, physical evidence and the condition of Lindsey's car.

According to Lindsey's federal complaint, the Flock hit three miles from the crash two minutes beforehand, ultimately helped her legal team argue that she was already beyond the crash location when the collision occurred. Technology can surface a lead. People still have to prove what that lead actually means.
FLOCK SAFETY CAMERAS NEED CONSTITUTIONAL GUARDRAILS BEFORE FURTHER DEPLOYMENT, TENNESSEE MAYOR ARGUES

Lindsey Isaacs spent 13 days in jail after investigators relied heavily on a license plate reader hit before charges were dropped. The case is fueling debate over how police use automated camera data. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Florida orders license plate readers off state highways

The debate over these cameras has now taken a major turn in Florida. On Aug. 31, the Florida Department of Transportation revoked permits for license plate reader systems within rights-of-way on Florida's state highway system.

FDOT cited the rapid growth of the systems along with reports of misuse and concerns involving data privacy and surveillance. Cameras covered by the order must be removed within 30 days. The agency also said it will stop issuing future permits for license plate readers within its jurisdiction.

However, that order does not eliminate every Flock camera in Florida. It applies to cameras within FDOT-controlled state highway rights of way. Local governments can take different approaches to cameras on city or county property. Several agencies have chosen to pull back further. Miami-Dade County, for example, announced that it would suspend its entire license plate reader program. Other Florida agencies plan to continue using cameras away from state highways.
Flock is adding new safeguards

Flock Safety has also announced significant changes to how its system operates. In August, the company announced that it was changing its recommended and default license plate data retention period from 30 days to seven days.
Flock also plans to require law enforcement customers to use its Audit Assistance tool by the end of 2026. The technology flags unusual search activity for review.

Case codes will also become mandatory for law enforcement searches by the end of the year. Flock says emergency searches can bypass that requirement, although those searches will be flagged for review. Those changes add oversight. Still, safeguards inside the software cannot determine whether an investigator has drawn the right conclusion from the information on the screen.
Your license plate can create a trail
Most of us probably drive past license plate readers without noticing them. A single plate scan may seem harmless. After all, anyone standing beside the road can see your license plate.
A searchable network changes the equation. Instead of someone seeing your vehicle once, a network of cameras can record when that vehicle passed particular locations.

We have already reported on Flock license plate cameras appearing at some Home Depot and Lowe's parking lots. We also reported on a Washington court ruling that found Flock license plate reader images can qualify as public records under that state's Public Records Act.

Lindsey told me she knew Flock cameras existed before her ordeal. She simply had no idea how much could ride on the information they collected. "I just thought it was like a traffic camera," she said. Today, her opinion has changed. "I feel very different about those cameras now."
POWERFUL CRIME-FIGHTING SURVEILLANCE GROWTH SPURS LAWMAKERS TO ISSUE WARNING: 'ORWELLIAN'
Lindsey Isaacs is suing two Florida Highway Patrol troopers after spending nearly two weeks behind bars in a case prosecutors later abandoned. (Volusia County Division Of Corrections)
What to do if police connect your vehicle to an investigation
If police tell you that your vehicle appeared in a license plate reader search tied to a serious crime, your own records could become important.

Save receipts and toll records that can help establish where you were. If your phone already stores location history, preserve that information too. Avoid changing or deleting anything related to the period investigators are asking about.

Doorbell cameras and security systems often overwrite older recordings. If footage could show your vehicle at home or somewhere else, preserve a copy as soon as possible. The same goes for dashcam video.

If authorities claim your car was involved in a collision, take detailed pictures and video showing its condition. Photograph and record each side of the vehicle and keep the original files with their date information intact.

A serious criminal accusation can escalate quickly. An attorney can help preserve evidence and communicate with investigators. Legal counsel can also examine whether the available data actually supports what police believe happened.
Kurt's key takeaways

I'm torn on Flock cameras. If somebody burglarizes my home, I want police to have technology that can help identify the vehicle that drove away. If investigators are trying to locate a missing person, a license plate reader could provide a valuable lead. But Lindsey's story shows what can happen when a lead begins driving the investigation instead of helping investigators test what really happened. Her black Dodge Durango had no crash damage. Other evidence pointed toward a maroon Durango. The timing of the Flock hit ultimately helped her attorney argue that she could not have caused the crash. Yet she still spent 13 days in jail. As I told Lindsey during our conversation, "I can't stand when technology is used in ways that it was never intended for." That is where I land on this. The technology can be incredibly useful. The people using it still need to challenge what they think they know before someone loses their freedom. For more of Lindsey's remarkable firsthand account, listen to or watch my full conversation with her on The CyberGuy Report Podcast at Cyberguy.com/podcast/.

After hearing what happened to Lindsey, would you want Flock cameras in your community, or has this case changed how you feel about police tracking license plates? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

title: AI shopping carts could drive up your grocery bill
summary: AI-powered smart grocery carts are linked to 32% higher spending, according to new research, as Instacart Caper Carts expand across U.S. stores.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

Artificial intelligence is making its way into the grocery aisle, and it could have an unexpected effect on how much you spend. You grab a grocery cart, start working through your list and notice a screen on the handle offering directions, coupons and product suggestions. It can keep a running total and may even let you skip the checkout line. That sounds convenient. It also gives the store a new way to reach you while you are deciding what goes into your cart.

New research found that shoppers who chose a smart shopping cart spent 32% more on average than people using a regular cart. They also bought more items and stayed in the store longer. So the question for you is pretty simple: Does a smarter cart help you shop better, or does it make spending more a little too easy?
Here's how the study worked, where these smart carts are already showing up in the U.S. and how to use one without letting it push your grocery bill higher.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
NEW AMAZON AI SEARCH TURNS WORDS INTO SHOPPABLE IMAGES
Amazon’s Dash Cart uses a built-in screen and sensors to track purchases while you shop and can help you skip the traditional checkout line. (Amazon)
What researchers found about AI shopping carts

The research comes from Bayes Business School at City St George's, University of London. The study, published in the Journal of Business Research, looked at how digital shopping carts were associated with spending and shopping behavior. Researchers studied smart shopping carts at a well-known German supermarket chain during March 2025.

They analyzed 12,418 individual shopping sessions over the month. Of those trips, 9,422 involved shoppers actively using the smart-cart technology. These were grocery carts fitted with tablet-style screens on the handle. Shoppers could use the technology for digital shopping lists, personalized recommendations and in-store navigation. The carts also supported checkout-free payment.
Researchers recorded how much shoppers spent and how many items they bought. They also measured how long each shopping trip lasted. The differences were substantial.

Smart-cart shoppers spent 32% more on average than non-users. They also purchased 25% more items and spent 23% more time in the store. The spending gap grew during afternoons and weekends. Meanwhile, shoppers tended to spend the most time in stores during the evening.
Why retailers may love smart shopping carts

Those numbers naturally caught the researchers' attention because a cart that increases shopper engagement could become a valuable tool for stores. Dr. Sabrina Gottschalk, a lecturer in marketing at Bayes Business School and lead author of the study, said the findings suggest retailers could see significant revenue gains from the technology.

She pointed to special offers and new product recommendations as potential opportunities. The screen also creates another place for retailers and brands to advertise while someone is actively deciding what to buy. That last part catches my attention. The screen may help you find something faster. At the same time, it can put another product in front of you when you are already in shopping mode. Your grocery cart has essentially become another screen competing for your attention.
Did the AI shopping cart actually make people spend more?

There is an important limitation here. The study found an association between smart-cart use and higher spending. Because the researchers observed shopping behavior rather than randomly assigning shoppers to different carts, the results do not prove that the technology itself caused the 32% increase.

Someone choosing a smart cart may already have planned a bigger grocery run. A shopper with a longer list could also be more interested in technology designed to make navigating the store easier. Then researchers found another wrinkle.

They looked at shoppers who interacted with the smart-cart screen more than 20 times during a single trip. These "superusers" bought significantly more items and stayed in the store longer. However, they did not spend more money overall. Once screen interaction reached higher levels, spending and basket size eventually began to decline.

Researchers suggested that some of these shoppers may have been using the technology more for the experience than because they wanted to buy more. So the research does not prove that tapping a smart-cart screen automatically sends your grocery bill soaring. Still, a 32% difference in average spending is hard to ignore.
BABY BOOMERS HATE 10 THINGS ABOUT TODAY'S GROCERY STORES
Amazon’s smart cart technology is being expanded to more Whole Foods Market locations as retailers bring digital tools deeper into the grocery aisle. (Amazon)
AI shopping carts are already spreading across the U.S.

While this particular study happened in Germany, smart carts are already rolling through grocery stores here in the U.S. Instacart says thousands of its AI-powered Caper Carts are deployed across more than 100 cities. The company also said in May 2026 that Caper Carts spanned 15 states and were available across more than a dozen retail banners overall. U.S. retailers using the technology include Kroger and Schnucks, along with Wakefern banners such as ShopRite and Fairway Market. Weis Markets has also begun deploying them at select stores.

Caper Carts use cameras, built-in scales and other sensors to understand what shoppers put into or remove from their baskets. The screen can also deliver recommendations while customers move through the store. Amazon has a competing version called Dash Cart.

Its newest Dash Cart displays prices and keeps a running total as you shop. It can offer personalized nearby deals, help navigate the store and let shoppers bypass the traditional checkout line. Amazon says the newest version will expand to dozens of additional Whole Foods Market locations across the U.S. by the end of 2026. That means this technology could become a much more familiar part of your grocery run.
Your grocery cart can become an advertising screen

Here is where I think smart carts become especially interesting. A traditional shopping cart holds your groceries. A smart cart can also put promotions directly in front of you while you move around the store.

Instacart says its Caper Cart technology can use signals such as what is already in your basket and where the cart is inside the store to decide when to surface recommendations. The company says prompts designed to remind shoppers about forgotten items have increased average basket size in its own testing. Think about how powerful that can be.

You turn down an aisle and a promotion appears for something nearby. Something already in your cart could also lead to a recommendation for another product. Sometimes that could save you money or remind you about something you genuinely need. Other times, you may end up buying something that never appeared on your shopping list. Retailers have spent decades figuring out where to position products. Smart carts bring another version of that strategy directly onto a screen that moves through the store with you.
What your smart shopping cart may learn about you

There is also a data side to these carts that deserves attention. Instacart says its Caper Carts use basket-facing camera sensors and outward-facing cameras. They also rely on built-in scales and location-tracking systems.

The company says those systems can detect which products enter or leave the basket and how shoppers move through store aisles. Instacart also says its technology can connect physical shopping interactions with purchase history. That data can make the cart more useful. It can also help make recommendations more targeted.

That is why I would pay attention to the privacy settings connected to any grocery-store account or loyalty program you use. Take a look at what information the retailer collects and what controls it gives you over personalized advertising.
MARYLAND MOVES TO BAN SURVEILLANCE PRICING IN GROCERY STORES
Instacart’s Caper Cart uses AI, cameras and sensors to recognize items, show a running total and deliver offers as you shop. (Instacart)
How to keep a smart cart from increasing your grocery bill

You do not have to avoid an AI shopping cart simply because there is a screen attached to it. Some of the technology can genuinely make grocery shopping easier. The key is using those features without letting every recommendation change what you planned to buy.
Decide what you need before you enter the store. When the cart suggests something extra, compare it with the list you already made.
This could actually be one of the best features of a smart cart. Keep an eye on your total as you shop instead of waiting for the final surprise at checkout.
A recommendation may be useful, but remember why it appeared on your screen. The retailer benefits when another product lands in your cart.
Do not assume a coupon or promoted product gives you the best deal. Compare prices and look at the unit price when package sizes differ.

Here is a simple experiment you can do yourself. Compare what you spend during a few smart-cart trips with your regular grocery runs. You may discover the technology helps you stay organized. You could also find that those convenient suggestions are adding more to your bill than you realized. For more ways to cut grocery costs, check out our article on 8 apps that can cut your food bill.
Kurt's key takeaways

I like technology that removes some of the aggravation from grocery shopping. Seeing your running total can be useful. Getting out of the store without standing in a long checkout line sounds pretty appealing to me too. What I want you to remember is that the screen on your cart has another purpose. Retailers can use it to put offers and recommendations in front of you at exactly the moment you are deciding what to buy. That does not make every suggestion a bad deal. Some could genuinely save you money. Still, the 32% spending difference in this study caught my attention. As these carts become more common in grocery stores, I think we should pay as much attention to how they influence our shopping as we do to how much time they save us. Enjoy the convenience and take the discounts when they really help. Most of all, keep your shopping list and your budget in charge.

Would you grab an AI-powered shopping cart if it helped you skip the checkout line, or would knowing smart-cart users spent 32% more make you stick with a regular cart? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: How to stream safely while traveling outside the US
summary: A VPN encrypts your connection on hotel, airport and café Wi-Fi abroad, but streaming catalogs and live sports access still depend on provider rules.
story: Travel expert Lee Abbamonte discusses the risks posed by fraudulent wireless connections on commercial flights and what passengers should check before accessing the internet in the air.

Traveling abroad used to mean leaving your normal entertainment routine at home. Now, your streaming subscriptions can come with you. However, hotels, airports and cafés often mean unfamiliar Wi-Fi networks and different streaming catalogs.

If you want to stream safely while traveling outside the U.S., a VPN, or virtual private network, can help. It creates an encrypted connection between your device and the VPN server. That adds useful protection when you are on a network you do not control.

A VPN can also let you choose a server in your home country. That can be useful when you sign in to streaming services you already use. Still, content availability depends on the service, your subscription and local licensing rules. Here's what to know before you travel so you can protect your connection, stream more smoothly and avoid surprises along the way.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. INSTANTLY UPGRADE YOUR STREAMING: AT HOME AND WHEN TRAVELING
Travelers can use a VPN on hotel, airport and café Wi-Fi while accessing streaming subscriptions they already use at home. (Photo by Alex Pantling/Getty Images)
Why public Wi-Fi deserves extra caution

Free Wi-Fi makes travel easier. Yet you often do not know who runs the network, how it is configured or who else is connected. Most major websites and apps already use HTTPS encryption. Even so, a VPN adds another encrypted tunnel between your device and the VPN server. That can reduce what the local network can learn about your internet activity.

This protection is useful beyond streaming. You may check email, book a reservation or sign in to an account while you are away. Turning on a VPN before using unfamiliar Wi-Fi adds another layer of privacy. Of course, a VPN does not make every public network risk-free. You should still avoid suspicious Wi-Fi names, keep your devices updated and use strong account security.
Keeping up with your usual streaming services abroad

Streaming can get more complicated when you cross international borders. A service may offer one catalog in the U.S. and another in Europe or Australia. Licensing agreements, regional rights and company policies often determine what appears. A VPN can be useful here because it gives you a secure way to connect to the internet while you sign in to subscriptions you normally use at home. You can also choose a VPN server in the U.S. when you need a U.S.-based connection.

However, a VPN does not guarantee access to a particular show, movie, channel or sporting event. Streaming companies set their own terms of use and regional availability rules. A program you watch at home may therefore be unavailable at your destination. Before you travel, check your streaming provider's current policies and the availability of anything you especially want to watch.
Watch U.S. TV online in 3 easy steps
If you want a secure U.S. connection while traveling, set everything up before you leave. That way, you are not troubleshooting from an airport lounge or hotel room.

Choose a reputable VPN service and create your account before your trip. Look for one that offers U.S. server locations, apps for the devices you use and enough simultaneous connections for the people traveling with you.

Install the VPN app on every phone, tablet or computer you plan to bring. Then, sign in and test the connection before you leave home. This also gives you time to solve any password, installation or account problems while you still have a reliable connection.

Open your VPN and choose a U.S. server location. Once connected, open your streaming service and sign in normally. Websites and streaming services see the VPN server's IP address instead of your usual public IP address, while the connection between your device and the VPN server remains encrypted. Your streaming provider still decides what programming your account can access.
TRAVEL MISTAKE PUTS PHONE, LAPTOP AND STREAMING ACCOUNTS AT RISK
A VPN can encrypt your internet connection on public Wi-Fi and help protect your privacy while streaming during international travel. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
What U.S. TV can you watch with a VPN?

Streaming services have their own rules for VPN connections, regional access and travel. Netflix, Hulu, Disney+, Amazon Prime Video, YouTube, ESPN and Apple TV+ may handle VPN connections differently, so check your service before you travel.
The exact shows, movies, channels and sporting events you can watch also depend on your subscription and the streaming provider's regional rules.

That is especially important for live TV and sports. Broadcast rights can change by country, league and even individual event. If there is something specific you want to watch during your trip, check the service before you leave.
Streaming U.S. sports while you travel

A VPN can also protect your connection while you watch live sports through subscriptions you already have. That can be useful for football, basketball, baseball, hockey, tennis, cycling, golf and other events when you are away from home.

However, a VPN does not create a subscription or eliminate a provider's blackout rules. Your streaming service still controls access based on your plan, location and its current broadcasting agreements. For that reason, check the event and service before relying on it for a big game.
Set everything up before you leave

The best time to prepare is before you are standing in an airport with spotty Wi-Fi. Download the VPN app on your phone, tablet or laptop. Sign in and test it. Also, update your streaming apps before departure.

Next, sign in to the services you expect to use. Some platforms may ask you to verify your identity when they detect a new device or location. Handling that at home can save time later. If your service supports offline viewing, download a few shows or movies before you go. Offline downloads are especially useful on planes, trains and trips where the connection may be unreliable.
Choosing a VPN server for streaming

When you use a VPN, your traffic travels through the VPN server before reaching the internet. Distance can affect performance. If you mainly want extra privacy and do not need a particular country, choose a nearby server. A shorter distance can often improve speed and latency.

If you need a U.S. IP address for a service you normally use at home, connect to a U.S. server instead. If the stream slows down, try another server in the same country. A different location may have less congestion or better performance.
What to do if your stream is buffering

Not every streaming problem comes from the VPN. Hotel and airport networks can slow down when many people share the same connection. First, check the underlying Wi-Fi. Then, reconnect to the VPN or try another server.

Closing apps that are downloading files, backing up photos or running large updates can also help. If the connection still struggles, lower the video quality. HD and 4K video require much more bandwidth than standard-definition video. A trusted mobile connection may also perform better than crowded public Wi-Fi, depending on your roaming plan and signal strength.
THE TRICK TO SMOOTHER STREAMING AT HOME AND ON THE ROAD
VPNs can improve privacy while traveling, but streaming services still control regional access, blackouts and available programming. (iStock)
Streaming on Apple TV, Fire TV and Roku
Traveling with a streaming device can make a hotel room feel more like home. However, VPN setup varies depending on the device.
Apple TV: Some VPN providers offer dedicated Apple TV apps that you can install directly on supported models.
Amazon Fire TV and Fire Stick: Many major VPN services offer apps for compatible Fire TV devices.
Roku: Roku does not support traditional VPN apps directly. Instead, you generally need to connect it through a VPN-enabled router or another supported network setup.

Before packing a streaming stick, check whether your hotel television gives you access to an HDMI port. Also, remember that some hotel networks use a browser-based login page. That can make connecting a streaming device more complicated.
Why streaming catalogs change when you travel?

A streaming service may license a movie in the U.S. but not in France, Australia or another country. Another broadcaster or streaming company may hold the rights there. As a result, the same account can show a different catalog after you cross a border.

Live sports can be even more complicated because broadcasting rights often vary by market. That is why it helps to check availability before a trip. A VPN can protect your connection and change the location of the VPN server you connect through. However, it cannot change the licensing agreements behind a streaming service.
Which VPN should you choose for travel?

With so many VPN services available, I would focus on a few practical things. Look for strong encryption, an easy-to-use app, plenty of server locations and support for the devices you plan to bring. If you expect to stream while traveling, also check whether the VPN works well with the streaming services you use and offers servers in the countries you may need.

A VPN encrypts the traffic between your device and the VPN provider's servers, which can add an important layer of privacy when you are using hotel, airport or café Wi-Fi. Before choosing one, check that it supports your phone, computer, tablet and any streaming devices you plan to use. You should also compare how many devices can connect at the same time, especially if you are traveling with family.

I would also look closely at the provider's privacy practices, reputation and independent security audits. Free VPNs can come with limitations such as slower speeds, fewer server choices or questionable data practices, so read the privacy policy before installing one.
Remember that a VPN is a privacy and security tool. You remain responsible for following the terms of your streaming provider and any applicable laws.
For the best VPN software, see my expert review of the best VPNs for browsing the web privately on your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com/VPN.
Kurt's key takeaways

Streaming abroad is much easier than it used to be. Still, I would not wait until you land to figure out your setup. Install your VPN and update your streaming apps before leaving home. Sign in ahead of time, too. Then download something for offline viewing so you have a backup when hotel Wi-Fi becomes unreliable. I also like using a VPN on unfamiliar networks because streaming is only part of what we do online while traveling. You may use the same connection for email, travel reservations and other accounts. Finally, remember what a VPN can and cannot do. It can encrypt your connection and let you select the location of the VPN server you use. It cannot promise that every show, channel or game will be available everywhere you travel.

title: Gmail change may flood your inbox with political email
summary: Gmail's Verified Sender Program launches September 8, 2026, giving U.S. political committees a more reliable path to your personal email inbox.
story: Google General Counsel Halimah Delaine Prado joins 'Fox & Friends' to detail how Google is fighting AI-powered phishing scams.

If your Gmail inbox already feels crowded, election season may add another layer of noise. Starting Sept. 8, 2026, Google's new Gmail Verified Sender Program will give qualifying U.S. political committees a more reliable path to personal Gmail accounts. That means qualifying political committees will have a new way to improve the reliability of their email delivery, provided they follow Google's security, authentication and spam requirements.

The program applies to eligible candidates, parties, PACs and other registered political committees that meet Google's requirements. Campaign Verify's eligibility criteria focus on registration and program requirements, regardless of party label.
The bigger issue for you is control. You can still unsubscribe, block a sender, report unwanted messages as spam or create your own Gmail filters.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. DO NOT CLICK FAKE 'ACCOUNT RECOVERY' AMAZON EMAIL
Google’s new Verified Sender Program could make it easier for qualifying political emails to reach your Gmail inbox starting September 8. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
What is Gmail's Verified Sender Program?

The Gmail Verified Sender Program is scheduled to launch September 8 for eligible U.S. political committees. Campaign Verify says political organizations must verify their sending domains before they can participate. Eligible groups include candidates, parties, PACs and other political committees that qualify under the program. Google also requires participating senders to follow email security and compliance rules. One key requirement is a user-reported spam rate below 0.3% over a rolling 14-day average.

Getting verified alone does not guarantee that every campaign message will reach your inbox. Google says continued participation depends on senders following its requirements and maintaining positive recipient engagement. If a sender's average user-reported spam rate rises above 0.3% over a rolling 14-day period, the sender violates the program's policy and could be suspended or removed. Standard Gmail spam filtering would then apply.

So, this does not give campaigns unlimited access to your inbox. However, it changes how Gmail can treat eligible political email before you personally tell Gmail what you want. One more point: verification confirms the political committee's sending domain. It should not be read as Google vouching for every claim, fundraising pitch or link inside a message.
Why you may notice more political email

Here is the part that could get annoying. Gmail has long used automated systems to decide whether bulk email belongs in your inbox or spam folder. Under the new program, verified political senders that stay within Google's rules can receive more reliable delivery to personal Gmail accounts.

For someone who already receives fundraising appeals, petition requests or campaign updates, that could mean seeing more political messages in Gmail. Google tells CyberGuy the program grew out of an earlier pilot and says Gmail users will remain in control of what stays in their inboxes.

"Following our previous pilot, this program is designed to connect people with the emails they want to receive while keeping them fully in control of their inboxes. To participate, bulk senders must meet strict security and compliance requirements, ensuring that messages people receive are relevant, useful, and verified," a Google spokesperson told CyberGuy.

Google also points out that Gmail users can continue to mark a message as spam, block a specific sender and unsubscribe from unwanted mailing lists. The company says the new program does not turn off Gmail's broader security protections. Google says Gmail's filters continue to block more than 99.9% of spam, phishing and malware while using recipient feedback to help determine what people want to receive. Still, if more qualifying political messages reach you, some of the cleanup work may fall on you.
RUSSIAN HACKERS CAN STEAL EMAILS WITHOUT A CLICK
Gmail users can still unsubscribe, report unwanted messages as spam, block senders and create filters to reduce campaign email clutter. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
What happens if you mark a political email as spam?

This is where your own Gmail choices become important. According to reporting on the new program, if you mark a participating sender's message as spam, Gmail can use that feedback for your account. Future messages from that sender can then be routed to spam based on your preference.

Google's standard Gmail tools also confirm that messages you report as spam move into the Spam folder. Over time, reporting unwanted email helps Gmail identify similar messages more effectively. In other words, do not assume you have to live with every campaign message that reaches you.
Tips to cut down political email in Gmail
You have several ways to take back your inbox. Start with the least aggressive option and move up if the messages keep coming.

On a computer, open the message and look next to the sender's name. If Gmail shows an Unsubscribe option, click it and confirm. Google says some unsubscribe requests can take a few days to fully stop the mail. Gmail may also send you to the sender's website when a one-click option is unavailable.

If you did not ask for the message or the sender keeps emailing you after you tried to leave the list, select the email and click Report spam. That moves the message into Spam and gives Gmail another signal about what you do not want.

For a sender you never want to hear from again, Gmail lets you block that address. Future messages from a blocked sender go to Spam. Keep in mind that campaigns may use more than one sending address or domain. Blocking one address may reduce the flow without stopping every related message.

If the same sender or phrase keeps showing up, create a filter on your computer. Open Gmail, click Show search options in the search box and enter the sender, domain or other criteria you want to target. Then click Create filter and choose what Gmail should do with matching messages. You can archive them, apply a label or delete them automatically. I would be careful with broad keywords such as "vote" or "election." Those words can appear in news alerts, community messages and emails you actually want. A specific sender or domain gives you more control.
FAR-LEFT POLITICIANS STILL USING ACTBLUE AS 88-YEAR-OLD DISPUTES DONATING NEARLY $150,000 TO FUNDRAISING GIANT
As election season heats up, political email could become more noticeable in your inbox, making your own spam controls more important. (Photo by Ute Grabowsky/Photothek via Getty Images)

Political campaigns and other organizations can obtain contact information from many sources, including public records and commercial data providers. Reducing the amount of personal information circulating online may help limit some unwanted outreach.

A personal data removal service can do much of the cleanup for you. They can send removal requests to data brokers on your behalf and continue following up as your information reappears. This can reduce your exposure across data broker and people-search sites. However, it cannot remove information from government websites, so it will not stop every political email or message.

The less personal information that data brokers have available to package and share, the fewer places marketers and other organizations may have to find your contact details. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting Cyberguy.com.

Political email can also give scammers an easy theme to copy. If a message pressures you to donate immediately, verify your identity or click a link before a deadline, avoid using the link in the email when anything feels off. Go directly to the campaign or organization's official website instead. CyberGuy has covered how scammers use fake political donation requests and how political messages can hide scam links.

One of the best ways to reduce future clutter is to stop handing out your main email address everywhere. An email alias gives you another address that forwards to your inbox. You can use a separate alias for donations, petitions, newsletters or other sign-ups. If that alias starts getting flooded, you can shut it down without changing your primary address. For recommendations on private and secure email providers that offer alias addresses, visit Cyberguy.com.
This Gmail change arrives at a time when many people already feel buried by junk email, spam texts, robocalls and political messages.

We covered exactly that in our free CyberGuy LIVE class, "Sick of Spam?" The live session has ended, but you can still get the replay and our spam-stopping checklist. I walk you through ways to reduce junk email, cut down robocalls, curb political texts and clean up unwanted messages. Get the free CyberGuy LIVE replay and checklist at Cyberguy.com/cyberguylive/classes/#past-classes. That is worth doing before September 8, especially if your inbox already feels like a dumping ground.
Kurt's key takeaways

Google is giving verified political committees a new path to more reliable email delivery, but campaigns still have to play by Gmail's rules. Users also retain the power to unsubscribe, block senders and hit the spam button. From a security standpoint, verifying political senders can help make impersonation harder. From an inbox standpoint, however, you may still end up doing more of the sorting yourself if campaign volume picks up. My advice is simple: use Gmail's controls aggressively when a message keeps showing up after you have had enough. Unsubscribe from legitimate lists. Report suspicious or unwanted messages as spam. Create targeted filters for repeat senders. Then think about using an alias for future political sign-ups so your primary email stays cleaner. Google's 0.3% spam threshold also gives campaigns a strong incentive to avoid irritating recipients. The real test will come after September 8, when political email volume increases and Gmail users start voting with the Report spam button.

title: Pilotless cargo aircraft could change how packages move
summary: Elroy Air's Chaparral can carry over 500 pounds and fly 450 miles without a runway, and the FAA just tested it under a new federal program.
story: A medical drone takes off during testing as part of a program aimed at speeding up the delivery of critical healthcare supplies. The effort is focused on transporting lab samples, blood and donor matching materials between smaller communities and larger hospital hubs, where timing can impact diagnoses and treatment. Developers say faster, on-demand flights could help reduce delays for rural patients, who often face longer travel times for care, with future plans to expand the technology to carry transplant-related materials.

A broken pump on an offshore platform, or medical supplies needed after a hurricane can be tough to move quickly. The FAA just tested one possible solution: a hybrid-electric cargo aircraft that can take off vertically and fly without a crew onboard.

The FAA announced that Elroy Air and the Louisiana Department of Transportation and Development conducted a cargo demonstration at Houma-Terrebonne Airport in Louisiana. The agency says it was the first remotely piloted aircraft test flight under its eVTOL (electric vertical takeoff and landing) Integration Pilot Program, known as eIPP.

That may sound like a specialized aviation test, but the bigger story is what aircraft like this could eventually do. Elroy Air's Chaparral can carry more than 500 pounds, putting it in a very different league from the small delivery drones you may picture hovering over a driveway.

So, could pilotless aircraft like this eventually change how everything from emergency supplies to everyday goods moves across the country? Here's what the FAA is testing and why it could be a big deal.
MISSOURI TESTS MEDICAL DRONES TO SPEED UP RURAL HEALTH CARE
The Chaparral can take off and land vertically, allowing it to operate in places without a traditional runway. (Elroy Air)

Why this pilotless cargo aircraft test stands out

The FAA created eIPP to help the government learn how next-generation aircraft can operate safely in U.S. airspace. In March, the Department of Transportation selected eight projects across 26 states. Louisiana is one of the participants, and more test flights are planned through the rest of 2026. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said the Louisiana demonstration provides data that can help "turn these concepts from trial to deployment."

That line gets to the heart of this test. Chaparral has flown before. In December 2025, Elroy Air completed its first point-to-point cargo delivery with the aircraft. During that demonstration, Chaparral autonomously carried 213 pounds over a 2.6-mile flight. What changed here is the regulatory setting. The FAA now gets to study these flights as part of a federal program focused on bringing advanced aircraft into the national airspace.
How Elroy Air's Chaparral works

Chaparral looks more like a small cargo aircraft than the drone that might bring dinner to your house. It uses electric propulsion for vertical takeoff and landing. Then it transitions to wingborne flight for the longer part of the trip. A hybrid-electric powertrain gives the aircraft longer-range capability without requiring charging infrastructure at every stop. Elroy Air's current Chaparral specifications list a maximum range of 450 miles and a payload of more than 500 pounds.

The cargo system is unusual, too. Elroy designed modular pods that workers can load before the aircraft arrives. Chaparral can pick up a pod, fly it to another location and leave it there. That could reduce the amount of ground equipment needed at remote sites. Because it can take off vertically, Chaparral can serve locations that lack a traditional runway.
Pilotless still involves human oversight

There is an important detail behind the word "pilotless." The FAA described the Louisiana demonstration as remotely piloted. Elroy Air later said Chaparral completed a week-long series of flights autonomously with no pilot onboard while operating under Air Traffic Control oversight.

That means humans still play a role in overseeing these operations even when the aircraft handles the flight autonomously. As testing continues, regulators will have to determine how much human supervision is required and how the aircraft should respond to communication failures, changing weather or other unexpected problems.
DOORDASH GETS FAA APPROVAL FOR ITS OWN DELIVERY DRONES
Elroy Air designed the Chaparral to carry heavy cargo between locations, including remote worksites and areas that are difficult to reach by road. (Elroy Air)
Where Chaparral could be useful first

You probably will not see a Chaparral dropping an Amazon box onto your front lawn anytime soon. The aircraft targets what the logistics industry calls the middle mile. That means moving cargo between larger points in a delivery network rather than carrying one small order to your doorstep.

Elroy Air has pointed to offshore energy operations and industrial supply chains as potential uses. The company also sees an opportunity in disaster response, where damaged roads can make moving supplies far more difficult. For example, Chaparral could carry replacement equipment to an offshore facility without sending a crewed helicopter. After a major storm, aircraft like it could eventually help move heavier supplies into areas that ground vehicles struggle to reach.
Elroy Air said when it joined eIPP earlier this year that the program could include cargo operations across the Gulf Coast, including energy industry locations in Louisiana, Texas and Mississippi.
How this fits into the delivery boom

Delivery drones are starting to show up in more places, but most of them are still carrying pretty small loads. Amazon plans to expand Prime Air drone delivery to nearly 500 U.S. cities and towns by the end of 2026. Those drones are built for lightweight packages delivered directly to customers. We recently took a closer look at Amazon's huge drone delivery expansion and what it could mean if you live in one of the communities getting the service.
Meanwhile, other companies are working on the last part of the trip. Robot.com's R-dog uses wheeled legs to get over obstacles such as stairs and curbs while carrying deliveries.

Chaparral takes on a much bigger job. Instead of carrying one sandwich or a small box, it is built to move substantial cargo between locations. That could make heavy-duty delivery one of the first places where this kind of aircraft proves especially useful.
What happens next for the FAA program

The Louisiana flight represents one step in a much broader federal test program. The FAA says it will study these demonstrations, identify problems and refine procedures for advanced air mobility. Louisiana and the other eIPP participants plan additional flights through the rest of the year.

Watch how much human supervision the FAA requires as the technology develops. Regulators will also have to decide where these aircraft can operate routinely. Another major test will come when something goes wrong. Communication can fail. Weather can change. The aircraft will need dependable ways to respond safely when either happens. Those answers will tell us much more about how close pilotless cargo aircraft are to regular commercial use.
100 KODIAK DRIVERLESS TRUCKS ARE HEADED FOR PUBLIC ROADS
Elroy Air’s Chaparral hybrid-electric cargo aircraft takes flight as the FAA tests how remotely piloted aircraft could fit into U.S. airspace. (Elroy Air)
What this means to you

The biggest change could happen behind the scenes before you ever see one of these aircraft overhead. If heavy cargo can move faster between remote locations, companies could shorten some supply routes. Communities that are expensive or difficult to reach could gain another delivery option.
Emergency response could benefit as well. An aircraft that takes off without a runway could potentially keep supplies moving when damaged infrastructure slows trucks or traditional aircraft.
However, communities will want answers about noise and flight paths. Safety questions will be even bigger as these aircraft begin sharing more airspace with conventional aviation.
For you, the FAA's work now could eventually influence which autonomous delivery services reach your area and what safeguards come with them.
Kurt's key takeaways

What gets my attention here is how much work this aircraft could actually take on. We have watched small delivery drones inch closer to everyday use for years, but Chaparral is built for a much bigger job. It can move hundreds of pounds over real distances without needing a runway at every stop. I also like that the FAA is testing this in a real-world program instead of rushing it into wider use. Regulators need to see how these aircraft handle shared airspace, changing conditions and unexpected problems. The bar should stay high when you are talking about hundreds of pounds flying overhead. For now, I would keep an eye on remote worksites, disaster response and other places where moving cargo is difficult or slow. If these aircraft prove they can do that safely and reliably, they could end up changing a much bigger part of the delivery network.
