title: Autonomous excavators are digging with empty cabs
summary: Bedrock Robotics says its autonomous excavators are doing paid earthwork on active job sites in Texas and Nevada with no operator in the cab.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

If you have ever driven past a construction site and watched an excavator moving huge piles of dirt, you probably figured there was an experienced operator sitting in the cab. On some job sites in Texas and Nevada, there is nobody in that seat.

San Francisco-based Bedrock Robotics has autonomous excavators doing real commercial earthwork with no operator onboard. The company says the deployments follow a year of testing on active job sites with human supervision.

Seeing AI take over software tasks is one thing. Watching it control a massive excavator on a live construction site feels very different. Bedrock says this could help contractors deal with worker shortages and keep projects moving more efficiently. Here's how the technology works and what could come next.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats , has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com
100 KODIAK DRIVERLESS TRUCKS ARE HEADED FOR PUBLIC ROADS
Bedrock’s sensor and computing system gives an excavator the technology it needs to operate autonomously. (Bedrock Robotics)
Bedrock's autonomous excavators are working on real projects

Bedrock says its operator-free excavators are now active on major infrastructure projects. One machine is working on a Nevada water treatment facility with Sundt Construction. In Texas, Bedrock is working with Champion Site Prep on a multimillion-cubic-yard earthwork project.
The company also has a 1.2 million-cubic-yard civil sitework project with Zachry Construction Corporation. The current work centers on rough early earthmoving and foundation prep.

The company is concentrating on clearing earth, cut-and-fill operations and rough cuts before moving into more detailed work. That makes sense because earthwork comes early in a project. If crews fall behind there, everything that follows can feel the delay.
Bedrock says productivity is approaching human levels
Bedrock measures excavator productivity by the cubic yards of earth moved during a shift, a company spokesperson tells CyberGuy.

How much earth a machine should move depends on the project, soil conditions and the rest of the equipment involved. Still, the spokesperson says, "As of our deployments in August 2026, two years after the company was founded, we are already near human-level productivity."
How the Bedrock Operator makes an excavator autonomous

Bedrock calls its system the Bedrock Operator. The company designed it as a retrofit for existing heavy equipment. Bedrock says crews can install its sensor and computing package in a day without permanent changes to the machine. Once a site manager sets the initial plan, the software takes over the digging work. Bedrock says its machine-learning system can understand the surrounding area and plan movement. It can then carry out complex tasks.

The company says it trained the system on tens of thousands of hours of field work. However, there is an important detail about the current rollout. Bedrock is deploying new excavators that it outfitted and tested at its own facilities. When we asked when the system would begin operating on contractors' existing equipment, a Bedrock spokesperson said the company has no update to share yet but hopes to have more soon. So the retrofit model remains central to Bedrock's plan. The live operator-free deployments are still in an earlier phase.
An empty cab still comes with human oversight

Seeing a huge excavator move with nobody inside will probably make some people nervous. Bedrock knows safety will help determine how far this technology goes and says it comes first as the company expands deployment. The machines monitor their own progress while they work. If a machine gets stuck or cannot continue, the system can call for help.

When we asked how often a person needs to step in, a Bedrock spokesperson told CyberGuy, "It's relatively rare." If a machine encounters something unusual or gets stuck, someone monitoring the fleet can briefly intervene until the autonomous system is ready to take back over.

Bedrock also keeps a person in the loop. That gives the system a path to human support without requiring someone to sit in the cab all day. On active sites, that becomes especially important. People walk through work zones. Water trucks and other heavy equipment move nearby.

Bedrock says the safety response happens automatically. "If a person or unauthorized object gets too close to a Bedrock-equipped machine, the machine will automatically stop," the spokesperson said. The excavator stays stopped until the person or object has moved to a safe distance, with no manual intervention required.
HUMANLESS BIG RIG COMPLETES FIRST US FREIGHT RUN
The empty cab shows how Bedrock’s system can handle digging work without an operator sitting inside. (Bedrock Robotics)
Why Bedrock started with one of the hardest machines
Bedrock picked excavators for a reason. The company says excavators can account for about 25% of a contractor's fleet. They also take years to master.

Bedrock estimates that an operator may need five years or more to fully develop the skill. That creates a difficult staffing problem. Contractors need experienced people, yet many projects involve long stretches of repetitive earthmoving.
Bedrock wants autonomous equipment to handle more of that repeatable production work. Skilled operators could then focus on detailed jobs or supervise a larger operation.
We have seen autonomous excavators before. CyberGuy previously covered HEAP, a 12-ton robotic excavator that built a massive stone wall on its own.
What makes Bedrock different is where the technology is headed now. These excavators are doing commercial work on active job sites as part of real infrastructure projects.
Construction faces a growing worker shortage

The timing helps explain why investors are pouring money into this technology. Bedrock has raised more than $350 million. Its founding team includes former Waymo engineers who spent years working on autonomous vehicles.

Meanwhile, construction companies are struggling to find enough skilled workers. Bedrock cites industry estimates showing that roughly one in five construction workers is over age 55. Another estimate says more than 40% of the construction workforce could retire within the next five years.

The company also points to research showing that 92% of firms with open craft positions have difficulty filling at least some of those jobs. Those departures could hit contractors while demand remains high across many types of building projects.
Costs add another pressure point. Bedrock cites a McKinsey analysis that found large construction projects typically took 20% longer than scheduled and ran up to 80% over budget.

Then there is safety. Construction accounts for a disproportionate share of workplace deaths compared with its share of the overall workforce. Automation could help reduce exposure to dangerous tasks. However, companies will still need to prove that autonomous machines can work safely around people over long periods.

Bedrock also takes a firm position on what this technology means for equipment operators. "We do not expect operators to be replaced at all," a Bedrock spokesperson tells CyberGuy. In the near term, the company sees Bedrock-equipped machines working alongside existing crews because contractors do not have enough skilled operators to tackle every project. Longer term, Bedrock expects some experienced operators to move into supervisory positions overseeing autonomous equipment. The company compares that future role to becoming a "foreman for machines." At the same time, Bedrock says people who want to continue operating equipment themselves should still have a place in construction for years to come.
Bedrock wants machines to work together next

The long-term idea goes far beyond one excavator digging by itself. Bedrock wants multiple machines to coordinate across a job site. Bedrock co-founder Kevin Peterson described a future where an excavator could work alongside a bulldozer, truck and grader.

Instead of each machine operating as a separate tool, software could help coordinate the larger job. That could change project scheduling in a big way. A site manager might eventually assign the goal while a connected fleet determines how to move the work forward.
Bedrock says this coordinated model remains on its roadmap. For now, the company is scaling excavator deployments and expanding the types of tasks its system can perform.
Bedrock keeps a person in the loop to monitor operations and step in when the autonomous system needs help. (Bedrock Robotics)
What this means to you

Here's why this could affect you. Construction delays can hold up new housing, road projects and water infrastructure. If autonomous equipment can keep earthwork moving when contractors cannot find enough experienced operators, some projects could move faster and stay closer to schedule.

Bedrock says it sees autonomous machines working alongside people rather than eliminating operator jobs. In the near term, that could give existing crews more help with repetitive earthwork. Over time, some experienced operators could end up supervising groups of autonomous machines while others continue working directly in the cab.
Permits and material shortages can still slow a project down. Skilled workers also remain essential for planning, detailed work and handling situations the technology cannot manage on its own.

I'll be watching whether that near-human productivity holds up as these machines move onto more job sites. Bedrock says human intervention is relatively rare today, but I also want to see how that changes when one person is monitoring a larger fleet.

Safety will be the other big test. I want to see what happens when something unexpected enters the work zone. The more autonomous equipment we put around people, the more important that real-world track record becomes.
Kurt's key takeaways

What catches my attention here is that Bedrock has moved beyond showing what an autonomous excavator might be able to do someday. These machines are already doing paid work on active construction sites with nobody sitting in the cab. Bedrock now tells us the machines are nearing human-level productivity and that human intervention is "relatively rare." Those are encouraging signs, but I want to see how those claims hold up across more projects and over longer periods. I also like hearing Bedrock say directly that it does not expect operators to disappear. If autonomy helps contractors handle more work while experienced people take on tougher jobs or supervise the machines, there could be a real upside for both crews and the projects they build. The real test will come as Bedrock puts more of these machines to work. If they stay safe and productive around real crews, those empty cabs may become a much more familiar sight.

title: Should you use a separate computer for online banking?
summary: A dedicated banking computer isolates your financial accounts from malware and phishing, but passwords, SIM swapping and outdated software remain risks.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

When so much of your financial life lives online, protecting the device you use to access your money deserves some extra thought. Nancy from Baton Rouge, Louisiana, recently wrote to us asking whether keeping banking and investments on an entirely separate computer could provide another layer of protection.

"I've had several clients tell me they have bought a computer that is only used for online banking, financial institutions and anything to do with their investment accounts. Is this a good strategy for protecting some of your assets? What are the upsides and what are the downsides?"

Nancy, yes. Using a separate computer only for banking, investments and other financial accounts can add a meaningful layer of security. I especially like this approach for someone with substantial savings or retirement assets. It can also make sense if you simply want to keep your financial life separated from everything else you do online.
However, buying another computer will not make your accounts untouchable. How you set it up and how you use it are what make the strategy worthwhile.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats , has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed.

CYBERCRIME LOSSES NEAR $21B: 5 WAYS TO PROTECT YOUR MONEY
A dedicated computer used only for banking and investments can reduce exposure to many everyday online threats. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Why a separate computer for online banking can help

Think about what happens on the computer you use every day. You open email, click links and shop online. Maybe you also use social media, download documents or install browser extensions. All of that creates opportunities for malware, phishing attempts or malicious software to reach your device. A dedicated financial computer removes much of that exposure.

On this computer, you would skip email and casual web browsing. Online shopping would happen on another device. Ideally, you would install very little software beyond what the computer needs for security and accessing your financial accounts. That gives attackers fewer opportunities to reach the device you use to manage your money. Our guide to safely viewing your bank and retirement accounts online also explains why protecting the device you use is an important part of financial security.
The biggest benefits of a banking-only computer
The biggest advantage is isolation. If malware gets onto the laptop you use for email or everyday browsing, your dedicated financial computer remains separate.
There are several other benefits worth considering:

Less exposure to malware and phishing: You are not opening random links or attachments on the same computer that accesses your financial accounts.A cleaner computer: You can limit installed software and avoid unnecessary browser extensions that could introduce security risks.More control over where you sign in: You can bookmark your legitimate bank and investment websites and use those bookmarks every time.Everyday mistakes stay somewhere else: A malicious download or dangerous website on your regular computer is less likely to affect the device you use for financial accounts.
Less exposure to malware and phishing: You are not opening random links or attachments on the same computer that accesses your financial accounts.
A cleaner computer: You can limit installed software and avoid unnecessary browser extensions that could introduce security risks.
More control over where you sign in: You can bookmark your legitimate bank and investment websites and use those bookmarks every time.
Everyday mistakes stay somewhere else: A malicious download or dangerous website on your regular computer is less likely to affect the device you use for financial accounts.
For people who do not need to check investments constantly, that separation can be especially useful.
FAKE PASSWORD-MANAGER ALERTS COULD PUT YOUR VAULT AT RISK
Keeping your financial computer updated and limiting what you do on it can help strengthen its security. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
A dedicated banking computer still has weaknesses
This is where you need to be careful. A banking-only computer can reduce certain risks, but it cannot protect you from every way criminals may try to reach your money.

If you reuse a password that later appears in a data breach, having a separate computer will not solve the problem. Every financial account should have its own strong password. A password manager can help create and securely store unique passwords for you.

Many financial institutions still use text messages to send security codes. Criminals may try to hijack a victim's phone number through SIM swapping or an unauthorized number transfer. If that happens, they could potentially receive verification messages without ever touching your banking computer. Our guide on how to avoid a malicious SIM swapping scam explains how protections such as a carrier PIN or number-transfer lock can help reduce that risk.

Suppose you receive an alarming text on your phone claiming someone transferred thousands of dollars from your account. You walk over to the dedicated computer and type the website address included in that message. If the address leads to a phishing site, the separate computer cannot protect you from entering your login information there. That is why I recommend bookmarking your financial institutions' legitimate websites and using those bookmarks rather than following addresses sent through unexpected emails or texts.

A computer that spends most of its life sitting unused can create another problem. It still needs security updates. Operating system and browser updates regularly fix vulnerabilities that criminals may try to exploit. Keep automatic updates enabled and restart the computer when necessary. If you have not used the financial computer in several weeks, let it finish installing updates before signing into your accounts.
Strong passwords, secure authentication and account alerts still matter, even when you use a separate computer for your finances. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Tips for setting up a separate computer for online banking
If you decide to take this approach, keep the computer's purpose very narrow. The less you do on it, the more useful the separation becomes.
Keep Windows, macOS or ChromeOS updated automatically. Your browser should stay updated too. Do not keep postponing restarts when an important security update requires one.

Reserve it for your bank, brokerage accounts, retirement plans, credit cards and other important financial services. Avoid email and social media. Do your online shopping and everyday browsing on another device.

I would also keep strong antivirus software running on the dedicated computer. Look for protection that can detect malware, phishing attempts and other online threats in real time. Even on a computer with limited use, antivirus software adds another layer of protection in case a malicious website or other threat reaches the device. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com

Go directly to your financial institution's legitimate website and save it as a bookmark. Then use that bookmark whenever you need to sign in. Be especially careful with financial links that arrive through text messages or emails, even when they appear urgent.

Never reuse your banking password somewhere else. If another website suffers a data breach, criminals may try stolen usernames and passwords on financial accounts. A password manager can create strong, unique passwords and remember them for you.

Enable multi-factor authentication on every financial account that supports it. If your institution offers a passkey or physical security key, consider using it. An authenticator app may also provide stronger protection than receiving a verification code by text. For more on the differences, see our guide to whether bank text codes are enough to protect you.

Do not wait until your monthly statement arrives to discover suspicious activity. Set alerts for logins, withdrawals, transfers, new payees and password changes whenever your financial institution offers them. These notifications can give you an early warning when something happens that you did not authorize.
Is a separate banking computer necessary for everyone?

No. You can safely manage financial accounts from a well-maintained everyday computer if you follow strong security practices. Keep the computer updated. Protect each financial account with a unique password and use strong authentication whenever possible.

For many people, those protections combined with careful online behavior will provide strong security. However, I look at the equation a little differently for someone managing significant retirement savings or investment assets. The cost of a basic computer may be relatively small compared with the amount of money you are trying to protect. You also do not need an expensive machine for banking and investment websites.

If you decide the extra separation makes sense for you, take a look at my best laptops for 2026 and best desktop computers for 2026 at Cyberguy.com to compare current options. A dedicated machine can create a cleaner and more controlled environment for accessing your financial accounts. Just remember that the separation only works if you maintain it. Once the "banking computer" becomes the computer you also use for email, social media or general web browsing, much of that security advantage disappears.
Kurt's key takeaways

Nancy's question gets at something I wish more people thought about before a scam or account takeover happens. A separate computer for online banking can be a smart additional barrier, particularly when you are protecting significant savings or retirement assets. Keeping email, downloads and everyday web activity away from that machine reduces the opportunities criminals have to reach it. Still, I would never rely on the computer alone. Your passwords matter. Your phone number needs protection. Strong authentication can help stop someone who gets hold of a password, while account alerts can warn you when something suspicious happens. So, if buying a dedicated computer gives you greater control over how you access your money, I think it is a sensible strategy. Treat it as another layer in a larger financial security plan rather than a replacement for the protections you already need. title: AI robot pet could know your family too well
summary: The OlloNi SS1 AI robot pet uses a 4K camera and facial recognition to learn your family, but its removable Red Heart memory module raises questions.
story: The 'Cyber Guy' Kurt Knutsson cautions parents about AI-powered chatbot teddy bears, highlighting privacy risks as toys might collect children's personal details.

We've covered home robots that can fold laundry and others designed to become AI companions. Now there's one that wants to remember your family. The OlloNi SS1 is an AI robot pet that can recognize family members and pets as it moves around your home. OlloBot says it can learn your routines, respond to emotional cues and save memorable family moments along the way.

Here's where it gets really interesting. OlloNi has a removable "Red Heart" memory module designed to carry those memories into a future OlloBot. So, when the robot gets replaced, years of personalization could move right along with you.

I can see the appeal of that. I also think it's important to ask yourself this: How much of your family's life are you comfortable letting a robot remember? Here's how OlloNi works, what it can remember and the privacy questions to consider before deciding whether you'd want one in your home.
WOULD YOU PAY $8,000 FOR A ROBOT TO FOLD LAUNDRY?
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks.

You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com
The OlloNi SS1 artificial intelligence robot pet can recognize family members and pets, learn household routines and capture memorable moments with a 4K camera. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
What is the OlloNi SS1 AI robot pet?

The OlloNi SS1 is OlloBot's newest AI companion robot pet, developed by Hong Kong-based Ollobot Robotics Limited. Unlike a robot built mainly for chores, the SS1 is designed to interact with the people and pets living around it.

Two circular eye screens display expressions while a separate main screen handles information and direct interaction. The setup gives OlloNi a face that can react visually without relying on spoken responses every time.

A 4K camera with motion tracking helps the robot recognize individual family members and household pets. OlloBot says the SS1 gradually learns routines and preferences as it spends more time with a household. It also adapts to different communication patterns.
That puts OlloNi in a different category from a robot vacuum or a machine built mainly to handle physical work. The goal here is to make the robot feel increasingly familiar.
OlloNi wants to understand how you are feeling

OlloBot is also giving the SS1 what it describes as proactive emotional interaction. The company says the robot uses several types of information to interpret what is happening around it. That includes someone's tone of voice and facial expression. It can also learn behavioral patterns over time.
For example, OlloBot says the robot may notice when someone appears to be feeling low. Instead of waiting for that person to issue a command, OlloNi could approach and initiate an interaction.

We recently covered Familiar, another emotionally aware AI robot pet. That robot is also designed to learn routines and react to the people around it. OlloNi takes the idea in another direction by connecting that personalization to a memory system that can survive beyond the original robot.
A 4K camera can capture family moments for you

One feature I can see families using is OlloNi's 4K camera. With permission turned on, OlloBot says the SS1 can recognize moments such as laughter or celebrations and capture them automatically. Its AI-assisted Vlog feature can then edit the footage and add music to create home videos.
I like the idea behind this. When something memorable happens, someone usually reaches for a phone. That often means the person recording ends up watching part of the moment through a screen.
OlloNi could change that. Because the robot is already moving around the home, it could capture moments while everyone else stays in them.
But this is also where I would start thinking seriously about privacy. You are allowing a connected 4K camera to move around your home and decide which moments may be worth saving.
That is a lot of access to give any device, no matter how cute the robot looks.
OlloNi can become a moving window into your home

OlloNi also supports remote viewing and two-way voice and video calls. Unlike a camera sitting on a shelf, the robot can move around the home and follow activity. OlloBot says this could make remote check-ins feel more active for family members who live apart.

The idea could appeal to someone who wants to stay connected with an older relative or other family members from a distance. OlloBot's website also says its app can let you see and interact with OlloNi while you are away. The app is designed to show daily moments and memories the robot has captured.

However, remote access raises the stakes for security. A camera that can move around your house deserves strong account protection. Owners should know exactly who can connect to it and what happens if an account gets compromised.
The Red Heart lets OlloNi's memories live on

This may be the most unusual part of the SS1. OlloBot calls it the Red Heart. The detachable module has 16GB of RAM and 64GB of local storage. OlloBot says the module carries the robot's long-term memories and personalized information.

Now, imagine replacing the robot several years from now. Instead of starting over, OlloBot says you could move the Red Heart into a future-generation OlloBot. Family memories and personalized information could then follow you to the next device. That is a clever idea. Most gadgets become disposable once their hardware gets old. OlloBot wants the relationship you developed with this one to survive the upgrade.

At the same time, think about how personal that little module could become. Years of family life could potentially be tied to it. That makes the Red Heart something I would want protected every bit as carefully as the robot itself.
OlloNi SS1 privacy deserves a closer look

This is where I would slow down and read the fine print. OlloBot says the SS1 uses local encrypted processing and includes a physical camera cover. The company also says facial recognition and automatic family moment capture work with your permission.

Those are good things to see. Still, a robot that can move around your home, recognize faces and build memories over time deserves more than a quick glance at the privacy settings. OlloBot's current privacy policy was last updated July 6, 2026. It covers the company's store and broader services, including device and usage information collected when people interact with those services. The policy also says some information may be handled by outside vendors that provide services such as IT management, data analytics or cloud storage.

What I want to see next is something much more specific to the SS1 itself. If this robot can recognize your family and save moments inside your home, you should know exactly where that information goes. OlloBot should explain what stays on the Red Heart, what leaves the robot and how long anything gets stored.

I would also want a clear answer about deletion. If OlloNi spends years learning your routines and how your family interacts, you should be able to see what it knows and permanently erase that information when you want it gone.
AI WEARABLE WATCHES YOU TO PREDICT WHAT YOU NEED
OlloBot’s OlloNi SS1 uses a removable "Red Heart" memory module designed to transfer years of personalized memories to future robots. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
OlloBot's child privacy language needs clarification
There is another privacy point worth watching. OlloBot's Aug. 28 announcement lists children separated from their parents by distance among the potential users for the SS1.

Meanwhile, OlloBot's current privacy policy says its "services are not intended to be used by children." It also says the company does not knowingly collect personal information from children under the age of majority in the user's jurisdiction. That does not automatically mean there is a conflict.

The current policy appears geared largely toward OlloBot's store and broader services rather than offering a detailed privacy framework specifically for the SS1. Still, OlloBot should clarify how those terms apply when a product is designed to interact with families and potentially children inside the home. Parents should not have to guess.
What happens if someone gets your Red Heart?

This is one of the first questions I would ask about the Red Heart: What happens if you lose it? If your family has used OlloNi for years, that little removable module could contain a very personal history of life inside your home.

OlloBot says the SS1 uses local encrypted processing, which is encouraging. What I want to know is what happens when the Red Heart comes out of the robot. If someone finds or steals it, does the information remain encrypted and inaccessible? I would also want a way to remotely erase the module if it disappears.

The whole appeal of the Red Heart is that families could keep it for years and move their memories into a future OlloBot. If OlloBot wants us to hold onto something that personal for that long, I want to know exactly how it will keep those memories protected.
OlloNi also keeps track of its surroundings

OlloNi goes beyond watching the people around it. The robot also pays attention to what is happening inside the home. OlloBot says the SS1 includes temperature and humidity sensors along with ambient light and spatial sensors. That gives the robot more context about its surroundings. The company says those sensors can help with reminders and brief activity records tied to relevant interactions rather than continuous recording.
The OlloNi SS1 crowdfunding launch has been postponed
If all of this has you wondering what the robot costs, there is a catch. You cannot back the planned SS1 crowdfunding campaign right now.
OlloBot previously said it would launch the OlloNi SS1 globally on Kickstarter in August 2026. In July, the company narrowed that window to late August. Then the plan changed.

On Aug. 28, OlloBot announced that it had postponed the crowdfunding launch. The company pointed to recent changes in the U.S. regulatory and market access environment for robotic devices made abroad. OlloBot says it wants a clear path to market and fulfillment before moving forward.

For now, the company has not announced a new crowdfunding date. OlloBot says it will share an updated timeline through its official channels once one is confirmed. So, consider the SS1 a robot to watch rather than one you can order today.
What this means to you

OlloNi SS1 shows how quickly the idea of a home robot is changing. We have spent years watching robots get better at physical work. Now companies want these machines to learn about the people living around them. That changes what you need to consider before bringing one home.
With a robot like OlloNi, start by looking beyond the cute eyes. Find out what its camera records and who can access those recordings. Next, understand the memory system.

You should know what stays locally on the robot and what gets transmitted elsewhere. Also check whether you can permanently delete information when you want it gone. Remote access deserves attention too. Look for strong account security and controls that let you shut off features you do not use.

Finally, think about the lifespan of your data. The entire point of the Red Heart is to keep personalized information after you replace the robot. That makes long-term software support especially important.

We recently saw why connected robots deserve scrutiny when a security report raised concerns about a Yarbo robot mower. The issues involved remote access, cameras and home-network exposure. Yarbo later acknowledged the core technical findings and began rolling out fixes.

OlloBot has already said it uses local encrypted processing and includes a physical camera cover. Now I want to see the deeper security details behind those promises. We reached out to OlloBot with questions about data storage, remote access and Red Heart security but did not hear back before our deadline.
MAJORITY OF YOUNG ADULTS SAY THEY ARE 'MORE CONCERNED THAN EXCITED' ABOUT AI: PEW RESEARCH
The OlloNi SS1 can interpret facial expressions, tone of voice and behavioral patterns as it learns how people interact inside the home. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Kurt's key takeaways

OlloNi SS1 caught my attention because OlloBot wants this robot to become more personal the longer it lives with you. The Red Heart is the feature I keep coming back to. Instead of losing years of personalization when the hardware gets old, your family's memories could move into the next robot. I can see why that might feel special.

I can also see why some people will want the exact opposite. A robot that recognizes your family and captures private moments can learn a lot about what happens behind your front door. When those memories are designed to last for years, privacy becomes part of the buying decision from day one.

OlloBot's physical camera cover and local encrypted processing are good places to start. Before anyone hands over money, though, I want clearer answers about recordings and remote access. The company also needs to explain exactly what happens to information stored in the Red Heart. That does not make OlloNi a robot to fear. It makes it a robot that asks for a lot of trust.

title: 9 warning signs of identity theft you should never ignore
summary: Nine identity theft warning signs range from unfamiliar credit inquiries to SIM swap attacks that can quietly drain your bank account funds.
story: Cybercrime losses reached nearly $21 billion last year, prompting Kurt Knutsson to warn of increasingly sophisticated AI scams. He joins 'Fox & Friends Weekend' to break down the FBI data, highlighting that investment fraud alone cost victims $8.65 billion. Knutsson hosts a free live class to teach families how to protect their money and secure accounts.

Identity theft can start quietly. You may not see a drained bank account or a maxed-out credit card. The first warning could be a strange letter in the mail, an unfamiliar inquiry on your credit report or a password reset alert you never requested.

Those little clues are easy to brush off, but catching them early can give you more time to protect your money, credit and accounts. One unusual message does not automatically mean someone has stolen your identity, so do not panic. Instead, verify what happened and pay attention to anything else that looks out of place.
Here are nine identity theft warning signs you should never ignore.
CYBERCRIME LOSSES NEAR $21B: 5 WAYS TO PROTECT YOUR MONEY
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay
Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com

Identity theft can begin with subtle warning signs, including unfamiliar credit inquiries, password reset alerts, strange bills or unexpected account changes. (Ute Grabowsky/Photothek via Getty Images)
1) You receive a data breach notice
A company may contact you after discovering that customer information was exposed. The notice could come from a bank, retailer, employer, healthcare provider, insurer, school or another organization.

Read it carefully. Find out what information may have been involved, when the incident occurred and whether the company is offering steps such as password changes or credit monitoring. Save the notice with your other records.
A breach notice shows possible exposure, not confirmed identity theft. Still, it is a good reason to review your accounts and strengthen your security.
2) An unfamiliar credit inquiry appears
Check your credit reports for hard inquiries you do not recognize. A hard inquiry generally appears when a lender reviews your credit after you apply for credit.

Also look for new accounts, unfamiliar addresses, collections accounts or loans you never requested. Identity thieves may use stolen information to apply for credit before you notice anything unusual.
Check all three major credit bureaus rather than relying on a single report. Details can differ from one report to another, so reviewing only one may leave gaps.
If you find an inquiry or account that does not belong to you, contact the lender using a trusted phone number or website rather than contact information from a suspicious message.
3) You get bills or collection calls for accounts you never opened

A bill for a credit card, utility service, medical account or buy-now-pay-later purchase you did not make is a serious warning sign. So is a call from a debt collector about a debt that does not belong to you.
Do not ignore the notice simply because you believe it is a mistake. Ask the organization for details, dispute the account and keep copies of your correspondence.
Be cautious about sharing personal information with an unexpected caller. If you need to contact a company, find its official number independently.
4) Your bank, card or payment app shows unfamiliar activity

Review checking, savings, credit card, payment app, investment and retirement accounts regularly. Look for small test charges, unfamiliar withdrawals, new payees, password changes, profile updates or transfers you did not authorize.
Scammers sometimes begin with a small transaction to see whether an account is active. Other times, they try to take over the account entirely.

Contact the financial institution immediately through its official app, website or statement. Ask what steps are needed to secure the account, replace cards, investigate transactions and protect any linked accounts.
Turn on account alerts for purchases, transfers, password changes and other important activity. Alerts are useful, but they work best when you still review statements yourself.
5) A government notice does not match your activity

Pay attention to unexpected letters or online notices from the IRS, Social Security Administration or a state agency. Examples include a tax return you did not file, benefits you did not request or a claim connected to an employer you do not recognize.
Do not respond using a link or phone number in an unsolicited message. Visit the agency's official website or use a phone number from a statement or a previously verified account.
Keep every notice. Government-related identity theft can take time to resolve, and a clear record of dates and communications may help.
6) Your phone suddenly stops working or your number changes

A phone that unexpectedly loses service can have an innocent explanation, such as an outage or billing problem. But it can also be a sign that someone transferred your number to another device or took over your mobile account.

That is exactly what happened to Patricia Escriva, whose phone suddenly lost service before scammers used a SIM swap attack to get into her accounts and steal thousands of dollars. We broke down her story and what you can learn from it in The CyberGuy Report podcast: How hackers drain your bank account in minutes.

If your phone suddenly goes offline, and you cannot explain why, treat it as a warning sign. Contact your wireless provider right away from another phone and ask whether there was a recent SIM change, number transfer or account update. A SIM is the small card or digital profile that connects your phone to a mobile network.
Once your number is secure, review important accounts for password resets or login attempts. Ask your carrier about an account PIN or other protections against unauthorized changes.
HEALTHCARE DATA BREACH EXPOSES 3.75M PATIENT RECORDS

Unexpected bank activity, collection calls or government notices may signal identity theft and should be verified promptly through trusted channels. (Isabelle Souriment/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images)
7) You receive password reset or login alerts you did not request

An unexpected password reset email, multifactor authentication code or sign-in alert may mean that someone is trying to access an account. It may also be a fake message designed to trick you into clicking a link.

Do not share a verification code with anyone who calls or messages you. Open the account through its official app or type the website address yourself, then review recent activity and change the password if needed.

Start with your primary email account. Email often acts as the doorway to password resets for banking, shopping, healthcare and other services. Use a long, unique password and turn on multifactor authentication, which requires an extra verification step beyond your password.
Avoid reusing passwords. If one website is breached, a reused password may give criminals an opportunity to try the same combination elsewhere.
8) Your personal details suddenly appear in unusually convincing scams

A sudden wave of calls, texts or emails that use your correct name, address, family details or account information deserves attention. This does not prove identity theft, but it may indicate that personal data is circulating among scammers.

Be especially cautious when a message creates urgency, demands payment, asks for a verification code or tells you to move money to "protect" it. Banks, government agencies and legitimate companies do not need you to hand over a one-time code to keep your account safe.
Instead of replying, contact the organization through a trusted channel. Then review your accounts, credit reports and recent security alerts.
9) Your address, account profile or identity information changes without permission

An unfamiliar mailing address on a credit report, a changed email address on an account or a notification that your identity was verified somewhere you do not recognize can signal an attempted takeover.
Review account recovery information, authorized users, linked devices and connected apps. Remove anything you do not recognize and change the password from a trusted device.

If the change involves a bank, credit card, phone provider or government account, contact that organization promptly. A small profile change can be an early step in a larger attempt to control the account.
What to do if you spot one of these signs
First, slow down and verify the information. A suspicious text may be a scam, and a legitimate account alert may be the result of a family member's purchase or a forgotten subscription.
If the activity is confirmed, or you cannot explain it, take these important steps:
Use a trusted number or official app. Ask the organization to secure the account and investigate.

A credit freeze restricts access to your credit file, making it harder for someone to open new credit in your name. Place a freeze with all three major credit bureaus if appropriate for your situation.
A fraud alert asks lenders to take extra steps to verify your identity. It provides another layer of protection and works differently from a credit freeze.
Change important passwords, use a password manager to create and store strong, unique passwords, review recovery settings and add account protections through your wireless provider.
Check banking, credit cards, payment apps, investments, retirement, healthcare, utilities and government services.
Save breach notices, screenshots, dates, names, dispute numbers and copies of letters.

If you confirm that someone has used your identity, report it to the Federal Trade Commission at IdentityTheft.gov. The site will help you create an FTC Identity Theft Report and build a personalized recovery plan. You can also use that report when working with credit bureaus, businesses and debt collectors to dispute fraudulent accounts or information. Some companies may also ask for a police report.

If your information appears in a breach, you may not be able to remove it completely. Focus on making the exposed information less useful. Freeze your credit, secure your accounts, limit unnecessary public information and keep watching for new warning signs.
Where identity theft monitoring services fit

You can take many important steps to protect yourself, including checking your accounts, using unique passwords and freezing your credit. An identity theft monitoring service can add another layer by watching for signs that your personal or financial information may be misused.

Depending on the service and plan you choose, monitoring can include credit reports, checking and savings accounts, investments and 401(k) accounts, bank account takeovers, home title changes, phone takeovers, identity verification, dark web exposure, data breaches and social media activity.

That broader monitoring can be helpful because identity theft can show up in more places than your credit report. If fraud occurs, restoration support may also help reduce the burden of dealing with calls, paperwork and disputes.

Monitoring works best as an added layer of protection rather than a replacement for good security habits. Continue reviewing your accounts, watching for unusual activity and acting quickly when something looks wrong. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at Cyberguy.com
NEW BANK SCAM LAWS COULD STOP SUSPICIOUS PAYMENTS
A phone that suddenly loses service could signal a SIM swap, potentially giving criminals access to accounts tied to the victim’s phone number. (Celine Frohnapfel/picture alliance via Getty Images)
Kurt's key takeaways

Identity theft often gives you warning signs before serious damage is done. A strange charge, an account you do not recognize or even a password reset alert you never requested can be your cue to take a closer look. Trust your gut when something feels off, verify what happened and act quickly to lock down your accounts and credit.

A few minutes spent checking now could save you a much bigger headache later. The key is to stay alert without living in fear. Keep an eye on your accounts, use strong security protections and know what steps to take if your information ends up in the wrong hands.

title: ‘I’m coming home’: Last words haunt a 9/11 daughter 25 years later as she builds a legacy in his honor
summary: Kayla Fallon Smith lost her father in the 9/11 World Trade Center attacks at age 8 and now runs a nonprofit offering equine therapy to veterans.
story: 25 years after losing her father at Cantor Fitzgerald, Kayla Smith opens up about her final morning phone call with him and the equine-assisted therapy program she built to help others heal from trauma.
"I'm getting out. I'm coming home."
Those were the final words of William Lawrence Fallon Jr. before he was killed in the 9/11 terrorist attacks on the World Trade Center 25 years ago.
He worked as an IT manager for Cantor Fitzgerald and was just 38 years old when he was killed.
I LOST MY WIFE ON 9/11. PLEASE LET THIS 25TH ANNIVERSARY BELONG TO THE FAMILIES
An old photo shows Kayla Smith and her sister posing with their father, William Lawrence Fallon Jr. (Kayla Smith)
His daughter Kayla Fallon Smith was 8 years old when she learned her father would not be coming home.
Before the attacks, Smith, now 33, said her father – who always commuted into work early – would call the house phone in the morning to wish her and her sister well before they would head to school.
📩 Send me a story idea: kelsie.cairns@fox.com
📸 Instagram: kelsiecairns_tv
🎥 Facebook: Kelsie Cairns
He went in early so he could leave earlier in the afternoons to take her to dancing school after her school day.

"That was the kind of man he was. I remember he would get up and work out in the morning before even going to work, so you'd hear the weights dropping in the house. I do remember that as a kid," Smith said.
Those quick and light-hearted morning phone calls to his daughters set the tone for the day.
Kayla Smith and her late father pose for a photo on the beach. (Kayla Smith)
"He would tell us what the skyline looked like. Sometimes it would be cloudy below him and he couldn't even see the street, but it'd be sunny up there," she said.
FRANK SILLER: 'I LOVE YOU, BROTHER' -- THE 9/11 LOSS THAT INSPIRED A MISSION OF SERVICE
Smith remembers hearing her father's voice for the last time on Tuesday, Sept. 11, 2001.
Kayla Smith and her father pose for a lakeside photo on a boat. (Kayla Smith)
"I spoke to him on the house phone that day, as I always did," she said, to which he said on the phone, "Have a good morning," she said.
"I'm sure I said something like, 'I love you, have a great day'," Smith said.
Her dad called again that fateful morning – sometime after the first tower was hit.
SALVATION ARMY RESPONDER OPENS UP ON 9/11 CANCER BATTLE, PHONE CALL THAT CHANGED HIS LIFE
This time, her mother answered the phone.
"He said something to the degree of, 'I'm getting out, I'm coming home,' and that was it," she said.
Smith's mother replied and said, "What are you talking about?" He responded and said, "Turn on the news."
After that he hung up.
9/11 DEATH TOLL KEEPS GROWING DECADES LATER AS TOXIC EXPOSURE HAUNTS SURVIVORS
His family never heard from him again.
William Lawrence Fallon Jr., 38, was an employee at Cantor Fitzgerald when he was killed. (Getty Images: MediaNews Group; Kayla Smith)
"Those words haunt me a little bit," Smith said. "Every year, grief is different. It doesn't go away. It's a myth when people say that time heals all wounds; it doesn't."
In the last 25 years of growing up without her father, Smith has turned her pain and grief into purpose. She's devoted her life to helping others living with grief and mental struggles.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

Smith is a licensed mental health counselor who founded Trails of Purpose – a nonprofit organization that provides free mental health counseling and equine-assisted therapy to military members, veterans, first responders and their families.
"As I was getting my graduate degree, I started to experience equine-assisted therapy, and I really—it just clicked for me," she said.
William Lawrence Fallon Jr. holds his daughter Kayla Smith. (Kayla Smith)
She went on to say, "I never experienced that as a kid, and I had a lot of trauma therapy growing up. The resources were abundant for 9/11 victims, and I never experienced equine therapy."
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS
She started her organization in 2019.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE
"I needed a place to just be when my brain always felt on fire. I think I've created that, and it's seeming to resonate with other people."
William Lawrence Fallon Jr. is one of the thousands of names engraved at the National September 11th Memorial reflecting pools. (Kayla Smith)
SEND US A TIP
Trails of Purpose has offered 30,000 hours of free mental health counseling and equine-assisted therapy to military members and first responders.
GOT A TIP?
"The horses, and the connection that they have when when words don't seem to to come, the horses can just be with you," she said.

"I created the thing that I think I needed: community and understanding, and a place that's safe, and quiet, and a respite," she said.

As she helps others heal, Smith said she'll never stop sharing her father's story.

title: Charlie Kirk supporters return to site of assassination 1 year later: ‘We are still standing’
summary: Turning Point USA returned to Utah Valley University to reclaim the space where Charlie Kirk was assassinated, unveiling a new statue in his honor.
story: Sage Lloyd says students who witnessed Kirk’s assassination refused to walk away or be silenced as a new statue was unveiled.

One year after Charlie Kirk was assassinated at Utah Valley University, the people who stood feet from him when he was killed returned to the campus Thursday night in what Turning Point USA (TPUSA) described as a deliberate effort to "reclaim" the space in his honor.

"We’re doing an event in Utah right now at UVU, a deliberate act reclaiming that space in his honor and for his legacy," TPUSA spokesman and "The Charlie Kirk Show" Executive Producer Andrew Kolvet told Fox News host Jesse Watters Thursday night.
Andrew Sypher, TPUSA’s chief field officer, told the gathering at UVU in Orem that he had been standing about 10 feet to Kirk’s left when the fatal shot rang out on Sept. 10, 2025.
CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSINATION: NEW UVU PRESIDENT SAYS IT WILL CONTINUE TO ‘HOST THE FRAYS,’ EMBRACE FREE SPEECH
A view of the location where Charlie Kirk was shot one year ago. (Alec Thornock for Fox News Digital)
"Steps from these doors is the ground where evil unfolded," Sypher said. "We did not come back to rehearse the crime scene."
Instead, Sypher said, they returned because "this is where they tried to end him" and "this is where we refuse to let the last word be a gunshot."
ERIKA KIRK URGES CONSERVATIVE STUDENTS NOT TO BACK DOWN IN FIRST SCHOOL YEAR SINCE CHARLIE'S ASSASSINATION
For the students of UVU’s TPUSA chapter, the anniversary marked a return to the campus where some witnessed Kirk’s assassination.
"A year ago, our lives changed forever," chapter President Sage Lloyd told the crowd.
Lloyd said students experienced "fear, grief, confusion, and heartbreak" and had every reason to walk away.
INSIDE CHARLIE KIRK’S EFFORT TO DEVELOP THE NEXT GENERATION OF CONSERVATIVE VOICES

People gather around a large wooden cross on a grass lawn in a campus courtyard at Utah Valley University in Orem, Utah, Thursday. Turning Point USA hosted its "Freedom Built to Last" memorial service to mark the first anniversary of founder Charlie Kirk's death at the courtyard site. (Getty Images)
"We could have packed our bags. We could have stepped away," she said.
Despite the tragedy, the TPUSA chapter stayed.
"The same students who witnessed a political assassination are willing to stand up, speak out and keep moving forward," Lloyd said.
"We can let it define us through fear, or we can let it strengthen us through courage," she added. "The Turning Point chapter at UVU has made our decision, and we chose courage."
Sypher also revealed what he said was a text Kirk sent him on the morning he was assassinated.
SURVEILLANCE VIDEO TIMELINE TRACKS ACCUSED CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSIN ACROSS UVU CAMPUS BEFORE FATAL ROOFTOP SHOT

Floral tributes and a prayer vigil sign are placed next to large concrete planters at Utah Valley University in Orem, Utah, Thursday, at the exact campus location where Turning Point USA founder Charlie Kirk was fatally shot one year ago. (Getty Images)
"Andrew, I’m not here to pick a fight. I am here to show them kindness," Kirk wrote, according to Sypher.
"That was the assignment this time," Sypher said. "To talk with students who hate you. To share the truth, and to not become cruel doing it."
Soon afterward, Kirk was fatally shot.
"Charlie’s assassination did not put our faith to death," Sypher told the crowd. "It woke it up."
The service was marked with worship performances and video tributes to the fallen conservative leader, as well as an unveiling of a new statue to stay on campus at UVU.
ERIKA KIRK PENS ESSAY ON GRIEF AS READERS GAIN INSIGHTS INTO WRENCHING PAST YEAR
Kirk’s widow, Erika Kirk, separately marked the anniversary with a black-and-white photograph from their wedding showing the couple holding hands.
Across the image were two words: "...until Heaven."

The university closed its campus for the one-year anniversary. UVU itself did not organize the memorial, but university President Dr. Jon Anderson previously told Fox News Digital the school supported TPUSA using campus space for its event.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Lloyd closed her remarks with a message about what returning to UVU meant for Kirk’s student movement.
"Our chapter is still here, we are still speaking, and we are nowhere near done," she said. "And that is how his voice lives on."
Fox News Digital's Michael Ruiz contributed to this reporting.
Jasmine Baehr is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital, where she covers politics, the military, legal debates surrounding life and family policy, as well as faith and culture.

title: Juror on Lindsay Clancy trial says 'we let down Lindsay' following mistrial
summary: A Lindsay Clancy trial juror says the jury "let down Lindsay" after a lone holdout prevented a unanimous not guilty verdict in Massachusetts.
story: Fox News national correspondent Bryan Llenas sits down with defense attorney Kevin Reddington to discuss the mistrial in the Lindsay Clancy case and Reddington’s motion seeking a not guilty finding by reason of insanity.
A juror on the high-profile Lindsay Clancy murder trial in Massachusetts said she believes the jury "let down Lindsay" and that it was "hard to separate the children from what our task was."

Clancy was on trial for strangling and killing her three young children in January 2023 after sending her then-husband, Patrick, out to pick up medication and takeout. When he returned, he found Clancy injured outside after an apparent suicide attempt and the children unconscious in the basement. Two children died that night, while the third was airlifted to a Boston hospital and died several days later.

The trial ended in a mistrial last week after the jury failed to reach a unanimous verdict. Eleven jurors sided with finding Clancy not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility — Massachusetts’ version of an insanity defense — while one holdout favored finding her criminally responsible.

"Everybody says you're not supposed to feel like you failed, but you have a task to come out unanimous. And we tried everything we could to get to that end. And I feel like we let down Lindsay," Paula, 65, who was one of the jurors who sided with the majority, told WCVB.
LINDSAY CLANCY LAWYER SAYS HE PLANS NEW MOTION TO DISMISS AFTER JURORS SPEAK OUT ON MISTRIAL: REPORT
A juror on the high-profile Lindsay Clancy trial in Massachusetts said she believes the jury "let down Lindsay." (Greg Derr/Pool The Patriot Ledger via AP)

Clancy's legal team did not dispute that she killed her children but argued that she should not be found criminally responsible because she was suffering from postpartum psychosis. Clancy also admitted in court filings to killing her three children, but claimed that severe mental illness left her not criminally responsible.

Paula said the jury's majority believed that Clancy needed help and that the healthcare system failed her, adding that she thinks the medical community should do more to support women with postpartum mental health issues.

"There was a clear indication that the medical community failed her and not just her, but her whole family, because something like that affects the whole entire family. And if everybody can be educated in a better way, then it will help the whole family unit," Paula said.

After attorneys made their arguments, Paula said the jurors were sent to deliberate with 297 pieces of evidence, including Patrick's emotional 911 call, which she said some jurors had trouble listening to during deliberations.
"We all tried to help each other. It was hard to separate the children from what our task was, and it was very emotional," she said.

The jurors polled themselves at the start of deliberations, at which point eight believed Clancy was not guilty due to lack of criminal responsibility, two thought she was guilty and two were undecided, Paula said.
The majority eventually came to the belief that Clancy was not guilty due to lack of criminal responsibility.

Lindsay Clancy's legal team did not dispute that she killed her children but argued that she should not be found criminally responsible because she was suffering from postpartum psychosis. (Boston Globe via Getty Images)
Prosecutors argued during trial that Clancy was criminally responsible for the killings despite evidence that she suffered from mental illness.
"We did not start out 11 to one," Paula said. "Everybody had different opinions and different reasons and different ways that they got there."
Paula said the majority had a hard time understanding why the one holdout wanted to vote to convict Clancy.

"We did not feel that he was following the law because he admitted that he had doubt at different times, that he had doubt about the case that was presented, and the way that the rule read to all the rest of us is if we had doubt, then we could not convict her of first-degree murder or second-degree murder or manslaughter," Paula said.
The foreperson then sent a note to the judge saying the jury could not reach a verdict and accusing the holdout of refusing to apply the law on reasonable doubt.
Judge William Sullivan called up each of the jurors and individually asked them if they could apply the law as he had explained it, and they reportedly answered in the affirmative.
"The judge has to believe that people are telling him the truth. And so, you know, 11 people told the truth and one maybe didn't. And I will never know why," Paula said.
Paula said she believed it would have been worth restarting deliberations with an alternate if the court had removed the holdout.
Lindsay Clancy was on trial for strangling and killing her three young children in January 2023 after sending her then-husband, Patrick, out to pick up medication and takeout. (Pool)
ACCUSED NC KILLER MOM PLANS INSANITY DEFENSE — AS RETIRED JUDGE SAYS MORE MAY FOLLOW LINDSAY CLANCY STRATEGY
"If our holdout juror had given us evidence to support his reasoning, we would have felt differently about what we told the judge," Paula said.
Other jurors have also spoken out in recent days to take issue with the holdout's position.
"He had the hardest time getting off the fact that Lindsay viciously killed her children," juror Kellie Farina previously told NBC10 Boston.

On Thursday, Clancy's defense filed a motion arguing the prosecution failed to meet its burden and asked the judge to enter a required finding of not guilty, which the defense argues would prevent a retrial.

title: Patrol sergeant accused of murdering sheriff’s captain in yearslong romantic dispute over woman they dated
summary: Sgt. Nekime Matu Oxendine is accused of fatally shooting Cumberland County Sheriff’s Capt. Adam Bean after a confrontation outside a woman’s home.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A North Carolina highway patrol sergeant has been indicted in the murder of a sheriff’s captain following a years-long romantic dispute involving a woman both officers dated, according to authorities.

North Carolina State Highway Patrol Sgt. Nekime Matu Oxendine, 44, reportedly shot Cumberland County Sheriff’s Capt. Adam Bean on March 27 outside the woman’s home in Hope Mills following a confrontation between the two men, according to authorities and CityView.
Police arrived to find the woman, Tara Lynn Whitman, performing CPR on Bean as Oxendine remained nearby, according to search warrant filings. Bean was pronounced dead at the scene, officials said.
The fatal shooting followed years of escalating tension surrounding Whitman’s relationships with both men, state investigators wrote in court filings.
FORMER COLLEAGUES DETAIL CHP CAPTAIN’S SPIRAL BEFORE ALLEGED MURDER-FOR-HIRE PLOT AGAINST HUSBAND
Cumberland County Sheriff’s Capt. Adam Bean was fatally shot on March 27 following a domestic confrontation. (Cumberland County Sheriff's Office)
According to investigators, Oxendine had displayed persistent jealousy and insecurity over the years regarding Whitman’s connection to Bean.
According to the warrant, Whitman began dating Bean in 2022 after ending a long-term relationship with Oxendine. She eventually ended that relationship and returned to Oxendine.
FLORIDA DEPUTY KILLED EX-GIRLFRIEND OVER A TV, THEN HIMSELF, SHERIFF SAYS

While Whitman was with Bean, Oxendine appeared to exhibit increasingly concerning behavior, according to text messages cited in the warrant. Whitman and Bean had described some of his behavior as "stalking," documents reported.
"I seen u have been talking to Adam!!! Best wishes!!!" Oxendine wrote in one message.
"Better tell that Mother F—er to get ready too!!! " he added.
Oxendine also sent messages questioning Whitman’s decision to stay with Bean, demanding to know the truth and claiming he knew where Bean lived, according to the warrant.
In December 2025, Whitman eventually resumed her romantic relationship with Oxendine, moving out of the home she shared with Bean.

FILE — The Cumberland County Jail building is pictured in North Carolina. Cumberland County Sheriff’s Capt. Adam Bean was fatally shot following a romantic dispute, authorities said. (Derek Davis/Portland Press Herald via Getty Images)

For the next three months, however, Oxendine continued to show insecurity over Bean, asking Whitman whether Bean was more attractive and accusing him of having the power to "lure u in and out of my life on demand." He also sought continued reassurance about Whitman’s commitment, according to the warrant
Then, on the night of March 27, Bean asked Whitman to come to his residence after work to talk. Whitman initially agreed but later stopped responding to his messages.
When Whitman did not show up, Bean messaged her, "F— it, I’ll come to you," and threatened to blow his car horn and cause a scene if she did not come outside.
When Bean arrived, he became irate after seeing Oxendine’s vehicle parked outside, according to the warrant.
Oxendine stepped outside and fired about two warning shots into the ground. Bean continued advancing toward him, and Oxendine then opened fire two to three more times, according to the warrant.
Bean collapsed onto his back in the yard, according to the warrant. Police said they found a handgun and magazine nearby.
Oxendine has been charged with first-degree murder.

FILE — A North Carolina State Highway Patrol vehicle drives through high water. Sgt. Nekime Matu Oxendine, a state highway patrol sergeant, was indicted in Bean’s killing. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Bean had served with the Cumberland County Sheriff’s Office for 20 years and most recently served as assistant chief of detectives with the rank of captain.
He was posthumously recognized with the Merit Award for his outstanding service, forward-thinking leadership, initiative and lasting contributions to the Cumberland County Sheriff’s Office.
Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

title: Family of critically missing DC mother says police still treating home as active crime scene
summary: Antoinette Forbes' sister says alarming discoveries inside the Washington, D.C., home prompted police to reclassify her as critically missing.
story: Antoinette Forbes' sister says family friends found her dog alone inside the home with her phones, wallet and car left behind after she disappeared.

The sister of a Washington, D.C., mother who vanished last week said a series of alarming discoveries inside her home immediately signaled something was wrong as police continue investigating her disappearance after reclassifying her case as a critically missing person.

Antoinette Forbes, 53, was last seen around 3 p.m. Friday at her home in the 3200 block of Nebraska Avenue NW, according to the Metropolitan Police Department. Police are asking anyone with information about her whereabouts to come forward.

According to family friend Elizabeth Northrup, police initially classified Forbes as a missing person before reclassifying her as critically missing in less than 24 hours. Under Metropolitan Police Department guidelines, a critically missing person is someone believed to be in danger or facing life-threatening circumstances.
"I knew immediately something was wrong," Forbes' sister, Aileen Forbes, told Fox News Digital.
'WONDERFUL' CA NURSE AND MOTHER VANISHES AFTER GOING TO CASINO, CAR FOUND ABANDONED AT MOUNTAIN PARK: FAMILY
Antoinette Forbes stands beside her son in Washington, D.C., in an undated family photo provided by her family. Her son has been blurred to protect his identity. (Aileen Forbes)
The sisters had spoken over FaceTime on Saturday morning while making plans to visit their mother in Florida over the holidays.
"It was just a fairly ordinary check-in with my sister, with whom I have regular contact — daily contact by text or on FaceTime," Aileen said. "We were just talking about our plans for the holidays."

By Labor Day, Aileen said she had tested positive for COVID-19 and texted her sister because she has an underlying health condition that can make the illness more dangerous. When repeated texts and FaceTime calls went unanswered, she grew concerned.
She contacted close family friends who live near Antoinette's Washington home. The friends, who had a key to the house, entered the home and immediately noticed several troubling signs.
FAMILY CHECKS LAS VEGAS MORGUES IN DESPERATE SEARCH FOR MISSING NEW YORK GRANDMOTHER
Antoinette Forbes smiles while wearing a navy blue baseball cap in an undated photo provided by her family. (Aileen Forbes)
"The text I got from Margarita ... I think something happened to me that made my heart stop," Aileen said.

The friends found Antoinette's dog, Max, alone inside the home after he had gone to the bathroom indoors, suggesting he had been left alone for some time, Aileen said. Her car remained in the driveway, while her phones and wallet were still inside the house.
The family immediately contacted police.
Aileen said investigators have told the family the home is being treated as an active crime scene and that no one, including relatives, has been allowed inside.
NEW DETAILS REVEAL MARRIAGE IN CRISIS BEFORE ANA WALSHE MURDER CASE IN FOX NATION SPECIAL

A Metropolitan Police Department missing person poster asks the public for help locating Antoinette Forbes, who was last seen Sept. 4, 2026, in Northwest Washington, D.C. (Metropolitan Police Department)
"No one has access to Antoinette's home, not even me," Aileen said. "In some ways, it's my home too, and I have not been able to step foot in it."
She said detectives have not provided significant updates but have remained in contact with the family and continue accepting information that could aid the investigation.
"I know that they have been working tirelessly since Monday afternoon ... around the clock," Aileen said.
Aileen said nothing about her sister's life suggested she would voluntarily disappear.
"Antoinette has a full, rich life," she said. "She's an incredibly successful woman professionally, personally. She's a happy woman."
She described her sister as a devoted mother whose world revolved around her 10-year-old son, Nathan, and the family's dog, Max.

Asked what she would say if her sister could hear her, Aileen responded, "Antoinette, you know how much we love you. You know who loves you. Keep the faith. We are not going to give up. We are going to bring you home."

Police describe Forbes as 5 feet, 2 inches tall, weighing approximately 115 pounds, with black hair and brown eyes. Anyone with information about her whereabouts is urged to contact the Metropolitan Police Department.
