title: Vance positions himself as a fighter for family values and a ‘national birthright’
summary: The vice president drew on the birth of his fourth child and the one-year anniversary of Charlie Kirk’s death in his GOP midterm convention speech.
story: DALLAS — Vice President JD Vance on Thursday offered his young family — in particular, his newborn son — as a model and a window to the future that the potential 2028 presidential contender envisions for America.
In a speech here at the Republicans’ midterm convention, Vance broadly criticized Democrats who he said do not share his values.

He also homed in specifically on two Democratic candidates this fall in Michigan: Senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed and Will Lawrence, who is seeking a House seat. Vance seized on Lawrence’s since-deleted social media posts that were critical of the nuclear family.

“I’ve thought a lot, ladies and gentlemen, about what is the birthright of this newest of Americans, my little boy,” Vance told the crowd at American Airlines Center. “And I think about what the Democrats have said about our shared birthright as Americans or, frankly, the lack thereof.”

He added a moment later, “To the radicals who wish to abolish my family and the thousands and millions of other families all across our country, we have a simple message for them: Stay the hell away from our kids!”

Vance’s speech on the convention’s closing night represented something of an unofficial passing of the torch from the term-limited Trump to his 42-year-old vice president, who is seen as a leading candidate for president in two years. At one point, the audience broke out with chants of “48! 48!” Vance would be the 48th president if he succeeds Trump.

“We’ve got to take care of business this November,” Vance replied, sticking to his common refrain when he is confronted with speculation about his White House ambitions. “Then we’ll worry about what comes next.”

Later, in a moment that captured the unique dynamic of playing understudy to a president who relishes being the center of attention, Vance passed the torch back. Trump, who spoke for an hour and 45 minutes the night before, returned to the stage for closing remarks that lasted about 25 minutes.

While Trump’s words Wednesday and Thursday effectively made the midterms a referendum on his time in office, Vance offered a more forward-looking case that at times scanned as his case for what should come next.
“I can’t help but think about what it is that we’re fighting for and what it is that we want for all of our children,” Vance said. “What I want for my family, I want for your family, too.”

He added: “This country was handed down to us by our parents and their parents before them. We received this national birthright, and we are going to fight for it by electing Republicans this November.”

A person close to Vance told NBC News that he will begin giving a White House bid more serious thought after the November elections and is not necessarily expected to reach or announce an immediate decision. Republicans routinely mention Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio as Trump’s two likeliest successors. Rubio, who ran for president in 2016, has said he does not plan to run and has signaled that Vance will have his support if he does.

Another potential 2028 contender, Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, spoke during Thursday’s convention program. He focused his remarks tightly on 2026 races, leveling criticism at Democratic Senate candidates such as El-Sayed and Texas state Rep. James Talarico.

“As one Democrat president put it long ago, before his party had lost their ever-loving minds, we have a rendezvous with destiny,” Cruz said, invoking Franklin Roosevelt. “Together, we must stand and fight for the Constitution. We must stand and fight for freedom. We must stand and defeat the communists. We must stand and defeat the Islamists.”

Cruz, who also ran in 2016, has made several moves over the last year to position himself against Vance. Those moves have not escaped Vance’s notice. When he was asked at a White House briefing last week about Cruz’s prospects, Vance offered a sarcastic reply: “Clearly, Ted is a very authentic and likable guy, and I’m sure he’ll do great.”

Vance, like others who spoke Thursday, also used his speech to reflect on his friendship with conservative activist Charlie Kirk on the first anniversary of his assassination. He offered a message to Kirk’s two young children.
“I hope that one day they will watch and they will know and they will understand what I’m trying to say to them tonight,” Vance said. “History will record that your father was a great man.”
At another point, Vance was briefly interrupted by what he said was a protester waving Mexico’s flag.
“Well, my friend,” Vance responded, “if you love Mexico so much, get your ass over there. I’ll buy you the plane ticket.”
Add to Google
Add to Google
Vance, known for his conservative populism, also made overtures to more moderate and independent voters.

“Look, I’m not asking anybody to agree with me on every single issue. I’m not asking anybody to agree on every single policy of the administration,” he said. “What I am asking you to do is to recognize the contrast with the radicals and recognize the achievements of the last 18 months. We have done a lot, my friends, and we can do a lot more if we fight together.”

Vance reserved his vitriol for Democrats and the progressive left. He went on an extended riff against El-Sayed, who last month mockingly wondered whether Vance would take his Indian American wife, Usha Vance, back in time to meet his late grandfather. Vance also alluded to El-Sayed’s alliance with Hasan Piker, a Twitch streamer who previously said on a livestream that “America deserved 9/11.” Piker has since apologized for the remark, which has become a staple of Republican campaigning this year.

“This is who the Democrats are now,” Vance said. “They’re the party that can find sympathy for the terrorists who perpetrated 9/11, but they say that people with names like James Vance are incapable of loving people with names like Usha. And they couldn’t be more wrong.”
Known previously for a bestselling memoir that chronicled his rough childhood, Vance has been on a fast political rise since he won a Senate seat in Ohio in 2022.

Just days after he survived an assassination attempt in 2024, Trump selected him over Rubio and others to be his running mate, opening doors that have helped position Vance as an heir apparent. Vance is the Republican National Committee’s finance chair — an unprecedented move for a sitting vice president that has given him an opportunity to connect with big-money donors who can be helpful to his political career.

On Thursday, for example, Vance headlined an RNC fundraiser here that brought in $2 million, two people familiar with the event said. He also headlined a breakfast for conventiongoers from Michigan, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, Ohio and Hawaii. Another speaker at that event, Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, referred to Vance’s backstory and explicitly promoted him as a 2028 candidate.

“Every single study would have told you that that kid will probably not make it in life. And what is he today? The vice president of the United States,” said Moreno, whose remarks were heard by NBC News before an organizer told a reporter to leave the event, which was not intended to be open to media.
“I think there’s a chance,” Moreno added, “that in two years when we’re together again for a convention that we’ll be nominating him as the next president.”

Moreno, who supported Rubio’s 2016 campaign for president, said Vance is his first choice for president and that he, like others, does not believe Rubio would run against him. Moreno, noting the recent birth of Vance’s fourth child, also said he believes he will take his time to make a decision.

“I think he’s going to do a lot of soul-searching,” Moreno said. “He does have four little kids. Being president of the United States is not a small job. It is soul-sucking. Running for president is beyond comprehension.”
Moreno added, “If he calls me and asks if he should run, I’d say, ‘Hell yes, and how can I help?’”

In other conversations around the convention, Vance’s and Rubio’s names topped the lists of many delegates and party leaders when they were asked whom they could see at the top of the 2028 ticket. Others took more of a wait-and-see approach.

“You know, I can name, you know, half a dozen people that are great, starting with our vice president, our secretary of state, numerous governors and senators,” said Vince Galko, a former top official at the Pennsylvania Republican Party. “We have a spoil of riches right now and a great bench to pull from.”

title: Organizers of Hong Kong’s Tiananmen Square vigils sentenced in national security case
summary: Three pro-democracy activists in Hong Kong who organized annual vigils for victims of China’s 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown were sentenced Friday under a national security law that critics say has stifled dissent.
story: HONG KONG — Three pro-democracy activists in Hong Kong who organized annual vigils for victims of China’s 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown were sentenced to prison terms between five and over seven years Friday after being convicted under a national security law that critics say has stifled dissent in the Chinese territory.

Lee Cheuk-yan was sentenced to seven years in prison, while Chow Hang-tung was sentenced to seven years and three months. Both had pleaded not guilty to charges of inciting subversion under the Beijing-imposed law.
A third defendant, Albert Ho, 74, was sentenced to five years and two months after pleading guilty, which can result in a shorter sentence.
Both Lee and Chow, who have been in custody continuously since they were charged five years ago, had pleaded for reduced sentences after the verdict. They had faced a maximum of 10 years in prison.

All three were leaders of the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China, which for three decades held annual candlelight vigils in honor of those who were killed on June 4, 1989, in a Chinese military crackdown on pro-democracy protesters in and around Beijing’s Tiananmen Square. The vigils, which drew tens of thousands of people a year, were the only large-scale public commemoration on Chinese soil of the Tiananmen crackdown, discussion of which is heavily censored in mainland China.
The alliance itself, which was also convicted, was fined 1.5 million Hong Kong dollars ($190,000) as part of the sentencing.

The trial, which began in January, was heard by three government-appointed judges who ruled last month that the alliance’s longtime call to “end one-party dictatorship” in China was an unlawful form of incitement to overthrow the country’s ruling Communist Party.

The United States, along with many other Western governments and the United Nations, condemned the Aug. 21 verdict as a further sign of Hong Kong’s deteriorating freedom of expression. The Tiananmen vigils “sought only to remember the past and honor the lives lost in that assault,” Assistant Secretary of State Riley Barnes said in a post on X.

During the trial, Lee, 69, a former lawmaker, told the court that the alliance was not calling to eliminate the Communist Party, but rather to allow the Chinese public to decide who governs them through free and fair elections.
The judges said the defendants were not being tried over their political views.
Chow, 41, a barrister who represented herself in court, said in her mitigation statement that the 206-page verdict “boils down to saying that pursuing democracy is a crime.”
“Believing that dictatorship is wrong and democracy is right — if that isn’t a belief, then what is?” she said.
Chow added that she had “no regrets” about her activism, saying she “would rather be a criminal than a person who betrays their conscience.”

Hong Kong, a former British colony, returned to Chinese rule in 1997 with the promise that its civil liberties would be preserved for at least 50 years. But residents of the once-freewheeling city have seen their freedoms significantly eroded since Beijing imposed a controversial 2020 national security law, which has also been used to jail other pro-democracy activists such as former media tycoon Jimmy Lai.

title: Singer D4vd sued by parents of teen girl he is accused of killing
summary: Celeste Rivas Hernandez’s parents are suing the singer D4vd, accusing him of wrongful death after he was charged in the 14-year-old girl’s murder.
story: Celeste Rivas Hernandez’s parents are suing the singer D4vd, accusing him of wrongful death after he was charged in the 14-year-old girl’s murder.
Mercedes Martinez and Jesus Rivas are also suing D4vd’s mother and managers, accusing them of negligence. D4vd’s real name is David Anthony Burke.

The lawsuit, filed Thursday in Los Angeles County Superior Court, outlines much of the evidence presented at a multiday evidentiary hearing in July about the pair’s relationship, which prosecutors said began when Celeste was 13 and ended after she threatened to expose him. Text messages revealed at the hearing showed that she had gotten pregnant by Burke and had an abortion.

Her decomposed and dismembered remains were found in September 2025 in the front trunk of Burke’s Tesla at a Los Angeles impound lot. Prosecutors said the car had been left on a street near his home and impounded at Hollywood Tow after someone reported an abandoned vehicle.

Burke, 21, was arrested in April at a house in the Hollywood Hills neighborhood, Los Angeles police said. He has pleaded not guilty to charges of murder, continuous sexual abuse of a child under the age of 14 and unlawful mutilation of human remains. He remains in custody awaiting trial.

The lawsuit accuses Burke of using his position of authority to “influence and control” Celeste, “including by providing her a concealed cellular telephone to maintain contact outside her parents’ knowledge, using false identities, and arranging and paying for her travel.”

The suit says that on the night she died in April 2025, Burke sent an Uber vehicle to pick her up from her family’s home in Lake Elsinore in Riverside County. After she arrived at his home in the Hollywood Hills, Burke stabbed her, prosecutors allege. Prosecutors said he used chain saws to cut her body apart in his garage.

Celeste’s parents say in the lawsuit that because of the decomposition, they had to wait more than a week after her remains were found for an identification and that some parts of the body were never recovered.

The suit accuses Burke of wrongful death, as well as battery, sexual battery, childhood sexual assault, assault, false imprisonment, human trafficking and intentional infliction of emotional distress. It also alleges that Burke engaged in human trafficking by causing or inducing Celeste “to engage in commercial sex acts.”

“The money, food, shelter, designer gifts, travel, a ring, and a promise of future marriage that Burke gave to Decedent were given on account of the sexual acts, satisfying the commercial-sex-act element,” the suit says. “Because Decedent was a minor, neither her purported consent nor any mistakes as to her age is a defense.”

Burke’s publishing and merchandising companies are also named as defendants in the lawsuit, which claims they were the vehicles that helped fund the alleged abuse. Listed as co-defendants are Josh Marshall and Robert Morgenroth, Burke’s managers; their company, Mogul Vision; and Burke’s live-in security guard, who the suit alleges drove him to pick up Celeste from her parents’ home in 2024.

The suit also lists Burke’s mother, Colleen Burke, as a co-defendant and says she approved and funded “arrangements that housed Decedent and enabled Burke’s access to her.” All co-defendants are accused of failing to protect a minor and negligence.

It was not immediately clear whether Burke had an attorney representing him in the lawsuit. Contact information could not be found for Burke’s companies or his security guard. Marshall, the owner of Mogul Vision, which employed Morgenroth, did not immediately respond to a request for comment on behalf of himself, the company or Morgenroth. Messages left at numbers believed to be associated with Morgenroth and Colleen Burke were not immediately returned.
The suit requests a jury trial.
Celeste’s parents asked for the death penalty this week.

“If the death penalty were activated, it would be perfect for this kind of human being, devoid of feelings ... and without conscience, who only caused pain to our daughter, our family, and the world that supports our precious daughter,” they said in a statement on what would have been Celeste’s 16th birthday.

title: Two researchers who left Anthropic and Google warn AI could become ‘uncontrollable’
summary: After Jacob Coxon roiled the AI industry with his viral departure from Anthropic, two more researchers are speaking out about their concerns over AI safety.
story: Citing fears that AI systems may soon spiral out of human control and potentially kill all humans, two more researchers from Anthropic and Google DeepMind who recently left their coveted positions are sounding the alarm about risks from advanced AI systems.

Joe Benton, who used to lead a safety research team at Anthropic, and Josh Engels, who used to work on AI safety research at Google, told NBC News in their first interviews since they left that they see an urgent need to boost transparency about incidents at the cutting edge of AI given the rapid pace of AI development.
Advances in AI research “could speed up the pace of progress from merely blistering at the minute to uncontrollable” rates of development, Benton said in an interview with Tom Llamas.
“There are no adults in the room,” Engels added. “People are trying their best, but there is no one coming to save us.”

Benton and Engels spoke with NBC News in the wake of a viral social media post from former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, who left Anthropic on Tuesday. In his post on X announcing his departure, Coxon highlighted his extreme concern about the pace of AI development and the risks he believes it poses to the future of humanity. The post has been viewed more than 155 million times, spurring calls from legislators to hold special sessions of Congress to take action and sparking a wave of AI employees to speak out in support of his concerns.

Benton and Engels both pointed to the recent cyberattack against AI startup Hugging Face, carried out in July by autonomous AI systems powered by an unreleased OpenAI model, as part of the reason for shifting their work now.

“If you look at some of the recent incidents, these were not cases where humans told the models to do something bad,” Engels said. Instead, OpenAI’s AI systems autonomously decided to hack into Hugging Face’s systems, create a sort of illicit message board to exchange information and even expose some of OpenAI’s own computing infrastructure to the open internet.
“The models decided that the best way to to accomplish their task was to commit really egregious actions, to commit crimes,” Engels said in an interview with Christine Romans.
OpenAI said that it has since strengthened its safeguards and that newer public models, including its most recent Astra system, more reliably follow human instructions.

An Anthropic spokesperson said in a statement Wednesday: “We have always been transparent that AI will bring both enormous benefits and unprecedented risks. To address these risks, we continue to build models with some of the strongest safeguards in the industry.”

Benton managed a group at Anthropic dedicated to creating ways for humans and weaker AI systems to supervise more capable AI systems. He said that he is particularly worried that the public does not have significant insight into how AI systems have already exceeded the bounds of human instructions and that the lack of transparency could only get worse as systems become more capable.
“At the minute, basically all of the transparency about these risks that is coming from the companies is entirely voluntary,” Benton told NBC News.

In a blog post released Wednesday, OpenAI’s head of global affairs, Chris Lehane, agreed that the status quo is insufficient. “Today, frontier laboratories largely set their own rules for managing frontier risks,” Lehane wrote. “Democratically accountable standards, independent verification, and meaningful transparency would replace that fragmented system of private governance.”
No federal law mandates that the largest AI companies, like OpenAI and Anthropic, share reports when agents or AI systems act beyond humans’ control.
Add to Google
Add to Google

Benton and Engels are joining METR, one of the world’s leading AI safety nonprofit research centers, to work on investigations into incidents or episodes in which AI strays from human directions or intentions. METR aims to create scientific ways to evaluate how AI systems could cause catastrophic risks and empower researchers and the public to sway their development.

“I left because I think I can have more positive influence on the development of this technology by helping to foster public transparency from outside these companies and to shed light on the risks,” Benton said.

The researchers joined growing numbers of AI safety researchers raising awareness about today’s AI systems following Coxon’s post Tuesday. Marcus Williams, an OpenAI employee who works on monitoring the activity of AI agents, wrote Thursday afternoon on X, “Unless there is AI regulation or a coordinated slowdown between labs, human extinction in the next few years seems very likely.”

Geoffrey Irving, who was the chief scientist at the United Kingdom’s AI Security Institute and served stints at Google and OpenAI, seemed to agree Wednesday on X. “I think we have a ~50% chance of all dying as a result of superintelligence, mostly due to actions in the next few to 10 years.”

AI researchers have referenced the possibility that AI systems could potentially begin to improve themselves without human input, creating the potential for AI systems to either purposely or incidentally kill humans.

Benton said he was most worried that the pace of technological improvement could lead to this sort of digital or artificial superintelligence, in which AI systems are more capable than humans across most tasks. “All of these companies — and this is something I witnessed firsthand at Anthropic — are pretty directly trying to race towards automating the process of AI R&D itself,” he said.

Benton suggested that there’s a chance AI systems could come to exist as a sort of separate species before long. “We’re probably going to go from a world where we have very capable systems now to a world where potentially we are co-inhabiting a world with AI agents that are much, much smarter than humans at some point in the next few years,” he said.

Engels said many people outside the AI industry might not fully appreciate just how intelligent today’s AI systems already are — and how capable they might soon become. “We’re building these systems that are generally intelligent,” he said. “They can generally do what people can do, and soon they might be able to generally do what people can do, but better.”
Both researchers said they were excited to shift their attention to more public efforts to highlight the latest AI progress, so people can make more informed decisions.

“There are many reasons people are excited and racing forward, Engels said, citing huge potential upsides and benefits from AI. But he added that “we should progress as society aware of the risks and okay with where they’re at.”
“I am worried that stuff might end up progressing too fast for us to get our act together in time,” Benton said, “unless we worry about it now.”

title: Prosecutor who led ‘grand conspiracy’ probe of Trump targets resigns without charging anyone
summary: Joe diGenova, 81, was part of a group that tried to overturn the 2020 election.
story: Joe diGenova, the 81-year-old Trump loyalist who had headed a sprawling investigation in the Southern District of Florida that targeted President Donald Trump’s perceived political enemies, has resigned from the Justice Department.
“It was an honor and a privilege to serve the president and the department,” diGenova said Thursday.
Asked why he is leaving, diGenova declined to comment.
“I’m moving on,” he said.
ABC News first reported diGenova’s departure.

While diGenova resigned from the Justice Department and was not fired, a source familiar with the determination told NBC News that Justice Department officials had already lost confidence in his leadership skills and his ability to run the investigation.

Justice Department leadership felt the investigation was not moving quickly enough, even though diGenova was provided with a team of Justice Department lawyers from Washington, according to the source familiar with the determination, who said the hope is the probe can get back on track with those attorneys at the helm.
For now, a specific person will not be named to take diGenova’s place, and the investigation is expected to move forward without delays.
The Justice Department declined to comment on diGenova’s resignation.

DiGenova, a top federal prosecutor under President Ronald Reagan, was part of Trump’s efforts to overturn the 2020 election in his favor. He made headlines this year when it was revealed that he would head the Florida-based investigation into Trump’s foes.

DiGenova’s probe has not produced any prosecutions, though shortly before he resigned there was a recent burst of activity in the wide investigation. The Justice Department is seeking testimony from multiple former officials before a federal grand jury, people familiar with the probe told NBC News. The Associated Press first reported the subpoena activity.

The probe reached back a decade, revisiting a Justice Department inquiry into Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election. That posed a major hurdle for the investigation, given that the activity took place nearly a decade ago, far outside the typical five-year statute of limitations for most federal crimes.

DiGenova stepped in to replace career prosecutor Maria Medetis Long, who had objected to advancing an investigation into former CIA Director John Brennan, whom Trump allies were pushing to be charged for allegedly false testimony.

The grand conspiracy investigation was taking place in a legal district that has historically been advantageous for Trump, overseen by the Trump-appointed U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Florida, Jason A. Reding Quiñones, and using a grand jury in a Fort Pierce court run by U.S. District Judge Aileen Cannon, a Trump-friendly judge.

Then-acting Attorney General Todd Blanche appointed diGenova in April, shortly after Pam Bondi was fired. DiGenova, joined by his wife, Victoria Toensing, whom he brought into his team along with Rudy Giuliani and Sidney Powell, was part of a group that repeatedly tried and failed to overturn Trump’s 2020 election loss.

title: Heart damage may occur from getting too much light at night while we sleep, study finds
summary: Too much light exposure during sleep may lead to potentially harmful changes in the structure and function of the heart, a new study suggests.
story: Exposure to light during nighttime sleep may lead to potentially harmful changes in the structure and function of the heart, according to a study published Wednesday in the European Heart Journal.

Previous research had shown a link between nighttime sleep while exposed to light and an elevated risk of coronary artery disease, heart attack, heart failure and stroke. The new study is the first to examine how it also affects the structure and function of the heart.

Changes to the heart — known as remodeling — can help explain the elevated risk for heart problems associated with too much nighttime light, said lead researcher Dr. Lu Qi, of Tulane University’s Celia Scott Weatherhead School of Public Health & Tropical Medicine.

“The takeaway is clear: darkness deserves recognition as a vital sign, as essential to cardiovascular health as blood pressure control and clean air,” Dr. Thomas Münzel, an environmental cardiologist at the University Medical Center of Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, and colleagues wrote in an accompanying editorial.

The researchers analyzed data from 11,071 participants enrolled in the UK Biobank, a massive database that began recruiting participants in 2005 and collects data about demographics, health and lifestyle. The people in the study wore light and motion sensors on their wrists for seven days, and a few years later, they were given MRIs of the heart. They did not have cardiovascular disease starting out.
Add to Google
Add to Google

The researchers compared people who were exposed to almost no nighttime light during sleep to people who were exposed to at least 3 lux — lux is a measurement of illumination — which would still be a very dim room, said Kristen Knutson, an associate professor of sleep medicine at Northwestern University’s Feinberg School of Medicine who has no connection to the study.
Your closed eyes, however, would be able to detect the light, she said.

Street light leaking through window shades, clock radio illumination and LED lights on equipment like room air purifiers or humidifiers were possible sources for nighttime light in the study, said Qi.

After adjusting for demographic, lifestyle, health and environmental factors, the researchers found that any increase in light exposure above 3 lux during nighttime sleep was associated with measurable, subtle cardiac damage.

For example, participants in the highest light exposure group had, on average, a 2.4% larger left ventricle (a chamber of the heart), a 1.5% thicker heart wall and a 1.9% reduction in the heart’s ability to contract, compared with participants sleeping in the darkest rooms.
Each of those changes in the heart looks small, but they have been linked with cardiovascular disease and stroke.
“If we look at the various different functional and structural outcomes together, they are pretty considerable,” Qi said.

In fact, the researchers looked for those kinds of health events. They found that after up to 10 years of follow-up, the highest light exposure group showed a 29% increased risk of heart failure, a 24% higher risk for heart attack, a 33% elevated risk for stroke and a 26% increased risk for cardiovascular death compared with the lowest light group.

Nighttime light can affect how long someone sleeps, and the paper found that nearly half of the changes in the heart’s structure and function could be attributed to lack of sleep. Another potential pathway could be nighttime light’s effect on the body’s circadian rhythm system.

That system, or clock, controls 24-hour patterns in a wide range of areas, from sleep, to hormones, to blood pressure, to inflammation, among others. Nighttime light can confuse the body’s circadian system, which can lead to cardiovascular consequences down the road, said Knutson.

The paper has limitations. The participants wore the wrist sensor for only a week. It also measured only illumination, not light spectrum, and so the study couldn’t say anything about the impact of different kinds of light, for instance LED light versus fluorescent light, on heart remodeling. In addition, the participants were mostly white, and so the results may not apply to other racial groups.
Most important, the study was observational, and so it can’t be firmly established that nighttime light caused the heart changes.

A future study about nighttime light could include people who start out with cardiovascular disease or are at high risk for it, said Knutson. “Are they more vulnerable, less vulnerable?” she asked. Future studies could also include measurements of the light spectrum and the body’s circadian rhythm.

The study’s implications are clear, wrote Münzel and colleagues. People can make simple and inexpensive fixes, such as installing blackout curtains, using warm-colored bedside lighting and covering the small standby LEDs on household electronics.
Cities can also take action, from using dimming and motion-activated streetlights to shielding streetlights so they don’t shine into buildings.

The study, the editorial said, provides a crucial link between “a planet growing ever brighter at night, and the clinical reality unfolding inside our chests: hearts that are becoming stiffer, weaker, and less efficient.”

title: CDC warns of a summer spike in rabies exposures
summary: A spike in exposures to rabies across the U.S. this summer has prompted the CDC to issue a health alert.
story: A spike in rabies cases among animals this summer has led to a rise in human exposures across the country, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention warned Thursday.

In a new health advisory, the CDC urged doctors to be on the lookout for possible exposures and to administer vaccines and treatments as needed. The agency also warned the public to avoid contact with wildlife and sick mammals, and to seek medical care if someone is bitten or scratched.

The CDC sent the advisory through its Health Alert Network, the primary communication channel the agency uses to disseminate urgent public health information to doctors, hospital networks and health officials.

Rabies is a rare but potentially fatal viral disease that must be treated before symptoms start. It spreads primarily through bites or scratches from an infected animal. Wildlife such as raccoons, skunks, bats and foxes are the most common carriers in the U.S.

The CDC’s warning comes less than two weeks after North Carolina officials announced that three baby goats at a mobile petting zoo had tested positive for rabies, potentially exposing hundreds of people.
The state health department launched a search to track down anyone who came into contact with the goats, saying Tuesday that rabies shots had been recommended for more than 260 people.
The petting zoo, Farm Adventures, said the goats were too young for vaccination and had been bitten by a skunk found in their pen. Four goats were euthanized to prevent further spread, it said.

“Several high-profile rabies outbreaks and mass rabies exposure events have highlighted the importance of performing careful rabies risk assessments and following evidence-based recommendations for administering PEP [post-exposure prophylaxis],” the agency said.

That post-exposure treatment typically includes a dose of an antibody medication that prevents infection, called human rabies immune globulin, and at least four doses of a rabies vaccine. The regimen is nearly 100% effective if administered quickly after exposure, according to the CDC.

From July through August, the CDC said, it received 17% more rabies-related inquiries than during the same period last year and also received reports from at least eight state health departments about the increased use of rabies shots, or of errors in the administration of the post-exposure regimen.
Not getting the shots before symptoms begin — typically, within weeks to months of an exposure — can lead to severe brain disease and death.

More than 6 million people in the U.S. report animal bites each year, and around 100,000 are treated for rabies exposure. But fewer than 10 people in the U.S. die from rabies annually. A combination of pet vaccinations, animal control programs and human testing and treatment has significantly reduced the risk.

Rabies exposures typically peak in the summer, since people tend to spend more time outdoors, which increases their odds of encountering wildlife. Hawaii is the only state in the U.S. that is free of rabies.

In its health alert, the CDC warned the public to keep a distance from wildlife and to never approach animals that appear sick or injured. In such cases, contact local animal control, the agency said.
“If you have pets, keep them up to date on rabies vaccines and away from wildlife when possible,” the CDC said in the alert.
The agency also advises people to wash any bites or scratches right away with soap and water.

Rebecca Lanning, whose family visited a dinosaur exhibit in Mocksville, North Carolina, on Aug. 15, previously told NBC News that she had been shocked to learn that her 4-year-old had been exposed to rabies. The exhibit included the mobile petting zoo with the goats that later tested positive.
She rushed her son to the doctor for his first shots of the vaccine series.
“My fear is that if he was feeding the goats, and he’s 4. Who’s to say that he didn’t touch his mouth or eyes?” Lanning said. “I don’t want to bury my child.”

title: The political risk behind Trump’s $5,000 pledge: From the Politics Desk
summary: In today’s edition, Jonathan Allen digs into President Donald Trump’s latest promise to voters.
story: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.

In today’s edition, Jonathan Allen digs into President Donald Trump’s latest promise to voters. Plus, Henry J. Gomez has the details on Vice President JD Vance’s message to battleground state Republicans at the midterm convention.
— Adam Wollner
The political risk behind Trump’s $5,000 pledge

There are plenty of reasons President Donald Trump received criticism for promising last night to hand out $5,000 to every adult American if voters keep Republicans in charge of the House and Senate in November’s midterm election.

To some on the left, it sounded like a bribe — though it is surely legal for politicians to promise public policy outcomes as they seek votes. To some on the right, it sounded like a plan straight out of the socialist playbook.
And the president of the nonpartisan Center for a Responsible Budget, Maya MacGuineas, had a few choice words about deficit spending.

“This proposal is fiscally dangerous, economically backwards and fundamentally unserious,” she said in a statement. Her organization estimated the proposal would cost $1.2 trillion to implement. Economists have also noted that a cash infusion of that size, far bigger than any of the Covid stimulus packages, would almost certainly cause further inflation.

Of course, he would need Congress to go along because it controls the nation’s purse strings. And that’s why, regardless of the substantive, ideological and ethical objections the plan has engendered, it’s risky politics.

Even some Trump voters are frustrated with what they say are the broken promises of the president’s second term. He said he wouldn’t start new wars. He said he would end inflation. He said he would stop the fighting between Russia and Ukraine on his first day in office. None of those things have happened. It’s not clear that anyone who isn’t squarely on Team Trump will believe that they can score a bonus payment by voting for a Republican this fall.

He has a credibility problem with independents and some Republicans. That makes it harder for him to be an effective surrogate for GOP candidates in the midterms and to regain his own footing. President Joe Biden experienced a similar phenomenon after playing down inflation, illegal immigration and his own aging.

By promising to boost the bottom line for every adult American citizen by $5,000, Trump has created an expectation that it will be difficult, at best, for him to fulfill. Is it possible, if Republicans control both chambers of Congress in 2027, that he could twist enough arms to pass the money through the filibuster-proof reconciliation process? Sure.

But the whole plan is so antithetical to conservative economic dogma — and so reliant on deficit financing — that it’s hard to see Republicans developing an appetite for it as he is on his way out of the presidency.
That would leave Trump with another broken promise.
Vance calls on battleground state Republicans to ‘nationalize’ the midterms
DALLAS — Vice President JD Vance urged Republicans from several battleground states to “nationalize” their midterm elections this fall.

“We have two things that we’ve got to do in order to win these midterm elections,” Vance said during remarks at a private breakfast here today with GOP leaders and activists from Michigan, Ohio, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, according to audio obtained by NBC News from a person who was in the room.

“Number one, we have to remind the American people of all the good things that we’re doing,” he said, “and number two, we have to remind the American people of how effing crazy the Democrats have become over the past couple of years.”

Vance, who is viewed as a likely candidate to succeed term-limited President Donald Trump in 2028, added: “We’ve got to nationalize this election. We’ve got to talk about all the crazy things the Democrats are doing.”

Vance singled out Abdul El-Sayed, the party’s Senate nominee in Michigan. Vance has been particularly critical of El-Sayed, having traveled last week to Michigan to make an explicit case against him. This morning, with Michigan delegates in the room, he called El-Sayed a “nut job.”
“I think Abdul El-Sayed may very well be the person who wins Republicans the midterms in November because he’s such a crazy person,” Vance said.
The remarks, which were closed to the media, came ahead of Vance’s speech tonight at the Republicans’ midterm convention. (Follow along with coverage on our live blog.)

title: Hillary Clinton warns the U.S. has let its guard down on terrorism 25 years after 9/11
summary: Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton warned Thursday that the Trump administration isn’t doing enough to monitor and thwart terrorists who still pose a threat to the U.S., 25 years after the 9/11 attacks.
story: Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton warned Thursday that the Trump administration isn’t doing enough to monitor and thwart terrorists who still pose a threat to the U.S., 25 years after the 9/11 attacks.

“I worry a lot that we’ve let down our guard on counterterrorism, and I don’t say this to scare anybody or to exaggerate, but I think we are not paying enough attention to resurgent terrorist actions,” Clinton said in an interview with NBC News’ Andrea Mitchell at the VOICES 25th Anniversary Symposium, an event reflecting on the attacks.
Clinton, who was a U.S. senator from New York on 9/11, said that there have been many “close calls” with terrorist plots in the ensuing quarter century and some that succeeded.

“The threat did not go away — it receded — but it is still there, and there are still many thousands of extremists in the world who wish us a great deal of ill,” she said. Clinton argued that the U.S. needs to overcome its internal divisions and confront threats from both nation-state adversaries, like Russia, China and Iran, and nonstate adversaries, like terrorist groups.

She lashed out at President Donald Trump for spending so much attention on his planned White House ballroom. “When you’re more interested in building your ballroom than figuring out what the intelligence is coming out of Afghanistan — that is absolutely contrary to any kind of sensible decision-making,” she said.

Clinton accused the Trump administration of dismantling parts of the federal government, including within the State Department, that traditionally collected intelligence and evaluated these terrorist threats. As a result, she said, the U.S. doesn’t have “eyes and ears in a lot of these countries,” including in western Africa, where she said extremism is taking hold.

The administration cut thousands of jobs across the federal government last year as part of the Elon Musk-led Department of Government Efficiency effort, including at the CIA and the State Department.

“I am increasingly concerned because I don’t think we are focused. I know there are very dedicated people still in the government, you know, in the FBI, in the intelligence agencies. I understand that,” she said. “But they don’t have ... the resources, and they’re not given the kind of mission focus that they need right now to adequately do their jobs.”
Reached for comment, the White House referred NBC News to the Department of Homeland Security.

A spokesperson for DHS told NBC News in an email: “Despite multiple Democrat shutdowns of DHS, the Department is more than equipped to keep Americans safe in an ever-changing threat landscape. DHS has been recruiting, reforming, and modernizing at a record pace—including in areas of counterterrorism.”

During the interview, Clinton also reflected on the revelations about the toxic air quality in Manhattan after 9/11, recalling her experience at ground zero. “It looked like a black curtain,” she said. “There was particulates. ... There was, you know, acrid smells. My throat hurt.”
Asked if misleading information about the air from the Bush administration at the time was deliberate, bad science or an effort to reassure the public, Clinton said it was “all three.”

“I think that there was a certain element of some leaders being unwilling to face the truth because they wanted to get the economy going,” she said. “They wanted to get Wall Street open. They wanted people to feel like normalcy was possible, and so they either deliberately ignored or they didn’t ask the right questions.”

She also responded to Jon Stewart, comedian and 9/11 health advocate, who said that the U.S. has lost nearly 10,000 people to 9/11-related illnesses, which is three times as many people as the nearly 3,000 killed in the twin towers.

Addressing the fact that there are people experiencing these health effects that aren’t registered for programs intended to help these victims, Clinton said, “There needs to be a concerted effort to fund this expanded outreach and screening and treatment. And I would hope that the city, the state and the federal government would join together to do that.”

title: 15-year-old survives after fishing boat capsizes off Alaskan island, killing his brother and cousin
summary: The teen was rescued Monday after he was found clinging to the overturned vessel about four miles east of St. Lawrence Island, the Coast Guard said.
story: A 15-year-old boy survived days at sea after a fishing boat capsized off an Alaskan island, killing his older brother and cousin.
The teen was rescued Monday after he was found on the overturned vessel about 4 miles east of St. Lawrence Island, in the Bering Sea, the Coast Guard said in a news release.
Darren Toolie-Noongwook said his family is mourning the death of his brother Sidney, who provided for the family, and “spoiling the hell” out of Parker, the teenage brother who survived.

Video obtained by NBC affiliate KTUU of Anchorage showed the moment the teen was rescued. The boy, appearing to wear a black hoodie underneath a coat with green pants and black boots, is seen kneeling on the vessel.

The group was on an 18-foot fishing vessel near the island when it capsized. The Coast Guard said it was notified of the overdue vessel Sunday night but was unable to begin searching until the next morning because of weather and poor visibility. The boat had last been seen Friday departing Savoonga.
Toolie-Noongwook said the family works in commercial fishing, which requires them to stay out on the water for days at a time.
It’s a difficult and physically taxing job, he said, and the crew were exhausted when a fishing line got caught in the boat’s motor.

“Once the motor got caught in the fishing line, they tried to untangle it, but they couldn’t because of how bad it was tangled,” Toolie-Noongwook said, recounting what Parker had told the family. “So they were just sitting, and then later on at the end of the night, the weather got bad and the boat flipped.”

Sidney was running to get a life jacket to Parker when he got tangled in the lines and the boat flipped. Parker and their cousin were able to climb on the top of the overturned boat together, but Sidney was “the first to go,” Toolie-Noongwook said.
Parker and their cousin were together through the night until, Toolie-Noongwook said, his cousin started to panic.
“The other crew member — our cousin — he started freaking out, and he jumped ship,” he said. “And he only swam five to six feet, and he sadly had drowned.”
Parker was alone on the top of the boat but felt safe knowing that his older brother was “watching over him,” Toolie-Noongwook said.

“He was sitting on his knees, just praying the whole time,” Toolie-Noongwook said. “He said he believed he was going to make it. He believed that he was gonna be found and he was gonna be safe, and it happened.”

The teen was located around 3 p.m. Monday and rescued by Northwest Explorer, a “nearby good Samaritan vessel,” with the help of watch standers at the Coast Guard Arctic District command center, according to the Coast Guard.
“Before departing the scene to refuel, the HC-130 aircrew deployed a line of flares to guide the Northwest Explorer to the overturned vessel,” the Coast Guard said.

Adam White, captain of the vessel that found the teenager, told NBC News that his crew were returning back from a NOAA survey when they received a message from the Coast Guard. After having received coordinates for a survivor, White altered their course to look for Parker and prepared supplies to keep him warm.
The seven scientists and six crew members on board all kept their eyes on the water to see whether they could find him.
“When he finally came into view, it was elation from everybody,” White said. “Everybody cheered.”

Parker was unable to get to the rafts near him, stuck on the top of the overturned boat about 8 miles from his last known position, White said. The crew blasted its horn “to give him some hope” that help was on its way.

“We were lucky enough, because the kid was so tough, so strong that that he was able to grab a hold of a heaving line that we threw to him,” White said. “And he was able to hold on while we sort of reeled him in. And I just, like, can’t believe how tough this kid is.”
White said the teenager was “moderately” hypothermic once they were able to get him on board. They were able to raise his body temperature until they could get him medical attention.
White was able to meet Parker’s family, which he described as overwhelming.

“We gave each other a really long hug, and they just, they had a lot of joy,” White said. “Obviously, there’s a lot of pain in their eyes — there’s a lot of sorrow. It’s just so much, so much mixed emotions.”
Rear Adm. Bob Little, the commander of the Coast Guard Arctic District command center, said its hearts go out to the families, friends and communities affected by the tragedy.

“We are grateful for the incredible efforts of the motor vessel Northwest Explorer, Federal, State, Village first responders and mission partners who assisted in the effort that resulted in a life saved,” Little said.
The family were together when they got the news that Parker was alive. Toolie-Noongwook said they are grieving together.

“It’s going to be a long, long process because of how, how painful this was,” he said. “We’re so happy that he [Parker] survived, but the trauma that comes with it, it hurts us. We’re all in pain for him.”

title: Rick Springfield recalls killing a man in Vietnam while he was there performing for troops
summary: “It’s hard for me to face that I was responsible for the end of a life,” the “Jessie’s Girl” singer said in an interview with Joe Rogan.
story: Rocker Rick Springfield recalled this week how, as a teenager, when he performed for U.S. forces in Vietnam, they came under attack and he killed a Viet Cong — haunting him to this day that he “was responsible for the end of a life.”

The Australian singer-songwriter became an ’80s superstar with his megahit “Jessie’s Girl,” but in 1968 he was an unknown 17-year-old musician who had traveled to Southeast Asia to entertain American troops at the height of the Vietnam War.

Springfield, 77, recounted that harrowing experience on an episode of the “Joe Rogan Experience” posted on Tuesday. He said he was staying at a U.S. Navy encampment in the Marble Mountains near Da Nang when they suddenly came under attack.

“We met these guys, and we really got along well, and we stayed overnight with them, and we all got in the bunkers, in the perimeter bunkers, and I stayed in the radio shack,” he recalled. “And we got attacked, and I’m throwing mortars down the freaking tube of the radio shack.”
In the heat of the moment, Springfield said he was haphazardly loading a launcher and “could have easily lost a hand.”

“It was like the movies,” he told Rogan. “They said, ‘Hey, you want to throw some mortars down the tube?’ And it was John Wayne time, you know. I mean, as a young kid, I didn’t really understand what I was doing.”
But what began like a scene from an action film gave way to the cold, hard realities of war.
“I’d thrown a mortar down and it had hit somebody, and they came in the next day and said, ‘Hey, you got one! You got one!’” Springfield said.
“That’s really the one thing I brought back with me that I couldn’t really find a place for that to land,” he said, saying that it feels like it happened to “another guy” in “another place.”
Rogan asked, “How long did that sit with you for?” and Springfield said the experience has never left him.

“I think it’s still there,” Springfield replied. “It’s hard for me to face that I was responsible for the end of a life, even though it’s distant and it’s war and I didn’t really have anything to do with it and didn’t really know what I was doing.”
Springfield also vividly recalled how unpopular the war was with the Americans fighting it in Vietnam.
“All the ones I met were, ‘Dude, I don’t know why we’re here. I don’t know what I’m doing here,’” he remembered.
The “Love Somebody” and “Don’t Talk to Strangers” singer wrote about the Vietnam incident in his 2010 memoir, “Late, Late at Night.”
“That was a war situation but it is still something that to this day sends a shiver down my spine,” Springfield wrote in the memoir.

title: How often do you really need to wash your jeans? Here’s what experts say
summary: According to experts, you should wash your jeans every few wears — or more often if you get them really dirty. Plus, here are the best detergents for washing jeans.
story: With all the content available online these days, it can be hard to figure out what’s real and what’s hype. While we don’t always have the answers, we have a direct line to people who do — which is why we present to you our series The Internet Made Me Ask, where we have experts break down the truth about some of the buzziest trends on our timelines, like whether honey is good for your skin.

Taxes, death and the “can I wear this” sniff test — they’re all certainties in life. And, whether we’d like to admit it or not, we’ve all grabbed a piece of clothing off the floor (or the chair) and inhaled to see if it’s wearable. While certain pieces of clothing require washing after every use (yes, we’re also talking about lucky underwear), other items can get by with fewer spin cycles. Jeans are one of those items. You don’t need to clean them after every wear — but how often should you wash your jeans?

“Overwashing jeans can cause them to fade, lose their shape and weaken the fabric,” says Daniel Feliciano, co-founder and CEO of Clotheslyne, an on-demand laundry service. “But not washing your jeans enough can lead to bacteria buildup, odors and even skin irritation.”
So, what’s the ideal washing schedule for your denim? To answer that question, I spoke more with Feliciano and another laundry expert — plus, I got their tips on how to clean your jeans.
Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter.
How often do you really need to wash your jeans?

There is no one-size-fits-all answer on how often you should wash your jeans. If you wear your jeans to a baseball game where you may sit in something sticky or spill beer on them, the answer will be very different than if you just occasionally throw on a pair for some quick errands. That said, you can follow a general rule of thumb: “In most cases, jeans can be washed every four to five wears,” says Morgan LaLonde, a brand manager for Whirlpool Laundry. The general rule is if your jeans look or smell dirty, wash them. If not, wash them every five or so wears.

If small areas become soiled (say, you spill a bit of coffee on them) but they otherwise smell okay, you don’t necessarily need to throw them in the wash. If the stain is small enough, you can try spot-treating it, says LaLonde.
Does sticking your jeans in the freezer clean them?

Some say that rather than washing your jeans, you should put them in the freezer to clean them. It may sound like sorcery but it actually works — kind of. Freezing your jeans can make odor-inducing bacteria lie dormant, says Feliciano.

But just because your jeans may smell less funky doesn’t mean they’re clean. “Freezing them is a temporary solution — it doesn’t actually remove dirt or oils,” adds Feliciano. “A thorough washing is much more effective.”
What is the best way to wash your jeans?

Both experts recommend following the care instructions on your jeans’ tag. But generally speaking, you should use cold water and the delicate or gentle cycle of your washing machine, says Feliciano, adding that a mild or gentle detergent is best.

It’s fine to wash your denim with other items, though if they are a darker wash (think indigo or black) and new, you may want to wash them solo the first few times. The dye used on dark denim may bleed during the first few washes, so if you want to avoid the possibility of other clothes soaking up that dye, wash them on their own.

Another tip: “Turn your jeans inside out to protect against direct exposure to detergent, which could fade them more quickly or lead to faster wear and tear,” says LaLonde. Finally, if your jeans are embellished or ripped, Feliciano suggests placing them in a mesh washing bag before tossing them in your machine to protect rips from becoming larger or embellishments from falling off.
The best detergents to use on jeans

Feliciano and LaLonde both recommend sticking with a mild detergent for washing jeans. “For dark blue or black jeans, opt for detergents specifically made for dark clothing to prevent any fading,” adds Feliciano. Below are detergents that fit those requirements and that have at least a four-star average rating from 1,000 or more shoppers.
Tide Free & Gentle Liquid Laundry Detergent

This mild detergent is free of dyes and perfumes, making it a great hypoallergenic option that can clean all your laundry — including your jeans. This is my go-to detergent and I find that it does a great job at cleaning my toddler’s t-shirts, workout leggings and my favorite wide-leg jeans. The detergent is also available in pods.
Molly's Suds Liquid Laundry Detergent

If you like natural cleaning products, consider this detergent from Molly’s Suds. According to the brand, it’s mild and made with plant-derived active ingredients. The detergent comes in a handful of scents — including lavender, peppermint and unscented.
Seventh Generation EasyDose Free & Clear Laundry Detergent

Seventh Generation’s EasyDose detergent is super concentrated, so a little goes a long way. You’ll get at least 66 loads from the 23-ounce bottle, making it a great option for those who have to lug their stuff to a laundromat or apartment laundry room. The mild detergent is free of dyes and fragrances, making it gentle on materials and your skin, according to the brand.
Woolite Darks Protect Liquid Laundry Detergent

If you have dark blue or black jeans, consider washing them in this detergent from Woolite. It’s formulated specifically to maintain the color of darker clothing items and prevent fading, according to the brand. A bottle gets you through 33 loads and the cap can be used to measure your detergent.
Perwoll Renew & Repair Liquid Detergent

Like the detergent from Woolite, this option is also made specifically for dark or black clothing. Not only does this formula help prevent fading, but it can also help restore darker colors and make them look less faded, according to Perwoll. You’ll get up to 24 loads from one bottle and the cap can be used to measure what you need.
Should you put your jeans in the dryer?

Resist the urge to throw your jeans in the dryer. It might be quicker, but your jeans will hold up better if you stick to air drying them whenever possible. “Drying your jeans in a dryer can cause them to shrink, fade or cause damage to fibers,” says LaLonde. “Remove them from the washer and pull the seams taught so the jeans lay flat. Then hang them up to dry completely before wearing them.”
If you don’t have time to air dry, opt for a low- or no-heat dry cycle, and use dryer balls to keep your jeans tumbling instead of balling up, suggests LaLonde.
Frequently asked questions

If you buy light or medium wash jeans, there’s no reason to wash your jeans after buying them, according to experts. However, if you buy indigo jeans, you may want to consider a quick wash. Indigo dye may rub off on your skin, shoes or furniture if it hasn’t been washed.

Baggy jeans can generally go longer between washes than slim or skinny styles. Because the fit is looser, the fabric doesn’t sit directly against your skin the way tighter jeans do, so it absorbs less sweat, oil, and body odor over the course of a day. That means you can often get away with wearing baggy jeans five to ten times — sometimes more — before they actually need a wash.
Meet our laundry experts

At NBC Selected, we work with experts with specialized knowledge and authority based on relevant training and/or experience. We also ensure all expert advice and recommendations are made independently and without undisclosed financial conflicts of interest.

title: Dolly Parton’s First Posthumous Song, ‘Bound to Ride,’ Features Her Beloved Sense of Humor
summary: Two weeks after her death, Dolly Parton’s fans are getting to hear the icon’s first song released posthumously.
story: Two weeks after her death, Dolly Parton’s fans are getting to hear the icon’s first song released posthumously.

The country music legend and actor died following “a brief battle with cancer” her estate announced Aug. 25. She was 80. As the news was reported, tributes poured in from her peers and fans. They reflected on Parton’s impact in the industry, from hits like “9 to 5” to “I Will Always Love You” and “Jolene.”

Now, they’ll have the opportunity to listen to a new song from her once more, as Parton is featured on an upcoming all-star tribute album titled “Where the Soul Never Dies: Celebrating 80 Years of The Stanley Brothers.”
She added her vocals to the track “Bound to Ride,” which the country duo recorded in 1964, and the single has been posted on YouTube ahead of the album’s release on Oct. 16.

Parton originally recorded her part around 2022 in her personal studio, Rolling Stone reports. The album is also set to include vocals by Willie Nelson and Sierra Ferrell, Dierks Bentley with Della Mae, and Steve Martin and Ed Helms, among others.
Following Parton’s death, her longtime manager Danny Nozell shared a lengthy list of all the projects that the country superstar had been working on and was excited to bring to life.

“Dolly worked up until the day she died. She loved seeing her dreams come to life, and loved knowing her work brought people joy,” Nozell said in a press release. “Ever the planner, Dolly worked with the team that she handpicked, for the past several years to build a project roadmap that will guide us for decades to come.”
Among Parton’s future plans are Dolly Dolls, Dolly’s Cup Of Ambition Coffee, Dolly’s Dog Treats and her Broadway musical, among many others.
Her manager stressed that anything that is released on the singer’s official channels, Parton “placed her personal stamp on it.”
He added that they will continue to share more details on additional projects, including an avatar show, a biopic, docuseries, scripted series and a Billy The Kid animated series, “soon.”
For now, fans can enjoy listening once more to Parton and her beloved voice and sense of humor.

title: Alison Brie Goes Blonde and Confirms a New Role: ‘It’s For a Part!’
summary: Alison Brie just underwent a stylish and lighter hairstyle. The actor, known for her brunette locks, is now a blonde.
story: Alison Brie is back to blonde.
The former “Community” star debuted her new hair color at the 2026 Daytime Beauty Awards red carpet in Los Angeles on Sept. 9.
“They *do* have more fun?!” Brie said on her Instagram story, commenting on her new look.
As someone complimented her blondest ‘do to date, Brie revealed the reason for it.
“It’s for a part!” Brie said in a TikTok shared by “Entertainment Tonight.”
Just three days prior, Brie showcased her typical brunette look at the Creative Arts Emmys, where she supported her “GLOW” co-star Betty Gilpin and her win for “Widow’s Bay.”
This is not the first time she’s sported lighter locks. In 2019, Brie teased a new role with a transformation reveal on Instagram.
“When your husband asks you to ‘go blonde’ for a role... you say yes😉,” she wrote in the caption.
That “role” turned out to be the 2020 horror thriller “The Rental.”
Now, blonder than ever, and with a few inches off, fans are wondering what role called for the change.
Brie has recently starred in “Masters Of The Universe” and “Together.”

Brie is confirmed to appear in Peacock’s “Community: The Movie,” which has experienced ongoing production delays. In the original sitcom, however, which ran from 2009 to 2015, Brie’s character Annie Edison was a brunette.
Brie is also in cahoots with Alice Stanley Jr. for a female-driven horror comedy, but is said to be making her directorial feature debut rather than any on-camera work.

title: Cindy Crawford Describes Meeting Son of Ex-Husband Richard Gere
summary: Nearly 40 years after Cindy Crawford and Richard Gere stepped out as one of the iconic couples of the early 1990s, their children are now starring together on the FX show “The Shards.”
story: Nearly 40 years after Cindy Crawford and Richard Gere stepped out as one of the iconic couples of the early 1990s, their children are now starring together on the FX show “The Shards.”

Homer Gere, 26, and Kaia Gerber, 25, are part of the cast of the teen serial killer drama helmed by Ryan Murphy and posed together on the cover of the September issue of Vogue. Their parents posed together for Vogue in 1992, making the latest cover shot a full-circle moment between the children of the supermodel and the actor, who divorced in 1995 after four years of marriage.

Crawford, 60, shared on TODAY with Jenna & Sheinelle Sept. 10 what it’s like to see the two working together and how she first met Homer Gere, who is Richard Gere’s son with actor Carey Lowell. Gerber is the daughter of Crawford and her husband Rande Gerber.
“I had never met Homer,” Crawford said. “I met him while they were filming. He’s lovely, and Kaia enjoyed working with him.”
Crawford also expanded on how the two young actors deal with being labeled “nepo babies.”

“They’re both in the same situation,” Crawford said. “They understand it’s going to be a question they’re going to get asked, but at the same time they both work really hard and think they’re both doing a great job.”
Crawford emphasized that Gerber works hard for her modeling and acting career.
“Look, there’s pros and cons to having famous parents,” Crawford added. “And I know sometimes it feels like pressure, or she feels like, ‘Wow.’”
For example, her daughter can do a modeling shoot and commenters may bring up that her mother wore the look first.

“I’m like, ‘I know,’ because I can talk about my mom and no one knew who that was, and (Gerber) doesn’t have that anonymity,” Crawford said. “But she also understands that it does open maybe some doors.”
Gerber spoke to Vogue about what it has been like growing up in the public eye due to her mother.

“Fame was something that I was born into, so I didn’t experience what it was like to become famous,” Gerber said. “I kind of thought that my way of being raised was the most anonymous it could get under the circumstances, and then I met Homer. Like, there are no photos of him as a child online, whereas my entire childhood and teenage years are on the internet. I can only imagine. I’m 24 but … very interviewed.”
Gerber began modeling at 13 and was walking runways at 16, according to Vogue.

“I’ve only ever been a nepo baby, and I’ve only ever benefited in my career from it,” she said “But I also find myself doing it to other nepo babies, thinking, like, OK, show me why you deserve this job. I said to Homer — because the concept is daunting to him, having lived as an adult so far without that perception, whereas I sort of went through it when I wasn’t fully sentient — I said to him, ‘Homer, unfortunately with this show, it’s not like you’re just any unknown actor and people will judge you as an unknown actor.’”
Homer Gere did not begin acting professionally until appearing in a small role in the final season of HBO’s “Euphoria” earlier this year.
“I didn’t grow up in the industry at all,” he told Vogue. “I had never been on a professional set until last summer.”
He and Gerber also didn’t ignore their unique connection when they both joined the cast of “The Shards.”
“Twenty minutes into knowing each other, I was like, ‘Should we just acknowledge the fact that our parents were married?’ She was like, ‘Yeah. Cool,’” he told Vogue. “And that was it.”

title: AARP’s List of ‘Most Fabulous’ Gen X Actresses Honors Viola Davis and More Hollywood Stars
summary: Viola Davis leads AARP’s Movies for Grownups’ 25 Most Fabulous Gen X Actresses list.
story: Viola Davis is fabulous!

The Oscar winner tops AARP’s Movies for Grownups’ 25 Most Fabulous Gen X Actresses list, which “honors powerhouse female talent who continue to break barriers, command screens, and redefine what it means to be a Gen X actress in Hollywood,” according a news release.
The rankings pay homage to Generation X, which is classified as people born between roughly 1965 and 1980.

“Now, at roughly between the ages of 45 to 61, this generation of Hollywood actresses have not faded from the screen, but have built production companies, developed their own projects, and reinvented themselves behind the camera as directors, producers, and entrepreneurs fighting for equal pay and breaking stereotypes,” AARP’s Movies for Grownups said in a statement.
“They are far from slowing down and are doing the most ambitious work of their careers.”

Davis, 61, is the oldest person on the list and said in a statement connected to the honor, “My ability to overcome and to challenge and to believe in my ability is mine.” She survived a poor childhood marked by food insecurity to emerge as a critically acclaimed actor, winning a best supporting actress Academy Award for “Fences” and earning three other nominations in her career.

“When you come to Hollywood, I think women over 40, then over 50, you feel like you’ve just sort of disappeared and fallen off a cliff,” she told AARP’s Movies for Grownups. “Like you’re invisible. So, it’s nice to know that that’s not true. I feel like my value is going up. It feels fabulous.”

title: Elizabeth Acevedo Shares First Page of Novel in Verse, ‘Anger Is Only a Shadow’
summary: Elizabeth Acevedo previews the first page of her novel in verse “Anger Is Only a Shadow” and explains how it sets up the rest of her book.
story: It is a truth universally acknowledged that a good story starts with a good first line. In TODAY’s “Cold Open,” authors tease their buzzy upcoming release by revealing and explaining its first line, paragraph or page.

Either because of her own lactose intolerance, or her memory of what lunch would smell like at the detention center she used to teach at, Elizabeth Acevedo knew her next novel would open with the “visceral” image of indigestion.
“Here is the most important rule of this place: Don’t drink the milk,” reads the opening line of her novel in verse “Anger Is Only a Shadow,” out Sept. 15 from HarperCollins.

The book’s narrator is a rebellious young woman named Lil, who finds herself in juvenile detention due to her “instinct for freedom,” per the novel’s premise, inspired by Acevedo’s own experience working as a teaching artist at a detention facility in Washington, D.C.
“It felt like such a visceral image to begin with, this disruption of your bodily functions in a space where that is very much monitored and very much like, not OK,” Acevedo tells TODAY.com.
The first page of the book is Lil “emphasizing the rules of this place,” both to herself and to the reader. Following the heading of, “Sunday, October 18,” it reads:

Here is the most important rule of this place: Don’t drink the milk. Trust, having the bubble guts is not the first impression you want to make. And while we’re on the subject, that’s an important rule too: don't make an impression.

Sit quiet, only slump so much in your chair, don’t look anyone in the face. Don’t avoid someone eyeing you either. And if you have to make an impression, let it be knuckle-size. Aldwin has been teaching me since I was little: know when to be brick-built, know when to be gentle. And here? Being soft don’t play here.

There are other rules you need to learn: Which YDR—youth development representative—you can joke with. When it makes sense to participate in an activity, or when it makes sense to stay your flat ass behind your door. What vent carries your voice into other units.
But the most important rule is Rule One: Don't. Drink. The. Milk.
The first page of the novel represents what Acevedo pictured her novel in verse to be. And the Lil readers meet through that introduction is the same way Acevedo found the character.

“I thought I was writing a book about a juvenile detention facility and this young woman who is in there and is kind of snarky and telling us the rules,” she says. “The first page was such a guide in her voice, really.

“Before I had plot, before I knew what the main conflict was, I was just kind of following the most irreverent character I’ve ever written,” she adds. “I knew I had a character long before I knew I had anything else.”

The rest came later, including its structure. Acevedo originally thought the novel would be entirely prose poetry, consisting of “blocky text without paragraph indentation.” In the final draft, the prose blocks, accompanied by dates, guide readers through Lil’s daily life. These entries are broken up by poems.

Acevedo first drafted a poem in Lil’s voice titled “Where I’m From.” It sparked a motif, and the character turns one writing prompt from a workshop at the detention center into a series of poems, illustrating how she’s “revising versions of herself,” Acevedo says.
When Acevedo worked as a teaching artist, she says she brought in poems.

“It’s a fraught space,” she says of her time teaching at a detention center. “You come in, and you’re like, ‘Let’s be really vulnerable in a space where you all are very reluctant to share vulnerability.’

“That tension was so visceral for me, and also ... the young women would open up in ways I had never imagined,” she adds. “It’s almost like I was constantly surprised and also fully understood like, ‘You have been looking for an opportunity for people to ask you these things.’”
But the book isn’t just about Lil’s time in the detention center. The novel also asks: “What are the stakes once you’re outside?”
“Anger Is Only a Shadow” will also follow Lil once she’s on probation, weighed down by an ankle monitor and fearing for her big brother, miles away at college.

“So many young people I know when I was a school teacher had ankle monitors, and how does that affect how you navigate your life? And what would be the thing that would lead this character, who’s very impulsive, to potentially violate the rules of the ankle monitor?” Acevedo says. “That’s when the second part of the story, a story I never thought I would write about, came forth.”
The result is “two big stories” rolled into the novel: one about juvenile detention and one about navigating a family member who has mental illness.

“I have a sibling who was diagnosed with schizophrenia when I was in the early years of my college career,” she says. “Trying to do well in my own little world of academics, while also showing up for family, and the ways in which it can be so hard to know what that person needs ... It felt like I just have so many questions about this. I don’t have answers.
“Then that felt like the challenge: Isn’t that exactly what you need to write about?” she continues.

“I’m not going to lie, I wasn’t sure,” she adds. “These are two big stories and I’m writing a very short book, I don’t think it can happen. But somehow, somehow, it felt like the two pieces were supposed to be interlocked.”

title: Harry Styles Announces 2027 Dates for ‘Together, Together’ Tour In 12 New Cities
